en: Preface to the Lotus Sutra:
When I was young, I read the "Universal Gate Chapter" (*Pumenpin*) and the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.

Although I could not yet deeply understand their meaning, I conjectured based on my own intuition that these were allegories of the Buddha. Long ago, Master Li Wen of the Tang dynasty questioned Master Yaoshan about Chan...
The Master said, "What is it like when a malignant wind blows a boat adrift into the realm of ghosts? The Master replied, "Why does this little fellow Li Ao ask such a thing?

When Wen Gong’s face suddenly flushed with anger, the Master laughed and said, "To give rise to such a mind of resentment and hatred is precisely what it means for a malignant wind to blow one's boat adrift into the realm of ghosts.
Alas! Yaoshi may truly be called one who excels at awakening others.
Inferring from this, one knows that the blazing intensity of profit and desire is a pit of fire, while the drowning in craving is a sea of suffering.
A single thought of purity turns a fierce conflagration into a pond; a single moment of awakening brings the boat to the other shore.

Though bound by calamities and afflictions, one dwells in peace wherever one stays. Without fear or dread, I am like one whose shackles have fallen away of their own accord. When evil people encroach and oppress me, I meet them with...
Violence and injustice. I harbor no anger or envy; I am like a wild beast fleeing for its life.

Those who read this sutra should contemplate in this manner, and they will know that the Great Being of Potalaka speaks truly for the sake of humanity and does not utter empty words. Compiled by Zhen Dexiu of the Western Hills.
*Commentary and Forest of Evaluations on the Sublime Dharma Lotus Sutra*, Volume One.

(Tiantai says: It reveals the profound treasury of the secret, and is thus called "Mysterious" (Miao). It demonstrates the correct path of the provisional and the real, and is therefore titled "Dharma" (Fa).
It points to the original fruit of the distant past, and is likened to a lotus; it unites the perfect way of non-duality, and is compared to a flower.
Its sound constitutes a Buddha-work, and it is thus termed a "Sūtra" (Jing). At the beginning of this perfect exposition, it is designated as the "Preface" (Xu). This...)

It eradicates the attachment to the teachings of the "City of Manifestation" and abolishes the stagnant sentiments of the "Thatched Hut. It opens the provisional gate of skillful means and reveals the wondrous principle of ultimate reality.
It unifies the minor practices of various virtues and leads them back to the single vehicle of vastness. Its phrasing is extensive and its meaning profound;
no other sutra can surpass it.
Master Shanyu’s intention was as follows: In Sanskrit it is called *saddharma*; here it is translated as "Wondrous Dharma" (*miaofa*) or "Right Dharma" (*zhengfa*).
This is because the character *sa* contains two meanings; thus, the Qin version's "Wondrous Dharma" and the Jin version's "Right Dharma" are both without error.
It possesses ten wondrous meanings that are uniquely superior to other sutras, and is therefore called "wondrous. It is the True Doctrine of the One Vehicle and the Middle Way.
It is definitive; therefore, it is called "Correct" (Zheng). It upholds the True Principle as a model for all beings; therefore, it is called "Dharma" (Fa). Regarding the lotus:
in Sanskrit it is called *puṇḍarīka*, which here means "white lotus. White is the foundation of all colors, and the One Vehicle is the source of the other vehicles;
thus, it is taken as a metaphor, as seen in the passage at the beginning of this sutra where the white tuft of hair is first emitted.

The Light ultimately bestowed the carriage of the white ox; this is the meaning of that. As for the lotus flower, it dwells in the mud yet remains unstained, with cause and effect manifested simultaneously.
This is a metaphor for the aforementioned Sublime Dharma, which opens up the provisional to reveal the real, unifies the three vehicles into one, and clarifies the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Unlike other sutras, this work titles both the Dharma and its metaphor; thus it is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. In Sanskrit it is called *sūtra*, which here is translated as "Kie-king" (契經).
"Kie" (契) means to accord with principle and to accord with the capacities [of sentient beings]; "King" (經) means to string together and encompass the eternal Dharma.

It refers, therefore, to the teaching that accords with principle and harmonizes with capacity, hence it is called "Kie-king. Here, the character "Kie" is abbreviated for the sake of following the established brevity of the preceding title.
Bai Juyi’s Preface to the Golden-Character Sūtra on the Stone Wall at Fahua Monastery states:

"To open the way for superior awakening and entry into the wisdom and vision of all Buddhas, to deliver the boundless through the definitive meaning, and to extend the inexhaustible through the Perfect Teaching—nothing is more venerable than the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This sūtra is the foremost essence of the Three Vehicles and the complete secret treasury of the ten thousand Buddhas."
Preface, Chapter One.
Xianzi said: "This sutra consists of twenty-eight chapters: first, the Introductory Section (Nidāna) comprises one chapter; second, the Main Body (Śarīra) comprises nineteen chapters;
and third, the Dissemination Section (Pariṇāmana) comprises eight chapters."
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
(Furthermore, it is said: The *Avataṃsaka* proceeds through ten locations to fully manifest the Dharma-precepts;

the *Awakening of Faith* relies upon the Great Treasury of Luminosity to directly reveal the primordial source. This reliance upon a human city is similar [to the former] in clarifying the lotus as the union of defilement and purity.)
The meaning of this is that, according to where the ancient Buddhas resided, they demonstrated their ancestral succession in order to continue the Way of the Lamp of Wisdom.
The *Jiehuan* states: "Such a Dharma as this I have heard from the Buddha.

This was the very first proclamation when Ānanda ascended the seat during the compilation of the teachings (*saṃgīti*), intended solely to testify that there was a specific transmission of the Dharma. Rājagṛha is none other than the site of Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*).
It is attached to the city and is a subordinate territory of the kingdom of Magadha; it is among the human realms of the Western Regions.
Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa—translated here as "Vulture Peak"—is named after its shape. It is the dwelling place of ancient Buddhas;
because it was the abode of ancient Buddhas, it is called "Numinous Vulture."
He was accompanied by a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats. Their outflows were exhausted;
they were free from further afflictions. Having attained their own benefit, they had severed all fetters of existence and achieved mastery over their minds.
Jiehuan said: "The causes and effects of the three realms are all matters for others; knowing and severing [defilements] through merit is what is called one's own benefit.

Only then is one fit to be a field of merit for humans and devas, and thus is termed 'Worthy of Offerings' (Arhat). In the Vinaya texts, whenever it concerns those 'Worthy of Offerings,' one must reflect upon whether one’s own virtue and conduct are complete or deficient;
this is to cause one to reflect upon one’s own benefit. Indeed, it is for the sake of such reflection that one undergoes ascetic toil and sits upright while eating, holding [the bowl]..."

They prostrated themselves on their knees and received [the teachings] while standing in a reverential posture. If one lacks the virtue of benefiting oneself, the harm will not be slight (those who travel on foot should take note of this).
Xiangmai said: "The Buddha’s assembly consisted of no more than one thousand two hundred and fifty people; as for the current mention of twelve thousand,"
This also includes those gathered from other directions. "Arhat" translates in meaning as "Slayer of Thieves," also called "Worthy of Offerings," and also called "Non-arising.
When the mind of the profound abyss cannot maintain total unity, it clings to stillness and gives rise to consciousness; this flowing forth and rushing toward objects is called "outflow" (*āsrava*).
These various outflows refer to the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance; all of them take the deluded consciousness that clings to stillness as their basis.

The substance [of these afflictions] is the root of the afflictions of the three realms. These afflictions—namely greed, hatred, delusion, and the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)—serve as the conditions for the outflows (*āsrava*).

They ravage the *dharmakāya* and oppress the true nature; thus they are called "affliction-thieves. To speak of the exhaustion of outflows and the absence of affliction means that because the root is exhausted, the conditions no longer exist;
this is what is meant by "slaying the thieves. One's own benefit consists in the realization of knowledge and abandonment.

The affairs of delusion: those who possess the fetters of existence are precisely those whose karma is the habituation of delusion, serving as the cause for birth within the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
Since the fruit perishes when the cause is exhausted, this is called "non-arising. In the Lesser Vehicle, having concentration without wisdom is partial;
one who has not yet attained self-mastery is merely named "autonomous," whereas one who possesses both concentration and wisdom is fully liberated.
Their names were Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa,
Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākātyāyana,
Aniruddha, Kapphiṇa, Gavāmpati, Revata, Pilindavatsa, and Bakula.
Mahākauṣṭhila, Nanda, Sundarananda, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
Subhūti, Ānanda, Rāhula— such great arhats as these, who were well known to the masses.
(The Ekottarika Āgama states: Kauṇḍinya first attained realization; Uruvilvāca attained the assembly of offerings; Gayākāśyapa subdued all fetters;
Nadīkāśyapa was skilled in teaching and transforming; Kapphiṇa knew the constellations; Gavāmpati received celestial offerings; Revata was free from confusion.)

Pilindavatsa excels in ascetic endurance; Bakula lives out his full lifespan without premature death; Kuṭhivimśa is skilled in answering difficult questions; and Sundara is preeminent in physical beauty—each is the foremost in his respective field.
Jie-huan said: "This refers to the leaders among the twelve thousand people, who were of superior virtue and ranked among the ten great disciples.
The Buddha had ten great disciples who served as Dharma-ministers to the Dharma-King;

each was endowed with manifold virtues and manifested specialization as a skillful means to assist in the Great Transformation. Thus, Mahākāśyapa was foremost in dhūta practices, and Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom."
First: Maudgalyāyana excels in supernatural powers; Kātyāyanīputra in debate; Śāriputra in the divine eye; Pūrṇa in preaching the Dharma; Subhūti in understanding emptiness;
Ānanda in extensive learning; Upāli in upholding the Vinaya; and Rāhula in pure conduct—each occupies the foremost rank.
This is their standard enumeration, like the listing of the Ten Disciples of Confucius. Now, from Kauṇḍinya to Rāhula, there are two [groups].
As for these ten individuals, they were endowed with manifold virtues and fully manifested the transformation of the Dharma. Each also possessed supreme qualities.

There were eighty thousand Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, had attained *dhāraṇīs*, possessed the eloquence of joyful exposition, and turned the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma. They made offerings to the [Buddha] without...
He has encountered hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and planted the roots of all virtues in the presence of those Buddhas. He is constantly praised by all Buddhas;
he cultivates his body with loving-kindness, skillfully enters the wisdom of the Buddhas, penetrates great knowledge, and reaches the other shore.
His fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds, and he is able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
(Jie-huan said: "A Bodhisattva-mahāsattva refers to a great bodhisattva among bodhisattvas. Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi means 'unsurpassed, correct, and true.
Dhāraṇī means 'total retention,' signifying that one has attained all-knowledge and maintains all dharmas.
(Xiang-mai said: "When internal virtue is thoroughly realized, there are those who are transformed upon merely seeing [the practitioner]. As for external virtue..."

When [the Dharma] is heard universally, there are those who are transformed by hearing it; thus, those whom they deliver reach into the hundreds of thousands of countless beings—all of which are the virtue of the great Bodhisattvas, for there is nothing beyond the stages prior to the [Bodhisattva] grounds.

Furthermore, it is said: "Delightful Eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) refers to the conceptualization of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one is designated as being in the "stage of non-retrogression.
On the fifth and seventh stages, one attains *dhāraṇī* and preaches the definitive Dharma; this is called the "wheel of non-retrogression. All these are qualities of transcendence.
One who dwells in the stage of non-retrogression attains this path for their own abiding, while one who turns the wheel of non-retrogression sets it in motion [for others].
This Way benefits others; it is the virtue of self-awakening and awakening others. Those who cultivate themselves through compassion intend to provide for and succor others.
They skillfully enter the Buddha’s wisdom, meaning they are able to employ *upāya* (expedient means) and penetrate great insight (*mahāprajñā*).
Thus, that which is realized is luminous, and having reached the other shore, that which is accomplished is substantial. This is internal virtue. By means of this, one becomes fully fulfilled.
Because they manifest in this way, their names are heard everywhere; these are their external virtues. Thus, they are able to deliver sentient beings.

Their names are: the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Nityodyukta, the Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhura, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, and the Bodhisattva Śūradatta.

Sādhū. There were eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas present together, including Bodhisattva Ratnacandra, Bodhisattva Candraprabha, Bodhisattva Pūrṇacandra, Bodhisattva Mahābala, Bodhisattva Anantabala, Bodhisattva Trailokyasamatikrānta, Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, Bodhisattva Maitreya, Bodhisattva Ratnākara, and Bodhisattva Śāstṛ.
Such were the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who were assembled there.

This sutra establishes its foundation through wisdom; therefore, Mañjuśrī is placed at the head. This is because Mañjuśrī possesses great wisdom and sublime virtue, serving as the embodiment of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the teacher of all Buddhas, and the eye of the world.
In opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), none precedes him.
The other names each represent the virtues of this sutra. For it is through great wisdom that one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and by supporting that wisdom with compassion—

Having cultivated the intermediate virtues throughout, until the path is realized and people are rectified, the essence of the One Vehicle is fully realized and its application for universal practice is complete.
Those who have not yet attained the level of Samantabhadra—from Avalokiteśvara downward—all practice the conduct of Samantabhadra;

however, they initially establish their foundation through wisdom to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and only finally, upon completing their virtue through practice, do they behold Samantabhadra, each specializing in their respective stage.
[This is] the inscription. The Inscription on the Precept Ring states: "Avalokiteśvara assists with wisdom and practices compassion; Mahāsthāmaprāpta possesses great virtue and function.

With diligence and mindfulness, he does not regress, ceaselessly cultivating through billions of kalpas. Ratnapāṇi grasps the Dharma-jewels; Bhaiṣajyarāja responds to capacities and manifests [his power]."
Medicine: He fearlessly bestows all things through total renunciation. Jewel Moon: His awakened body is luminous and pure. Moonlight: He is able to dispel the darkness of ignorance. Full Moon:
He possesses both of the aforementioned virtues. Great Power: He bears the great Dharma. Immeasurable Strength: He remains unmoved in the face of objects.
Transcending the three realms, they do not manifest body or mind; Bhadrapāla skillfully guards right view; Maitreya continues the Buddha’s work through compassion;
Ratnakūṭa is able to gather and benefit; and the Guide leads those on wrong paths into the right. These are the leaders among the eighty thousand.
This is the introductory exposition of the sutra.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, who made offerings to him, revered him, honored him, and praised him.

For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he preached a Mahāyāna sutra titled *The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings*, which instructs bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas. Thus did the Buddha speak this sutra.
Having finished, he sat cross-legged and entered the Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meaning, his body and mind unmoving.
(Xiang Mai said: "This demonstrates that within the opening of a single principle—whether movement or stillness—all things without exception possess immeasurable meanings;
only then can one enter the Subtle Dharma.")
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* states: "Immeasurable meanings" refers to the arising of immeasurable dharmas from the single mark of reality (*ekadharmatā*).

That the assembly first hears the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* and, upon its conclusion, enters the samādhi of immeasurable meanings is for the purpose of initiating the sequence of the *Sublime Dharma*.
At that time, the Buddha emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception.
(Jiehuan said: "A single ray of light extends throughout, fully manifesting the wondrous essence. The white tuft of hair is the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment. Eastward..."
This is precisely the realm of Immovable Wisdom (Acalajñāna). The "eighteen thousand worlds" refers to the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) of sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses.

Furthermore, Nan-yüeh said: "Sentient beings are deluded regarding this fundamental luminosity and fundamental wisdom, thereby forming the eighteen realms, which act as self-imposed limitations and obstructions."
Because it is difficult to manifest the wondrous body, the Buddha first displays these auspicious omens before preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

This causes the practitioner to immediately and spontaneously give rise to their own fundamental luminosity (*mūlaprakāśa*), thereby illuminating and realizing fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Consequently, the realms of the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses all become the sphere of wisdom; there is no longer any limitation or delusion.
Being vast, penetrating, and perfectly interfused, it is therefore said that "eighteen thousand worlds" [are illuminated].
He also saw those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who had attained the Way through various practices;
he further saw bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the bodhisattva path with various causes and conditions, various inclinations, and various characteristics;
he also saw Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa, and he again saw Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa.
Later, he erected a stupa made of the seven precious substances over the Buddha’s relics.
(Xiang Mai said: "When one observes the myriad phenomena of the world from the perspective of the realm of consciousness, they are all entirely illusory and deceptive; none of them possess reality.")

Contemplating this from the perspective of one's own wisdom, such natures, characteristics, causes, and conditions, as well as such fruits and retributions from beginning to end, are all uniformly wondrous and luminous;

there is nothing that is not the true mark (*dharmatā*). If sentient beings were to have their original luminosity fully manifest and their fundamental wisdom appear before them, then it would shine forth universally and perfectly, no different from that of a Buddha;
the wondrous essence and true mark would be vividly clear within their own minds and eyes.

Furthermore, the southern inscription states: "Beginning with the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus practicing to attain the Way, next showing the conduct and characteristics of bodhisattvas and various buddhas, and finally reaching nirvāṇa and the erection of stupas—this is the manifestation of the beginning and end of all buddhas for sentient beings.
That a single ray of light shines to the east, pervading everywhere and appearing perfectly round; that which is so detailed is directly based upon the realm of wisdom to demonstrate all dharmas."
It is the true nature (*dharmatā*).
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought: "Now the World-Honored One manifests a sign of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*).
For what cause and condition does this manifestation exist? Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered into *samādhi*; this is inconceivable and manifests the rare."
"There is a matter that must be asked of someone; who is there capable of answering it?
He further thought to himself, "This is Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, who has already drawn near to and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas of the past.
He must surely have seen this rare phenomenon. I shall now question him. At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās [all gathered].
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and others all formed this thought: "This is a manifestation of the Buddha’s light and supernormal powers;

whom should we now question? At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to resolve his own doubts, observed the minds of the fourfold assembly—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as those of the devas, nāgas, spirits, and others gathered there.
He asked Mañjuśrī, "By what causes and conditions has this auspicious omen appeared?

This sign of supernatural power, emitting a great radiance that illuminates eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, allows one to see entirely the majestic adornments of those Buddha-fields."
Jiehuan said: "Maitreya, as the Lord who occupies the position next in succession, desires to bring about benefit for the future;

therefore, he manifests doubt here to question Mañjuśrī. Mañjuśrī, being the Eye of the World, desires to awaken the wisdom of the blind masses; therefore, he later provides a divination to corroborate it.
This is what is called 'assisting in the awakening'."
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva and the other great beings, the sons of good family, saying:

"As I contemplate it, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, now intends to proclaim the Great Dharma, to rain down the Great Dharma-rain, to blow the Great Dharma-conch, to beat the Great Dharma-drum, and to expound the Great Dharma-meaning. Sons of good family, regarding the Buddhas of the past..."

I have previously witnessed this auspicious omen: after emitting such light, he immediately expounded the Great Dharma. Therefore, you should know that the Buddha’s manifestation of light now is likewise so;
it is intended to cause all sentient beings to hear and understand this Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe.
Therefore, this auspicious omen has manifested.
(Jiehuan said: "The rain wets all with a single flavor; the conch resonates with a single sound to reach the subtlest; the drum issues commands to the multitude;
and the Dharma-meaning is revealed according to what is appropriate. (Jianan said: "Go at once to bear witness to this, so as to inspire the faith and compliance of the people. )
Furthermore, sons of good family, in the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata.
Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
(Asaṃkhyeya means "innumerable"; kalpa means "period of time.

To seek the origin of its radiance and the root of its beginning by tracing it back through innumerable and inconceivable kalpas—this radiance and this Dharma are indeed without beginning from the start, transcending all calculation and measure.)
The Buddha is named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp). The sun manifests the day and the moon manifests the night;
the lamp, however, illuminates what the sun and moon do not reach, penetrating the way of both day and night in an uninterrupted succession without end.
That Buddha’s wondrous wisdom is true illumination, possessing the virtues of these three together; therefore, this is his name.
The Precept Ring says: Of the ten titles of the Buddha, the first refers to the fundamental nature, the last to the traces [of manifestation], and the middle to his virtues.

"Fundamental" refers to the true nature, which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all things; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. "Traces" refers to his transformative activities as a human being and a World-Honored One (*lokanātha*), whom all revere;

therefore, he is called the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*). "Virtues" refer to the myriad virtues and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); because he is a field of merit for the worthy, he is worthy of offerings (*Arhat*). Thus, he is fully endowed with perfection.
Because he possesses the four wisdoms, he is able to know all things correctly and universally; thus he is called "One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*).

Because he skillfully enters the realm of worldly toil and exhaustively comprehends all phenomena, he is called "One Well-Gone and Knower of the World" (*sugata lokavidū*). Because he realizes that which is unequaled, he is called "Unsurpassed One" (*anuttara*).

Because he transforms sentient beings without violence and remains steadfastly unbending, he is called "Charioteer of Men" (*puruṣadamyasārathi*). As the model for the three realms, he is called "God among Gods" (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*).

The Master says: One who has perfected the awakening of both self and others is called a Buddha. In summary, this is a title for one who has come from the path of suchness, is endowed with all virtues, and is honored by the world in response to sentient beings.
He expounds the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end;

its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its phrasing is exquisite, it is pure and unadulterated, and it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy life (*brahmacarya*). For those seeking the state of a *śrāvaka*, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths.

He delivers beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death, leading them ultimately to nirvāṇa. For those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the twelve links of dependent origination.
For all bodhisattvas, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the six pāramitās, enabling them to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and achieve the knowledge of all modes.
(Xiangmai said: "The Four Truths are [the truths of] suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path. (Xiangmai said: "The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are:

ignorance as a condition, volitional formations as a condition, consciousness as a condition, name-and-form as a condition, the six sense bases as a condition, contact as a condition, sensation as a condition, craving as a condition, grasping as a condition, becoming as a condition, birth as a condition.
(Yi Nan said: "What is called 'nirvana' by the śrāvakas... (Regarding the pratyekabuddhas...)

The Bodhisattva Zhi said: "Regarding 'knowledge of all modes' (sarvākārajñatā): because śrāvakas weary of the suffering of birth and death and take the minor fruit of the truth of cessation, they are led toward ultimate nirvana.
Because pratyekabuddhas possess sharp wisdom and bodhisattvas possess great faculties, they bring it to completion through the knowledge of all modes.
This knowledge of all modes is possessed only by the Buddha."
The Jie-huan (Jie-ring) says: This passage describes how the Lamp of Wisdom likewise teaches the Three Vehicles according to what is appropriate within the One Vehicle.

The terms "beginning, middle, and end" refer to the teachings of the Three Vehicles; all of them respond to the capacities of beings and accord with the Path, such that there is nothing that is not wholesome.

Because they rely on provisional means to reveal the ultimate reality, their meaning is profound and far-reaching. Because they employ skillful means according to individual capacities, their expressions are ingenious and subtle. They are fundamentally based upon the One Vehicle.
It is pure and unadulterated; because it clarifies the bodhisattva practice, it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and white *brahmacarya*.

It is taught by means of the One Vehicle in response to the Three Vehicles; therefore, it is said that it "teaches in accordance with the Four Truths" and so forth. While the term "seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā*) is used regarding the Two Vehicles, it is not used regarding the Bodhisattvas.
This is because the Buddha appeared for the sake of the Great Matter, and his primary teaching was the Dharma for instructing Bodhisattvas. Therefore...
It was not sought; it was not something spoken out of a desire for other vehicles, but was spoken specifically because those who delighted in the Lesser Vehicle requested it.
Next there was another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa. Next there was another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa.
Thus, these twenty thousand buddhas all shared the same name: Sūryacandrapradīpa (Sun-Moon-Lamp Brightness). They also shared the same clan: Bharadvāja.
Maitreya, you should know that from the first buddha to the last, they were all of the same name, Sūryacandrapradīpa, fully endowed with the ten titles.
The Dharma they taught was good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end. Regarding the very last of these buddhas, before he had gone forth into homelessness, there was...

There were eight princes: the first was named Intention, the second Good Intention, the third Immeasurable Intention, the fourth Jewel Intention, the fifth Increasing Intention, the sixth Doubt-Dispelling Intention, the seventh Resonance Intention, and the eighth Dharma Intention.

These eight princes possessed majestic power and sovereignty; each ruled over the four continents under heaven. When these princes heard that their father had left the household life and attained [enlightenment],...
They all renounced their royal thrones to follow [the Buddha] into the homeless life, giving rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna and constantly practicing pure conduct.
All became Dharma masters who had already planted various roots of goodness under ten million buddhas.
This further cites the original beginning of Dīpaṃkara to clarify the origins of the transmission of the Sublime Dharma.
From the first Dīpaṃkara to the final Dīpaṃkara, there were twenty thousand Buddhas; Dīpaṃkara was the prince of the final Dīpaṃkara.
That their names and natures are identical clarifies that their Way is the same. Regarding the eight princes, it shows that the Sages manifest traces to represent [the truth].

This is the Dharma. Based on the lamp’s illumination, there are eight meanings. This signifies that from the wondrously luminous true mind (*tathatā-citta*), the meaning of wondrous observation emerges;
its functions are eightfold. (Furthermore, Nan said: "Prince Zhisheng possessed precious playthings. Hearing that his father had attained the Way, he abandoned them and departed.
His intention was the same as this: when the Mind-King leaves the house of the triple world, the eight consciousnesses are its children.")
It emerges accordingly; it is the same for all Dharma masters. Jiehuan said:
"The wondrous mind is fundamentally empty, yet it is capable of function; therefore it is called 'possessing intent. This is the wondrous existence."
Emerging from the wondrous mind, its application is never unwholesome; thus it is called the "Wholesome Intention" (*kalyāṇa-manas*), which is the wondrous goodness. Its measure is unfathomable;

thus it is called the "Immeasurable Intention" (*apramāṇa-manas*), which is the wondrous measure. It is utilized effectively in response to objects; thus it is called the "Precious Intention" (*ratna-manas*), which is the wondrous jewel.

It extends and proliferates across all categories; thus it is called the "Increasing Intention" (*vṛddhi-manas*), which is the wondrous increase. It is well able to awaken and comprehend; thus it is called the "Doubt-Dispelling [Intention]" (*vicikitsā-prahāṇa*).
The "intention" (manas) refers to this wondrous awakening. Responding to objects like an echo is called the "echo-intention"; this is the wondrous resonance.

Establishing the myriad dharmas is called the "dharma-intention"; this is the wondrous dharma. One who governs the four continents has not yet escaped the burdens of worldly things before leaving the household life.
Hearing that his father had attained the Way and relinquishing his position to leave home signifies departing from emotions and discarding burdens, thereby proceeding toward the Correct [Path].
This was the manifestation of his awakening.
At that time, the Buddha Sun Moon Lamp Brightness preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings*, a Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas and protected by the Buddhas.
Having finished preaching this sūtra, he immediately sat cross-legged in the midst of the great assembly and entered into the state of immeasurable...
The Samādhi of the Station of Meaning: body and mind unmoving. Maitreya, you should know that at that time there were twenty *koṭis* of bodhisattvas in the assembly who desired to hear the Dharma.
These bodhisattvas, seeing this light universally illuminating the Buddha-land, attained what they had never experienced before.
Desiring to know the causes and conditions for which this light was manifested, there was then a bodhisattva named Wondrous Light (*Prabhāsa*) who possessed eight... [qualities].

He had one hundred disciples. At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa arose from samādhi and, through the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu, preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
(These words mean that the assembly of the past saw this omen; those who wish to know its cause are like the present assembly. (Furthermore, it says in the South:

"The Wondrous Light was the former incarnation of Mañjuśrī. The reason the Dharma was previously preached by means of the Wondrous Light was because he served as the eye of the world and was able to realize this Dharma;
now, likewise, it is through his assistance that it is brought forth)."
For sixty minor kalpas, he did not rise from his seat. Those in the assembly who were listening likewise sat in one place for sixty minor kalpas;
their bodies and minds remained unmoving as they listened to what the Buddha taught, perceiving it as if it were the duration of a single meal.
At that time, there was not a single person in the multitude whose body or mind experienced weariness or fatigue.
Furthermore, [Nan] said: "These words refer to the power of the true knowledge and vision of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*;
it is not subject to displacement by the passage of time, nor is it diminished or increased by the duration of kalpas."
Jie-huan said: "In the past, sixty small kalpas were perceived by this assembly as being like the duration of a single meal;
now, fifty small kalpas are perceived as being like half a day. This is entirely due to attaining the Lotus Samādhi, such that one never tires on the Path."
After the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had preached this sutra for sixty intermediate kalpas, he spoke these words before the assembly of Brahmās,
Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, humans, and asuras: "This very day, at midnight,
the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa without remainder."
(Xiang Mai said: "Nirvana" is here translated as "extinction and deliverance" (*mie-du*). It means to extinguish all sufferings and cross over the sea of birth and death;
it is the designation for the fruit of the path of true permanence, not a designation for death or loss. "True permanence" is the fundamental source of the nature of living beings.
When sages return to original enlightenment, they do not sink into various delusions nor undergo various transformations; therefore, it is called "true permanence. It is with...)
What the Confucians call "returning so as not to be deluded" and what the Laozi calls "returning to one's destiny as the constant" (the meaning is the same).
Since the Sūtra has already proclaimed extinction and intends to entrust this great matter, the Buddhist scriptures likewise state that the Buddha will soon enter Nirvāṇa.
It is because he wishes to entrust the wondrous Dharma to those who are worthy. Regarding "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*):

those of the Hīnayāna loathe the suffering of birth and death and desire to quickly escape the triple world; they stagnate in partial truth, and their realization of the nature is not yet perfected, hence it is called "with remainder.

Those of the Mahāyāna transcend birth and death, seeing that there is neither regression nor emergence, remaining eternally quiescent; their realization of the nature is already perfected, hence it is called [“without remainder”].

There is no remainder. As for what is now called "entering nirvana," it is a demonstration of being liberated from illusory and delusive disturbances, returning instead to the fundamental truth of concentrated stillness.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakośa. The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa immediately bestowed upon him a prediction of enlightenment and addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"Kauṭilya, this Bodhisattva Guṇagañja shall next become a Buddha, named Viśuddhakāya, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having thus bestowed the prophecy, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa without remainder during the middle watch of the night.
(Xiangmai said: *Tathāgata* means "Thus Come One"; *Arhat* means "Worthy of Offerings";
*Samyaksaṃbuddha* means "Perfectly and Fully Enlightened. These are three of the ten titles, abbreviated here.)
Jie-huan said: "This is also like recording the names of the disciples at the end of a sutra as it is preached today.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for a full eighty minor kalpas, expounding it for the sake of others.
The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa all took Wonderful Light as their teacher; through Wonderful Light’s instruction and transformation, he caused them—"
Firmly established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these princes made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas and all attained the Way of Buddhahood;
the last among them to attain Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara.
(Nan said: "This Way arises from the luminous mind of original enlightenment and is constantly sustained by wondrous light.

The essence of wisdom continues in succession without end, like a single lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps; its brightness is inexhaustible and its radiance is non-dual. This is the great root of the Wondrous Dharma.
Therefore, I shall conclude my citations here. (Xiangmai said: "The parinirvāṇa of the Great Awakened One is likened to the extinction of fire after the wood is consumed.")
This is because, although the fuel may be exhausted, the transmission of the flame continues such that its end is unknown; this is what is meant by "non-extinction. Jie-huan said:
"Miaoguang, in the past you assisted Dīpaṃkara as the teacher of Dīpaṃkara; now you assist Śākyamuni to continue the Way of Dīpaṃkara.
The eight sons were born from Dīpaṃkara and were taught by Miaoguang; when they attained Buddhahood, [the lineage continued again]."
He was named Dīpaṃkara. Furthermore, Dīpaṃkara was the teacher of Śākyamuni.
Among his eight hundred disciples, there was one named Yaśaskāma. He was greedily attached to gain and offerings;
although he recited many sūtras, he did not master them and forgot much of what he had learned, which is why he was called Yaśaskāma. This man also planted various...

By virtue of the causes and conditions of these roots of goodness, he encountered immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, whom he served, honored, revered, and praised (and offered salutations).
[Furthermore, it is said that at the initial stage of his mind, Maitreya was attached to the gains and offerings of the Hīnayāna; therefore, among the various sūtras, he sought only fame.]

He said: "There was no realization; he had lost his right view. Because he encountered the teaching of the Lamp-Bearer (Dīpaṃkara), he was able to meet many Buddhas and advance toward the stage of a Bodhisattva bound for Buddhahood.
Maitreya, you should know that at that time, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light—was he anyone else? It was I myself. As for Seeking Fame..."
"O Bodhisattva, you are that very person. Seeing this present omen, it is no different from what occurred in the past. Therefore, reflect well:
today the Tathāgata shall preach a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*, the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas."
(Xiangmai said: "The accounts of manifesting auspicious signs are similar; what I have now surmised is only this.

Furthermore, the extensive citation of passages concerning the samādhi and the proclamation of entering extinction is intended to provide a hidden narrative of the beginning and end of this single sūtra; therefore, they are cited extensively, as all these matters accord with the subsequent text.")
Jie-huan said: "The events of the past and present correspond perfectly; thus, it can be inferred with certainty that he will preach the Lotus Sutra.
Chapter Two: 'Expedient Means.
As for 'expedient means,' it refers to the fact that the quiescent nature of all phenomena is inexpressible, and can only be revealed through expedient means."
He attained it for himself.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi and addressed Śāriputra: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable;
the gateway to this wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter, and is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
He is able to know. (The square brackets indicate: "This is the arising from the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings; it is the depth of the two wisdoms and the One Vehicle.
"The wisdom of all Buddhas" refers to the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real. The provisional wisdom expounds the Dharma; the real wisdom realizes the Dharma. As for that wisdom...)
The "Gate of Wisdom" (the phrase in parentheses indicates it refers to the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle).

Jiehuan said: "At the beginning of the sutra, when the thread of the discourse is first initiated, it is solely because of Mañjuśrī that [the Buddha] emerges from samādhi and immediately addresses Śāriputra."
This sutra establishes its foundation through wisdom and reunites provisional means with ultimate reality.

Mañjuśrī is the foremost of those possessing ultimate wisdom, while Śāriputra is the first among those possessing provisional wisdom. The intent behind addressing them is to lead the provisional toward the ultimate.
Why is this? The Buddha has personally attended upon hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of countless Buddhas;
he has fully practiced the immeasurable Dharma of all Buddhas with courageous diligence; his fame is universally renowned, and he has accomplished profound and unprecedented dharmas.
What is taught according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand in its underlying intent.

(Xiang Mai said: "That which is so profound and difficult is intended to lead through provisional means into the ultimate reality. By merging the three refuges into one, it seeks to inspire the two vehicles to aspire toward [the Great Vehicle]. )
Jie-huan said: "The term 'Shi' (釋) refers to the source of profound wisdom and profound Dharma. To have personally attended countless Buddhas is the profundity of what has been studied;
to have practiced immeasurable paths is the profundity of what has been accomplished; to have been courageous and diligent is the profundity of one's resolve;
for one's reputation to be heard everywhere is the profundity of accumulated virtue; and to have perfected the profound Dharma is the profundity of what has been realized."
What is taught according to what is appropriate is the profundity of skillful means; this is why it is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.

Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded the verbal teachings through various causes and conditions and various parables, using innumerable skillful means to guide sentient beings and cause them to leave behind all attachments. Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata, for the sake of...
One then knows and sees that those pāramitās are all already fully perfected.

(Furthermore, it is said: "The appearance of the World-Honored One and his various expositions, which guide beings through skillful means, all arise solely from the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate reality.")
Jie-huan said: "The *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya*) is provisional wisdom (*prajñā*). The *pāramitā* of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*) is ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Without the provisional, one cannot guide sentient beings; without the ultimate, one cannot detach from attachments. Therefore, both must be possessed. As for various attachments:
the coarse are the karma of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*); the subtle are the teachings of the Two Vehicles (*dvi-yāna*)."
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound, immeasurable and unimpeded.
His powers and fearlessnesses, his meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis penetrate deeply to the boundless. He has accomplished all unprecedented dharmas.
(Xiangmai said: "This praises the realization of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). This wisdom indeed encompasses all phenomena, just as space contains form;
it dissolves all marks, just as the ocean receives flowing streams. Therefore, its merit is vast, great, deep, and far-reaching.)"
Jie-huan said: "The Tathāgata’s power of true knowledge and vision is so vast that nothing is not encompassed by it, and so profound that nothing reaches its limit.

Therefore, regarding the four immeasurable minds, the four unhindered analytical knowledges, the ten powers and four fearlessnesses, the deep meditations and great concentrations, and all dharmas of liberation and the various gates of samādhi—each and every one he has deeply penetrated to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). As for all unprecedented dharmas, there is none..."
It is not by means of this that [the Tathāgata] achieves it.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is able to analyze all things in various ways and skillfully expound all dharmas; his words are gentle and pleasing to the hearts of the multitude.
Xiang Mai said, "This is the difficult task of preaching the Dharma through provisional wisdom.
Jiehuan replied, "The Tathāgata’s true skillful means have the power to discern the myriad dharmas and artfully teach the Three Vehicles.
He adapts his preaching to the capacities of beings; therefore, his words are gentle and supple, perfectly suited to the nature of things, and thus they gladden the hearts of the multitude."
Śāriputra, to speak in brief: the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas.
(Xiang Mai notes: This concludes the section on the functional application of the two types of wisdom and virtue.)
Stop, Śāriputra. There is no need to say more. Why is this? The Buddha has accomplished a foremost, most rare, and difficult-to-understand Dharma;
only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaustively realize the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
(Naizhi said: "Such a true reality (*tathatā*) is real in every encounter; to conceptualize it is to deviate from it, and to speak of it is to contradict it.

It is said that the class of Confucian scholars is generally unable to understand this, because they find it difficult to silently realize it within the very nature and characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), rather than seeking it outside of form and mind (*rūpa-citta*).")

Jie-huan said: "To refrain from further explanation serves only to manifest its profound subtlety all the more. This foremost dharma that is difficult to understand is the wondrous Dharma of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa);
it cannot be reached by words, and therefore need not be explained further. It cannot be attained by the mind, and therefore it is rare and difficult to comprehend.
It is not something produced by those of the Two Vehicles; thus, only a Buddha can fully fathom it."

That which is called all dharmas: such are their marks, such their nature, such their substance, such their power, such their activity, such their causes, such their conditions, such their fruits, such their retributions; thus are they equal from beginning to end.
(An added note states: The old [teaching] explains the ten dharma-realms—the four noble ones and the six ordinary beings—on the basis that each realm possesses ten suchnesses (*tathatā*).
These combine to form one hundred suchnesses across the ten realms, which are further subsumed as one thousand suchnesses across the hundred realms. These are then fused until they reach infinity.)
This clarifies the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) by means of the ultimate reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa). Furthermore, it is explained through the three contemplations:

emptiness is the suchness of characteristics; the provisional is the characteristics of suchness; and the middle is the suchness of characteristics. This clarifies the wisdom of contemplation by means of the ultimate reality.

However, this primarily elucidates the true reality of all phenomena, which is the ultimate discourse of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna); one should not regard it merely as the principle of suchness (tathatā).
This is explained by its nature; how much more so the ten suchnesses and the three contemplations, which constitute the perfectly interfused dharma of the Mahāyāna.
Within the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the One Vehicle, they share the same path yet differ in their tracks—let those who understand examine this.

Jie-huan said: "That which is called 'true reality' (śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa) as mentioned above is precisely this: the nature, characteristics, essence, and power of all worldly dharmas are equal from beginning to end.

That which can be perceived is the characteristic (lakṣaṇa); the fundamental basis of these characteristics is the nature (svabhāva). That which possesses form is the essence (ātman); that which provides utility is the power (bala).
What arises momentarily is activity (karma); what initiates the process is the cause (hetu); what assists the cause is the condition (pratyaya); and the ripening of conditions is the fruit (phala)."
The fruit of arhatship is the retribution; beginning and end constitute the root and the branches; exhaustion constitutes the ultimate.
All dharmas do not depart from these ten, nor does each individual dharma lack these ten.

Such [a description] is a term used according to phenomena to grasp their characteristics, meaning that all dharmas possess such marks, such natures, and so forth, up to such a beginning and end. As it is said:
Exhaustively investigated, there is nothing that is not the true mark (*dharmatā*). Extending this reasoning further:

all the various phenomena manifest before us—the straightness of pines and the curvature of thorns, the whiteness of cranes and the blackness of crows, the verdant hue of bamboo and the golden color of flowers—all these mundane conventional matters (*saṃvṛti*) are none other than the true mark.
Precisely because they are mundane conventions and yet are none other than the true mark, one realizes [it].
One who practices this should not impair their original nature (*tianzhen*), nor depart from its essential reality; rather, they should silently attain it beyond both form and mind.
This is called the foremost, rare, and difficult-to-understand Dharma.
At that time, among the great assembly, there were certain śrāvakas, arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who each had this thought:
"For what reason does the World-Honored One now so earnestly praise skillful means, saying: 'The Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand;
whatever he speaks, his underlying intention is difficult to discern,' such that it cannot be grasped by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?"
Furthermore, when the Buddha taught the meaning of a single liberation, we too attained this Dharma and reached nirvana;
yet now we do not know where this meaning leads.

[And the Southern Text says: "The two vehicles, upon hearing of the Buddha’s profound and difficult twofold wisdom, were unable to understand it and thus harbored doubts; consequently, they spoke as follows.
[From the words "The Buddha has said" onwards, all is a narration of the Buddha's previous discourse.]

Jie-huan said: "The Buddha taught that because those of the lower vehicles could not attain liberation through the various samādhis, they consequently equated the liberation of the two vehicles with the liberation of a Buddha, claiming they had already attained it.
They did not realize that for the two vehicles, liberation merely refers to being free from delusion;
in reality, they have not yet attained all-encompassing liberation."
At that time, Śāriputra, perceiving that the minds of the fourfold assembly were filled with doubt and that he himself had not yet fully understood, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, for what cause and by what condition do you so earnestly praise the Buddhas' foremost skillful means—the profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma?
Since the distant past, I have never before heard such a teaching from the Buddha. Now, the entire fourfold assembly..."
There is doubt; we only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this matter. At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak further.
If this matter were spoken, all the gods and humans in the world would be struck with alarm and doubt."
(Xiangmai said: "These are the words of Śāriputra posing the question. (Jiannan said: "The Buddha stopped and did not speak, because the Way is great while his capacity was small;
those who heard it would have been startled and filled with doubt.")
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying, "World-Honored One, I only pray that you will speak; I only pray that you will speak.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra, "In this assembly of mine now, there are no longer any branches or leaves; it consists purely of those who are true and real.
Śāriputra, it would be well indeed for such people of overweening pride to depart. Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for your sake."
(Jie-huan said: "The Buddha ceased [teaching] because of those with inferior faculties, while Śāriputra requested it because of those with superior faculties. Such is the urgency for the Dharma.
Now, branches and leaves are like the assembly of those at the periphery; the 'true reality' is like the assembly of those who have perfected virtue.")
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare intervals;
it appears but once in a long while, like the udumbara flower."
(And Nan said: "This wondrous Dharma is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This concludes what is meant by 'this Dharma is not to be understood through thought or discrimination. It can simply be understood without thought or discrimination.)
Jiehuan said: "The 'Direct Pointing' is the entire body of the wondrous Dharma. The udumbara flower—here called the 'Numinous Auspicious Flower'—appears once every three thousand years;
when it appears, a Golden Wheel-turning King emerges. This is used as a metaphor for the wondrous Dharma being for the sake of the one great matter, which is preached only at such a time."
Why is this? By means of countless skillful methods, various causes and conditions, parables, and discourse, I have expounded all dharmas.
These dharmas cannot be understood through thought or discrimination; only the Buddhas can know them. Why is this?
It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter.
"World-Honored One, [Nan said: 'The one great matter is precisely the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas, the wondrous mind of humans, and the true reality of the myriad dharmas.
There are neither two nor three; therefore it is called 'one. This is no small cause; therefore it is called a 'great matter.'"
Jie-huan said: "To say 'I expound through skillful means' clarifies the provisional; to say 'this Dharma is not to be understood through deliberation' reveals the real.
That which is beyond deliberation and discrimination is because it is detached from the conceptualizing mind.
Only a Buddha can know it; it is not the teaching of the Two Vehicles. 'The one great matter' refers to the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle."
Śāriputra, for what reason do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world? It is solely for the sake of one great causal matter.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that they may attain purity.
They appear in the world because they desire to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. They appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings...

It is for the sake of awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that he appears in the world; it is because he wishes to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that he appears in the world.
(And the Southern School says: This true knowledge and vision is possessed equally by sentient beings and Buddhas; it is primordially pure, yet humans alone [obscure it] with delusive objects.)
Being defiled and shrouded by radiance, one becomes lost in self-delusion;
therefore, the Buddha provides instruction so that one may realize their own original purity and awaken to it, no longer remaining lost. "Opening" means breaking through the covering of ignorance.
"Showing" refers to pointing out the true essence that was previously deluded about. "Awakening" means seeing through it with sudden, clear insight.
"Entering" means attaining profound realization for oneself and thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is called the path of the Buddha's knowledge and vision.
Jiehuan said: To explain the meaning of the preceding passage is to clarify the fundamental intent behind the appearance of the Buddhas.

"The Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers to the thorough realization of the true mark (*dharmatā*); it is true knowledge and true vision. In terms of the Dharma, it is called the One Vehicle of the Buddhas;

in terms of the cause, it is called the Great Matter; in terms of the fruit, it is called the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Therefore, it is said that the Buddhas appear for the sake of this one Great Matter.
I preach the Dharma for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle, desiring to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,
so that they may ultimately all attain universal and perfect enlightenment.
Śāriputra, it is for this one great cause and condition that all Buddhas appear in the world.
(Xiang Mai notes: This is the concluding explanation.)
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "All Buddhas, Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas. Whatever they do is always for a single purpose:
solely to use the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to instruct and awaken sentient beings.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sentient beings using only the Single Buddha Vehicle; there are no other vehicles, whether two or three."
(Jie-huan said: "Because the Buddhas appear for the sake of the one great matter, all that they do is always for this one purpose.
It is by this that they instruct bodhisattvas, it is by this that they manifest themselves to sentient beings, and it is by this that they preach the Dharma;
there has never been any other way.")
Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions is likewise so.
(And the salutation says: "The Way is the same throughout the ten directions.")
The Precept Ring said: "None have failed to proceed by this path.

Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past, through immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and expressions, have expounded all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; these teachings were all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. These...
Sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, will ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

Śāriputra, future Buddhas who shall appear in the world will likewise, through immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and expressions, expound the various Dharmas for sentient beings; these teachings are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. These...
Sentient beings who hear the Dharma from the Buddha will all ultimately attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

Śāriputra, in the present, throughout the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-fields in the ten directions, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bring great benefit to many and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings.
These Buddhas also employ immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and words.
Using these words, he expounds all dharmas for the sake of generating the seeds [of enlightenment]. These dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle.
Consequently, these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately all attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
(Jie-huan said: "Although hundreds of thousands of billions of countless Dharma-gates are taught, their reality is the One Vehicle of the knowledge of all modes;
this is precisely the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit. (And Nan said: "Though the verbal explanations are three, the ultimate reality is one.")
Śāriputra, these Buddhas teach and transform only bodhisattvas because they wish to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings,
because they wish to awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and because they desire to cause sentient beings to enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
(Jiehuan said: "Binding the fingers signifies returning to the same [state]. The reason 'opening' is not mentioned is that 'teaching and transforming' already carries the meaning of opening.

Śāriputra, I now do likewise. Knowing that all sentient beings have various desires and deep-seated attachments, I preach for them according to their fundamental natures, employing the power of skillful means through various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions.
Dharma. Śāriputra, all these are for the sake of attaining the Single Buddha Vehicle and the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvākārajñatā).
[Jiehuan says: This refers to the identity of the path of self-cultivation. It means that the Dharma I now preach accords with all Buddhas. Regarding various desires and attachments:
some rely on defiled karma and desire attachment to the five sensory objects; others rely on pure karma and desire attachment to minor fruits.]
Śāriputra, even in the worlds of the ten directions there are no two vehicles, let alone three.
(And the Southern edition says: "This conclusion clarifies the One Vehicle.")

Śāriputra, the Buddhas appear in the world during the five turbidities: namely, the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), and the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
It is thus, Śāriputra, that during the chaotic time of the turbidity of the eon, the defilements of sentient beings are heavy;

because they are characterized by stinginess, greed, envy, and jealousy, and have perfected all roots of unwholesomeness, the Buddhas, through the power of skillful means, divide the single Buddha Vehicle (*eka-buddhayāna*)— [...into three].** (Note: The source text ends abruptly. The standard Mahāyāna context implies the division into three vehicles.)

The three [vehicles] are explained separately. (Xiangmai said: "This means that the Sage initially employs the vehicles to save beings according to the times; he speaks of three only because it cannot be helped.

Yet, when one considers the ultimate goal, they are truly but the One Vehicle. Because of clinging to the five desires, deluded craving gives rise to affliction; this is the turbidity of affliction. )

Due to the causal conditions of desire, they fall into the three evil realms and the six paths of existence. Amidst the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), they receive subtle forms in the womb and experience an increase of manifold sufferings.

Amidst the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*), they enter the forest of false views and become attached to delusion, flattery, and crookedness. Amidst the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), they are fully possessed of the sixty-two views;
for ten billion kalpas, they do not hear the name of the Buddha, nor do they hear the True Dharma. This is the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

Jiehuan said: "The five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya) are all explained in relation to the nature (prakṛti). The nature is fundamentally profound and clear; when the five matters interact and disturb it, various sediments arise, which are called 'turbidity.
As for what is called the turbidity of the eon (kalpa-kaṣāya): 'eon' refers to time. When time abounds in evil matters, karma arises in a state of confusion and turbidity.
The turbidity of afflictions (kleśa-kaṣāya) refers, when analyzed, to the ninety-eight proclivities (anuśaya), and, when summarized, to the five [poisons] such as greed, anger, and delusion."
Dullness. The turbidity of phenomena obstructs events. The turbidity of sentient beings nourishes ignorance, causing the six realms of existence to become fragmented and various evils to arise;

this turbidity obstructs nature. The turbidity of views consists of sixty-two views when analyzed individually, and the five [wrong] views—identity view, extreme view, and so forth—when taken as a whole;
this turbidity obstructs principle. The turbidity of lifespan takes the karmic consciousness as its seed, which, through mutual interaction, brings about birth and follows along with...

The kalpas are shortened and diminished; one is submerged in birth and death. The turbidity of the kalpa has no separate essence; it is merely a designation established based on the intensification of the [other] four [turbidities].
○ Chapter Three: Simile and Parable.
Regarding the parables: those of superior capacity have already attained awakening through prior knowledge; those of middling capacity have not yet understood.

Therefore, the Teacher employs the shallow analogy of the three carts at a single gate to illustrate the profound reality of the three vehicles within the one path. There are nine such illustrations: namely, the burning house, the impoverished son, and the medicinal herbs.
The conjured city, the tied jewel, the dug well, the king’s topknot, the young father, and the physician—of these, two remain today.
At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy and, filled with delight, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, when I was always dwelling alone in the mountains, forests, or beneath trees, whether sitting or walking, I would constantly think: 'We have entered equally into the nature of dharmas; why is it that [the Tathāgata]..."
"Come! That we were delivered by means of the Hīnayāna teachings is our own fault, not that of the World-Honored One.
(Jiehuan said: "In daily life, one should emphasize what is common and record what is unique; this is not something the Buddha favors privately. The fault truly lies with us.
To 'enter the Dharma-nature together' means to realize the True Principle together.")
Why is this? If we had waited for the explanation of the causes by which one achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, we would certainly have attained liberation through the Mahāyāna.
However, not understanding the skillful means taught according to what was appropriate, we accepted the Buddha’s Dharma upon first hearing it, contemplated it, and sought realization therein.
(Jie-huan said: "The Buddha reproached himself. That which served as the cause was true wisdom, the direct cause of Bodhi.
Since the Buddha was certainly about to preach it, I did not wait for him. Upon first hearing the Four Noble Truths, I immediately accepted them in faith and quickly attained the lesser fruit;
this was indeed my own error)."
World-Honored One, from the past until now, throughout the day and night, I have constantly reproached myself.

But now, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma never before heard, all my doubts and regrets are severed; my body and mind are at ease, and I have attained a swift sense of peace and security.
Today I finally know that I am truly a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s own mouth, transformed by birth from the Dharma, and having obtained a share of the Buddha-Dharma.
(Jie-huan said: "To rejoice in what one has realized. "The birth from the mouth" refers to hearing a single sound. "The birth of the Dharma" refers to awakening to such a Dharma.
"The division of the Dharma" refers to obtaining a share of the Tathāgata’s treasure-house of knowledge and vision.)
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "I now declare before this great assembly of devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas:
in the past, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, I have constantly instructed and transformed you in the presence of twenty trillion buddhas."
You, too, have followed and studied under me for a long night. It was through my skillful means that I guided you so that you were born into my Dharma.
(The *Śīla-sūtra* states that Śāriputra had practiced the bodhisattva path for sixteen kalpas; the present mention of "twenty thousand koṭis of Buddhas" refers to that time.
"Following and studying for a long night" indicates that his correct wisdom had not yet been clarified.)
The Precept Ring says: This describes the original cause in order to clarify the basis for attaining enlightenment and receiving a prediction of future Buddhahood.
The statement that it was spoken "among the assembly of devas and humans" is intended to clarify the distant cause and the distant prediction, demonstrating that they are not false.
Śāriputra, in the past I instructed you to set your aspirations on the Buddha-way, yet you have now completely forgotten this and instead claim that you have already attained parinirvāṇa.
Now, wishing to cause you to remember your original vow and the path you were practicing, I preach this Mahāyāna sūtra for the sake of all śrāvakas;
it is titled *The Lotus of the Wonderful Law*, the teaching of the bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas’ mindful care.
(Śikṣānanda said: "In the past you already tied the jewel; now you have again shown it to me.

"Śāriputra, in a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas, you shall make offerings to many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, uphold the True Dharma, and fulfill the path practiced by Bodhisattvas. You shall then attain..."

He became a Buddha, named Padmaprabha (Flower Light). He was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat.
Furthermore, [the Master] said to the South: "Although those of the Lesser Vehicle have awakened to ultimate wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), they have not yet cultivated the Great Practice.

Therefore, they must pass through kalpas making offerings to the Buddhas in order to expand their great mind and accomplish the myriad virtues. Only when these myriad virtues are perfectly complete do they become a Buddha fully endowed with the Ten Titles;
this is not comparable to the Buddha of the self-nature’s original truth. This is what is meant by the Sudden Teaching’s 'transcending the immeasurable'."

Regarding "inconceivable eons": if one were to consider it solely in terms of right wisdom suddenly severing ignorance and suddenly perfecting the seed-wisdom, then the delusions of boundless eons would be extinguished all at once;
this is what is meant by "passing through boundless [eons] without becoming a Buddha."

The Precept Ring says: "Having already awakened to the wondrous Dharma, one shall attain the Buddha-way; therefore, one receives the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of becoming a Buddha. All texts concerning predictions consist of two parts:
first, the prediction based on making offerings to Buddhas and practicing the Way (the causal prediction); second, the ten titles, the kalpa, and the land (the resultant prediction).
This prediction of great causes and great fruits is intended to spur those of the Lesser Vehicle forward. As for the title "Flower Radiance" (Puṣyarasmi), "flower" symbolizes...
Regarding "causal practice": light is able to bring forth illumination because, from the very beginning, one has realized and brought forth this Way.

As for the fact that, even after receiving the Buddha’s prediction, one must pass through many kalpas before attaining the fruit: becoming a Buddha depends on wisdom, while attaining the fruit depends on practice.
The land is named Vimalā. Its terrain is level and even; it is pure, adorned, peaceful, and prosperous. Gods and humans are exceedingly numerous.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli, with eight intersecting roads bordered by cords of gold.

Alongside these roads stand rows of trees made of the seven treasures, always bearing flowers and fruit. The Tathāgata Puṣpārāma also teaches and transforms sentient beings through the three vehicles.
Śāriputra, although that Buddha appeared at a time when it was not an evil age, he preached the Dharma of the three vehicles by virtue of his original vows.
That kalpa was named Mahāratnavyūha. Why was it called Mahāratnavyūha? Because in that land, bodhisattvas were regarded as the great jewels.
Furthermore, it says: "If one turns back and seeks within, the marks of stainless purity are all the very ground of the mind (*citta-bhūmi*).
Matters of peace, stability, abundance, and joy are none other than virtuous nature (*guṇatā*). Defilement, attachment, and transformation constantly reside within persons.

If sentient beings do not undergo unbearable suffering, do not give rise to the karma of the three turbidities, and do not engage in deviant or sycophantic conduct, then they will truly be free from defilement, upright, and at peace."
"It is a land of stability, abundance, and joy.
Jie-huan said, "The adornments of a kalpa and a land are all due to the dependent retribution resulting from one's causal practices.

Because Śāriputra’s causal practice takes great wisdom as its foundation, the land is named 'Free from Defilement' (Vimalā). Because his causal practice elucidates and reveals the Dharma for Bodhisattvas, the kalpa is named..."
It is a Great Jewel Adornment, taking the bodhisattvas as its great jewels; it is pure and magnificent, thus lacking any defiled lands;
it is peaceful, secure, abundant, and joyful, thus lacking the suffering of the three calamities; and devas and humans flourish therein, thus lacking the three evil realms.

Regarding the mention of "eight intersecting roads," these are the confluence of the Eightfold Noble Path. Regarding the "rows of trees made of the seven treasures," these are produced from the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
Generally, all such environmental rewards (*niśraya-vipāka*) of the Buddhas are like this, for they are common to those who have cultivated the same causal practices.

If, however, one considers the environmental rewards of sentient beings, then the land is named Endurance (*Sahā*), the eon is named the Five Turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), and that realm is filled with pits and ravines.
The ground consists of sand and gravel; this is likewise due to the commonality of their past conduct.
Those bodhisattvas are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable, beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
It is not by the power of a Buddha’s wisdom that anyone could know this. When they wish to walk, precious lotuses receive their feet.

These bodhisattvas have not merely resolved their minds for the first time; they have long planted the roots of virtue and have purified their brahma-conduct under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas.
They are constantly praised by all Buddhas, always cultivate the Buddha-wisdom, possess true great supernormal powers, and are well-versed in [the Dharma].
The gateways to all dharmas are straightforward and without artifice; their resolve and mindfulness are firm and steadfast. Such bodhisattvas fill that land.
Śāriputra, the lifespan of the Buddha Puṣpārāma is twelve small kalpas, excluding the time when he was a prince and had not yet attained buddhahood.
The lifespan of the people in that land is eight small kalpas.
[The Precept Ring says: Except for the period when he was a prince, he alone recorded that after becoming a Buddha, his lifespan would be twelve kalpas.
After twelve minor kalpas had passed, the Tathāgata Padmaprabha bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavīrya the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "This Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavīrya shall next become a Buddha, and his name shall be Padma."
