With feet set in peace, he is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
His Buddha-land is likewise so.
(This refers to Śāriputra’s transformation of the record to Jianman, causing him to transmit and continue the wondrous Way.

As for the term "Nan," it is a suppressed designation for "Huazuan Anxing" (Flower-Adorned Peaceful Walking), which signifies that one carries the fruit while practicing the cause. That the Bodhisattva’s feet are supported by precious flowers signifies that one attains the realm by relying upon the cause.)
Jie-huan said: "After twelve minor kalpas have passed, it will be the time of his final extinction.

The wondrous Way of the Lotus Sūtra originated with Dīpaṃkara, was transmitted by Prabhāsa, and was continued by Dīpaṃkara [the Buddha]. From Buddha to Buddha it was handed down by hand; from light to light it was perpetuated.
Thus Śāriputra attained it and was designated as the Buddha Flower-Light (Huaguang). This was because he illuminated this Way, enabling all who possess eyes to share in it."
It is seen that Jianman (Dṛḍhavati) attained this; he was also titled Huazuan Anxing (Flower-Foot Peaceful Progress).
Thus, he followed this Way so that all who have feet might travel together by it. When Bodhisattvas reach his land, precious flowers receive their feet as they walk;
thus, none among those who follow his transformation fail to proceed by this Way.

At that time, the fourfold assembly, seeing Śāriputra receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before the Buddha, was filled with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight; each one removed the upper garment they were wearing.

To make offerings to the Buddha, Śakra Devānām Indra, Brahmā Sahāmpati, and countless sons of gods likewise offered celestial fine garments, celestial *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, and so forth, to the Buddha.
The celestial garments they scattered remained suspended in mid-air, revolving of their own accord. There were hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of celestial music in the sky.
In the air, they simultaneously performed [these acts], raining down various celestial flowers.
(Jiehuan said: "I leaped for joy, thinking that we too shall likewise surely attain Buddhahood.

Because the devas heard the sublime Dharma, they were able to transcend their innate obstacles; thus, they turned from the Hinayana toward the Mahayana and stripped off their garments as an offering to the Buddha.
To record his sincerity: it was as if he had unfastened the celestial bow-case and opened the celestial chest. His robe hovered in mid-air and rotated of its own accord;
this was surely the response to his focused devotion.
Jie-huan said: "Clothing is the sheath for a person; the nature-obstructions are the sheath for Heaven.
'Turning back' (huizhuan) is the meaning of 'dedication' (huixiang).
And he spoke these words: 'In the past, the Buddha first turned the Wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī; now he has once again ascended to the Unsurpassed.'"
The Greatest Dharma-Wheel.
(The Commentary on the Precept-Ring states: This means that in the past, the turning of the Four Truths was the smallest, whereas now, the turning of the One Vehicle is the greatest.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "These twelve hundred who have attained mastery over their own minds previously remained in the stage of training."
World-Honored One, the Buddha has constantly taught and transformed us, saying: "My Dharma can bring about liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death, culminating in ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

Those who were in training and those beyond training each considered themselves to have already abandoned the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), as well as views of existence and non-existence, and claimed to have attained *nirvāṇa*.

Yet now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, hearing what we have never heard before, we all fall into doubt and confusion. How excellent it would be, World-Honored One, if you would act for our sake—[for the sake of these four...].
The assembly explained the causes and conditions for this, so as to dispel their doubts.
[Jie-huan] said: "One who has mastery over the mind is an Arhat beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training are merely the Lesser Śrāvakas.

In the past, having received the Buddha’s teaching, they considered themselves to have reached the ultimate end; thus they ceased their pursuit of views and entered into quiescence. Now I hear that although they speak of *nirvāṇa*, it is not yet the true one."
...ceased. This is why there is doubt.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "Suppose in a kingdom, city, town, or village, there is a great elder who has reached an advanced age."
His wealth and resources are immeasurable; he possesses many fields, houses, and various servants.
(Nan says: This introduces the parable of the burning house to clarify that the former provisional teachings were all intended to transform the deluded.
(Xiang Mai says: This is an analogy for the Buddha-King transforming the three realms.)
Jie-huan said: "A country has cities, and cities have villages; this is like the trichiliocosm containing the three realms.
Within these three realms are the six destinies and the four modes of birth. Great Elder, the Tathāgata is like the father of all the world.

His years are now advanced, which is like his long-standing engagement with conditions; he wishes to enter parinirvāṇa. His wealth and provisions are immeasurable, which is like the [immeasurable]..."
The wealth of the Dharma consists of knowledge and vision; its many fields and houses are a metaphor for the field of merit consisting of skillful means and wisdom.
Servants are a metaphor for compassion that never tires, which assists the Right Path and engages with the various capacities of sentient beings.
His house was vast and spacious, yet had only a single door; many people—hundreds, two hundred, or even five hundred—dwelt within it.
(Nan Yue further stated: "This 'house' refers to its vastness and the multitude of people within it; it is a metaphor for the mass of suffering of the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
Jiehuan said: "The house is a metaphor for a single realm (*dhātu*). A single gate is a metaphor for the path of deliverance of a single vehicle (*ekayāna*).
The five hundred people represent sentient beings of the five destinies. As for the mention of one hundred or two hundred, these are counted sequentially starting from humans and devas."
The halls and pavilions were dilapidated and old; the walls and partitions had collapsed; the bases of the pillars were rotten; and the beams and rafters were leaning precariously.
Suddenly, fires broke out all around simultaneously, burning down the house and its dwellings.
(Nan-yueh further said: "This statement regarding 'the house being dilapidated and fire pressing in' is a metaphor for the body being oppressed by the suffering of old age.
Jiehuan said: "A family possesses halls, pavilions, and dwellings; these dwellings have walls, pillars, foundations, beams, and rafters.

All are decayed and rotten, on the verge of collapsing and thus unfit for habitation. This is a metaphor for the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of sentient beings within the three realms. Sentient beings possess..."
The four great elements, the life-faculty, and the physical body all undergo transformation and rapidly decay, being impossible to preserve.
Yet, within them, beings compete to create evil karma, scorched and boiled by the grief and afflictions of birth and death for the sake of the five desires and material gain.
Neither in the heavens nor among humans can one escape this; hence it is said that "all around, flames suddenly break out at once."
The sons of the elder, whether ten, twenty, or even thirty in number, were within this house.
(Furthermore, while "one hundred" was previously mentioned in reference to the five destinies, here "ten" is used in reference to the three vehicles;
this is because among the sentient beings of the five destinies, those who have been transformed by the teaching of the three vehicles amount to no more than one in ten.)

Jie-huan said: "When he speaks of 'five hundred people' and again of 'sons,' 'people' refers broadly to all sentient beings, while 'sons' specifically refers to those who have followed his transformation.
For example, the ten fingers represent the Bodhisattvas, and the twenty or thirty fingers represent the followers of the Two Vehicles."
When the elder saw this great fire rising from all four sides, he was immediately seized with great alarm and fear, and thought to himself:
"Although I am able to escape safely through this gate that is being consumed by flames, my children within this burning house are attached to their play and amusement;
they do not perceive, they do not know, they are neither alarmed nor afraid, even as the fire approaches their bodies and its agonizing pain cuts into them."
They do not feel weary or distressed, nor do they have the intention to seek liberation.
(And the commentary says: This refers to the elder’s rescue by means of analogy; observing the suffering of the six realms, he gives rise to great compassion.
Sentient beings vainly see gain and forget their true form, seeing profit and forgetting the truth. Those within the burning house are all like this.)
The Precept Ring says: "The four directions represent the old age, sickness, and death of sentient beings; these four marks are the root of all suffering.
To emerge safely from the burning house represents the Buddha’s eternal exhaustion of the suffering of birth and death, such that grief and affliction can no longer assail him.
That the children are attached to their pleasures, unaware and unafraid, represents those who cling to worldly delights and lack the heart of wisdom."
Śāriputra, that householder thought to himself: "My body and arms possess great strength;
I shall carry him out from the house using my lap or a small table. Then he further reflected: "This house has but a single door, and it is moreover narrow and small."

Furthermore, Nan said: "I was deeply contemplating a means to rescue [the child] from the burning house. I thought that by relying on the strength of my own body and limbs, I could manifest a subtle skill suited to a youth;
thus, I wished to secretly support him with my robe-sleeve and carry him out, or to lift him up using a desk or table."
Furthermore, he thought that the entrance was too narrow for this to be used; rather, he would simply use diligent skillful means to lead it out.
(The Tripitaka Master said: A *yike* [衣裓] is a vessel for holding flowers in the Western Regions, used when making offerings to persons of high rank.)
Jie-huan said: "This parable illustrates the intent behind establishing the teachings through seven days of contemplation.

The body and hands as a whole represent the Tathāgata’s powers of knowledge and vision, as well as his fearlessnesses. The secret use of the robe and bowl represents the possession of great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-bala*).

The desk upon which one may lean represents the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*). The narrowness of its door represents the inferiority of the minds of those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), who are unable to endure this Dharma."

The subsequent text states: "If I were to rely solely on the power of my spiritual transformations and the power of my wisdom to praise the Tathāgata’s powers of knowledge and vision and his fearlessnesses, sentient beings would not be able to attain liberation through them; therefore, I employ only skillful means to rescue and deliver them."
The sons were young and lacked discernment; they were attached to their play area and might fall into it and be consumed by the fire.
"I shall speak to them of things that cause fear: this house is already burning; you should quickly exit at once, lest you be harmed and destroyed by the fire.
Having formed this thought, he acted according to his deliberation and addressed all the sons: "All of you, come out quickly!"
Although the father compassionately enticed and exhorted them with kind words, the sons remained attached to their play;
they were unwilling to believe or accept his words, neither startled nor afraid, having no intention at all to escape, nor did they know what was fire or what was the house.
"What is the loss? They merely run about here and there playing;
they are nothing but fathers. (Jiehuan said: "I grieve for their ignorance. I shall clearly inform them of the harm so that they may know how to pursue what is beneficial. (Jiehuan said:
"These words refer to the delusion of the sons, which is like sentient beings being deluded by greed and desire; though they encounter great suffering, they do not perceive it as such.")
Furthermore, Nan said: "Since their indulgence has become so extreme, they do not know what constitutes suffering, what constitutes the body, or what it means to be poor.

They are merely deluded by themselves and pursue external objects, racing like a firebrand without turning back. Although they have encountered the Buddha-dharma, they do not follow its transformation."
He merely observes it.
At that time, the elder immediately thinks to himself: "This house has already been consumed by a great fire; myself and my children [are within]."
"If they do not emerge at the proper time, they will surely be consumed by fire. I must now employ skillful means to enable my sons to escape this calamity.
The father knew that each of his sons had their own particular preferences regarding various rare treasures and extraordinary objects.
Their hearts were inevitably filled with attachment, so he said to them: "These toys you may enjoy are rare and difficult to find.
If you do not take them now, you will surely feel sorrow and regret later. Such various carts—drawn by goats, deer, and oxen—are now outside the gate."
"It can be used for play. You all should quickly come out from this burning house. Whatever you desire, I shall give it all to you.
(The Southern commentary says: To merely urge them to come out quickly would frustrate their desires; since they could not be transformed by such means, [the Buddha] accords with what they wish.)
(He transformed them according to their desires. (Xing Jianzi said: "The Śrāvaka vehicle is the sheep cart;

the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is the deer cart; the Mahāyāna is the ox cart. (Xiang Mai said: "Sheep and deer are not things that can be harnessed for riding; they are merely objects of play and curiosity.
If the two vehicles were insufficient to bring one to the Way, they would be nothing more than the dharmas of frivolous discourse.")

The "precept-rings" (śīla-maṇḍala) are said to mean that the elder also feared being burned himself; this is an analogy for the Buddha manifesting the three precepts of the body to share in the sufferings of the people.
"Knowing what his son liked" is an analogy for knowing that all sentient beings have various anxieties, and thus he skillfully taught the three [vehicles] according to their respective natures.
The "chariot" represents the Dharma of fruition, which does not belong to the triple world; therefore, it is said, "it is now here."
That which can be used for play outside the gate is a metaphor for the joy of the Dharma (dharmasukha) by which one may amuse oneself.
The ox, being a great beast capable of pulling a carriage, is precisely a parable for those with great faculties (mahāmūla), who are fit for the Mahāyāna. The sheep and deer cannot pull carriages;
they merely resemble oxen and serve as toys for the young. They are expediently compared to those with small faculties (hīnamūla), who are fit for the Hīnayāna.
At that time, the sons, hearing of the rare and precious playthings described by their father, had their desires satisfied;
their hearts were each filled with vigor and resolve, and pushing one another aside, they vied with one another to run forth, contending to escape from the burning house.
Nan Yue said: "These words regarding the sons leaving the house are a metaphor for following their desires; thus, there is nothing that transformation does not accord with. Jiehuan said:
"Advancing is like pushing forward, and retreating is like pushing back; this is the momentum of vying to exit.
It is a metaphor for following the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties to discern among the three vehicles in order to seek liberation."
At that time, the elder saw that his sons had all emerged safely; they were sitting in an open space at a crossroads, free from all obstructions.
Their minds were tranquil, and they leaped for joy with great exultation.

(Nan said: "I first rejoice that my children have escaped suffering. [The passage on] 'sitting together in the open air by the road' etc., is like relying on the Four Noble Truths to construct a partial emptiness, yet not knowing how to progress further)."
Then the sons each addressed their father, saying, "Father, we pray that you grant us at once the playthings you previously promised:
the goat-carts, the deer-carts, and the ox-carts."

(Jie-huan said: "The sons leave the house and go to their father to request vehicles; this is like attaining the benefits of the three vehicles by means of causes, and subsequently grasping the fruits of the three vehicles.")
Śāriputra, at that time the elder bestowed upon each of his sons an identical great carriage.

These carriages were high and wide, adorned with various jewels, surrounded by railings, and hung with bells on all four sides. Furthermore, canopies were spread over them, likewise decorated with rare and miscellaneous gems.
Precious cords were interlaced across them, and hanging flower garlands were draped from them, layered and elegantly arranged.

A ceremonial mat was spread, upon which a vermilion pillow was placed. It was drawn by a white ox, whose hide was pure and clean, its form beautiful and well-proportioned, possessing great strength and walking with steady, level steps as swift as the wind; it was also attended by many servants who escorted it.

(And the Southern Text says: "After the parables of the three [vehicles] were taught, the One Vehicle was equally revealed to show that there is neither two nor three, thereby abolishing the provisional and establishing the real.

To summarize the parable: it refers to what follows, namely the various Buddhas' implements of recreation—such as meditative concentration and liberation—which consist of the singular mark and the single kind of pure, wondrous bliss.")

The *Jie-huan* (Precept Ring) states: "The chariot is a metaphor for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); the oxen are a metaphor for the Great Root. This represents the virtuous function of the One Vehicle’s Great Root.
That its matters are 'lofty and vast' means it rises high above the Three Vehicles and extensively encompasses the nine stages.

The various jewels are a metaphor for the ten thousand practices (*sāhasra-caryā*); the railings are a metaphor for *dhāraṇī*; the suspended bells are a metaphor for the transformative teaching through the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); and the canopy is a metaphor for compassion."
Compassion covers all universally. The various jewels are a metaphor for the manifold virtues, by which compassion is adorned.

The jeweled cords are a metaphor for the four vows, by which compassion is made firm. Hanging down flower garlands represents the outward distribution of wondrous causes, linked together like a necklace.
Spreading out layered, elegant mats represents the inward expansion of the power of patience, as supple as a mat. As for placing the crimson pillow:
To cause the mind to be appropriately engaged in *vitarka* and *vicāra* while remaining in silence is the Way.

As for "yoking it with white oxen," those who lack the pure and great faculties are incapable of this vehicle. That its hide and color are full and clean means it has received proper nourishment and remains unstained.
His physical form is beautiful and excellent; he fulfills his innate endowment without any defect. He possesses great strength and vigor, which is like being capable of undertaking great affairs.
His gait is level and upright, which is like faithfully treading upon the Great Way. His speed is like the wind, which is like attaining realization instantaneously in a single thought-moment.
Furthermore, he has many attendants, which are like the expedient means for benefiting sentient beings and assisting the Path.
Why is this? Because this great elder possesses immeasurable wealth; his various treasuries are all overflowing.
He then thinks: "My riches are infinite; it would not be right to give inferior, small carts to my sons."
(And Nan said: "This explains the reason for bestowing upon us all one great vehicle.
Jiehuan said: "For example, the Tathāgata possesses an immeasurable treasury of the Buddha-dharma, consisting of knowledge and vision, powers, and fearlessnesses."
I am able to provide sentient beings with the departure of the Mahāyāna.
These young children here are all my own sons; my love for them is without partiality. I possess such great chariots made of the seven treasures.
Their number is immeasurable; you should bestow [the gift] upon each with an impartial mind, without making any distinctions.
(Jie-huan said: It is like regarding all sentient beings as my own children; bestow the Mahāyāna equally upon them, so that no one is left to attain parinirvāṇa alone.)
Why is this? Because if I were to distribute these goods throughout the entire kingdom, they would still not be exhausted; how much less so for my sons.
(Jiehuan said: "This refers to the fact that all things flow toward it for support without ever being depleted.")
At that time, the sons each mounted a great vehicle; they experienced what they had never known before, for it was not what they had originally hoped for.
(Jie-huan said: This is like the two vehicles attaining Buddhahood, which exceeds their expectations.)
"Śāriputra, what do you think? Would this elder be guilty of falsehood in giving precious great chariots equally to all his sons?

(Jie-huan said: "The question suggests that while three were promised, only one was given; this is like beginning with a provisional means and ending with the ultimate reality. Thus, the beginning and the end would be contradictory, involving [the charge of deception]."')
"Is it not false?
Śāriputra replied, "No, World-Honored One. This elder merely enabled his sons to escape the calamity of fire and preserve their lives;
it is not false. Why is this? If they have preserved their lives, they have already obtained playthings."
This is the requisite for such a task; how much more so the subsequent skillful means to rescue them from that burning house.
[Jiehuan said: "The body is the foundation of the Way. When the foundation is complete, the Way is complete.

Therefore, the perfected person always casts aside material things to embrace the Way, thereby preserving the integrity of the body and nourishing life. Yet those within the burning house treat material things as mere playthings and do not value or cherish themselves."
This is merely to admonish him.
Jiehuan said: "Those who would risk their entire lives for the sake of playthings—surely the body itself is far more worthy of being cherished than material objects."
World-Honored One, even if that elder did not give so much as the smallest single chariot, he would still not have been guilty of falsehood. Why is this?
Because that elder had previously formed this intention: "By means of skillful expedients, I shall cause my sons to escape. For this reason, [he was not lying].
There is no falsehood here; how much less so in the case of the elder, who knows his own wealth is immeasurable and desires to benefit his sons by giving them all equally great chariots.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said."
(Śīlaka said: "This knot signifies the intention not to be deluded.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is likewise so; he is the father of all the world, having forever exhausted, without remainder, all fears, decays, afflictions, anxieties, and the obscurations of ignorance.
Jiehuan said: "To regard the four modes of birth as one's only child and to treat the three realms with equal benevolence.
Jiehuan said: "Fear, dread, affliction, and suffering are the painful characteristics of the three precepts; ignorance and obscuration are the root of suffering for the four modes of birth.
To exhaust these forever is the Buddha of Suchness."
They have fully accomplished immeasurable knowledge and vision, the powers, and the fearlessnesses.

Possessing great supernormal power and the power of wisdom, they are endowed with the perfection of skillful means and wisdom, as well as great loving-kindness and great compassion. They are ever free from weariness or indolence, constantly seeking what is wholesome to benefit all beings.

(Jiehuan said: "The powers and fearlessnesses of knowledge and vision are correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*). Expedient means, the perfection of wisdom, and skillful wisdom are provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Spiritual power and the power of wisdom serve to support correct wisdom; compassion without weariness serves to mobilize provisional wisdom.)
He enters this decayed and ancient fire-hovel of the triple world to deliver sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress,
and from the fires of ignorance, delusion, and the three poisons, teaching and transforming them so that they may attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He sees all sentient beings being scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress, and likewise...

For the sake of the five desires and material gain, they undergo various kinds of suffering. Furthermore, because of their greedy attachment and pursuit, they experience manifold sufferings in the present life:
the suffering of poverty and hardship, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of encountering the hateful and hostile.
While sentient beings are submerged within such various sufferings, they play with joy, neither perceiving nor knowing them; they feel no alarm, no fear, and do not give rise to [renunciation].

They feel weary [of the world] yet do not seek liberation. Within this burning house of the triple world, they run hither and thither; though they encounter great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity.
(Jie-huan says: "Born below" means that, out of compassion, he manifests birth within the household of the triple world to deliver the five [classes of beings].)

Regarding the multitude of those in the [six] destinies: because he has eternally exhausted his own ignorance and obscurations, he desires to deliver sentient beings from the obscurations of folly and ignorance;

because he has personally accomplished immeasurable knowledge and vision, he desires to cause sentient beings to attain Great Bodhi—namely, that he wishes for all beings to be no different from himself.
From the passage "seeing the various beings" below, the fires of the three realms are fully enumerated.
The "Hairs of Suffering" (Mao ku zhuang) describe the causes and effects of the three periods of time and the six realms of existence.

Jiehuan says: "The suffering of affliction constitutes the fruit-karma and belongs to prior causes; the suffering of pursuing the five desires, wealth, and profit constitutes the cause-karma and belongs to subsequent fruits.
The suffering of poverty and so forth arises from these preceding causes and fruits, thereby forming the karma of the six realms."
They transform into different species, sinking into decline without ceasing; this is truly cause for alarm and dread. Yet they rejoice in it without weariness, encountering it without anxiety;
they are truly obscured by the darkness of ignorance.
Śāriputra, having seen this, the Buddha thought: "I am the father of sentient beings;
I ought to uproot their suffering and distress, and grant them the immeasurable and boundless joy of the Buddha’s wisdom, so that they may sport therein. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata further thought:
"If I were to rely solely on my power of supernatural faculties and the power of wisdom, while abandoning skillful means, for the sake of all..."
Regarding sentient beings who praise the Tathāgata’s powers of knowledge and vision and his fearlessness: these sentient beings cannot be delivered by means of them. [Jiehuan said:

"The bliss of the boundless Buddha-wisdom is precisely the bliss of the One Vehicle Dharma; the Tathāgata’s powers of knowledge and vision and his fearlessness are precisely the essence of the One Vehicle Dharma.
Although they are sufficient to uproot suffering, they are not matters for ordinary worldlings; therefore, they cannot [be used to deliver them]."]
This is how they attain deliverance.
Why is this? Because these sentient beings have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction;
they are being burned by the burning house of the triple world. How, then, could they understand the wisdom of the Buddha?
(Śikṣānanda said: "The reason they were unable to attain deliverance by this means was that they were deluded by manifold sufferings.
Śāriputra, it is just as that elder, although his body and arms possessed great strength, did not employ it;
rather, through diligent skillful means, he strove to rescue his children from the peril of the burning house, and only thereafter bestowed upon each of them precious great chariots. Just so...
His arrival was likewise thus. Although he possessed power and fearlessness, he did not employ them;

rather, through wisdom and skillful means, he rescued sentient beings from the burning house of the triple world by preaching the three vehicles: the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddha-vehicle. He spoke these words:
"Do not take pleasure in dwelling within the burning house of the triple world; do not crave coarse and inferior forms."
These are sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. If one becomes greedily attached to them and gives rise to craving, one will be consumed by them.

(Jiehuan says: These words are a skillful exhortation to use the power of discourse to uproot their suffering. The five desires, such as form and so forth, are considered soft and beautiful by the world, yet they are regarded as coarse and debased by those who have transcended it.
They are all illusory delusions; being turbid and evil, they can trigger the karma of suffering and truly result in fire.)
It is the fuel for this fire. Therefore, when greed and attachment give rise to craving, one is consumed by it.
You must quickly escape the triple world; you shall then attain the three vehicles: the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha-vehicle. I now [speak] for your sake.
I guarantee that this matter shall never be in vain. You should simply cultivate diligence with vigor.
By these skillful means, the Tathāgata entices and encourages sentient beings, further saying: "You should know that these three vehicles of the Dharma are all praised by the sages;
they are sovereign, unbound, and free from dependence or seeking. By mounting these three vehicles, one employs the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*)."

By means of the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the meditative concentrations, the liberations, the samādhis, and so forth, they enjoy themselves and thereby attain immeasurable peace and happiness.
(These are the vehicles of the Threefold Dharma praised by the noble ones and honored by all Buddhas; because they enable one to leave behind birth and death, they are [praised].)
It is unconditioned; because it differs from conditioned phenomena, it has no basis for seeking.

Those who attain this vehicle obtain the untainted five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the four dhyānas, the nine successive attainments, the eight liberations, and all dharmas of samādhi, by which they are sufficiently entertained and liberated from the suffering of the three realms.
The Precept Ring said: "He shows them the three vehicles and praises their respective dharmas so that they may aspire toward them.

Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings who possess the nature of wisdom within and, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, receive it with faith, and practice with diligent vigor, desiring to quickly escape the triple world and seek nirvāṇa for themselves—this is called the Śrāvaka Vehicle. As it was for those...
The son seeks the goat-drawn carriage and emerges from the burning house.

(This refers to the initial Śrāvaka vehicle. [Jiehuan says: This distinguishes how the capacities and natures of the three vehicles are unequal, and how their attainment of the fruit differs, just as those sons have different toys.]
The *Jie-huan* says: "That which possesses the nature of wisdom within refers to the causal factor of the seed of faith; this excludes the icchantikas.

Because this causal factor exists within, one takes the Buddha as a condition to contemplate the principle of the Four Noble Truths. Hearing the voice [of the Dharma] and following the path is called the Śrāvaka-yāna.
Because their aspiration for speed is slight, it is likened to a sheep-drawn carriage."
If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, accept it with faith, apply themselves with earnest diligence,
seek spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), delight in solitary tranquility, and deeply understand the causes and conditions of all phenomena— this is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
It is like those sons who, seeking the deer-cart, emerged from the burning house.
[And the Southern text says: "This refers to the Pratyekabuddhayāna. This vehicle severs the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms, which is the same as the Śrāvaka [vehicle];

however, it further penetrates and severs the residual habits (*vāsanā*). Because its faculties and nature are sharp and keen, it ranks above the Śrāvaka; because its capacity is somewhat greater, it is likened to a deer cart.
The *Jièhuán* says: "Pratyekabuddha" is translated here as "Solitary Realizer" (*dújué*). It also encompasses the term "Conditioned Realizer" (*yuánjué*).

Because they appear in an age without a Buddha, observe the transformation of phenomena, and personally awaken to non-arising, they are called Solitary Realizers. Because they contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination and awaken to the principle of ultimate truth, they are called Conditioned Realizers.
Those who seek spontaneous wisdom and delight in solitary tranquility are Solitary Realizers; they possess profound knowledge of all dharmas.
"Pratyaya" refers to the Pratyekabuddha.
If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, receive it with faith, and diligently practice with vigor to seek all-encompassing wisdom;
The Buddha’s wisdom, self-existent wisdom, teacherless wisdom, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the powers, and the fearlessnesses;
out of compassion for immeasurable sentient beings, bringing them peace and happiness, benefiting devas and humans, and delivering all—this is called the Mahāyāna.
Because Bodhisattvas seek this vehicle, they are called Mahāsattvas. It is like those sons who, seeking ox-carts, emerged from the burning house.
(The Southern tradition says: "This refers to the Bodhisattva Vehicle. This encompasses all three vehicles and constitutes the great root for the accumulation of manifold wisdoms.
Its capacity is supreme; therefore, it is likened to an ox-drawn carriage.)
Jie-huan said: "All-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is the wisdom of the bodhisattva; Buddha-wisdom is the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
'Spontaneous' means being free from all forms of realization and grasping. 'Teacherless' means awakening not through another.

One is able to seek all forms of knowledge, as well as the vast and great virtuous functions of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, thereby compassionately benefiting and delivering others; for this reason, it is called 'Great'."
Bodhisattva Śāriputra,
it is like that elder who, seeing his children safely emerge from the burning house and reach a place of fearlessness,
reflects upon his own immeasurable wealth and bestows great chariots equally upon all his sons.

(This section cites the passage where the son sees [the chariots] and goes out to sit in the open air; it includes his own thought that the wealth is inexhaustible, as well as the passage concerning not giving him small carts, etc., which follows next.)
The Tathāgata is also like this. He is the father of all sentient beings.

When he sees immeasurable billions of sentient beings who, through the gateways of the Buddha's teaching, emerge from the perilous path of the three realms of suffering and fear to attain the bliss of nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata then reflects:
"I possess immeasurable, boundless powers of wisdom, the fearlessnesses, and all other qualities of a Buddha."

"O Treasure, all these sentient beings are my children; I bestow the Mahāyāna equally upon them, so that no one shall attain extinction alone, but rather I lead them all to extinction by means of the Tathāgata’s own extinction."

Furthermore, [the Master] said: "Combined, these clarify that one may transcend the suffering of the triple world and attain the bliss of nirvana; this refers to the provisional vehicle’s minor fruits.
When the Tathāgata brings about their extinction through his own extinction, this refers to the ultimate fruit of the Mahayana."

These sentient beings who have escaped the three realms are all provided with the various implements for enjoyment, such as the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*) of the Buddhas;
these are all of one characteristic and one kind, praised by the Sages, and capable of producing the supreme, pure, and wondrous bliss.
Śāriputra, it is just as that elder first used the three vehicles to entice his children, and afterwards gave them only the great chariots.
Adorned with precious treasures, it is the foremost in security. Yet that elder is free from the fault of falsehood. The Tathāgata is likewise; he is without falsehood.
Initially, he teaches the three vehicles to guide sentient beings, and subsequently, he delivers them by means of the Great Vehicle alone.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses.
This is the treasury of the Dharma, which can bestow the Mahāyāna Dharma upon all sentient beings, yet they are unable to receive it in its entirety.
Śāriputra, for this reason, you should know that through the power of the skillful means of the Buddhas, the One Buddha Vehicle is distinguished and taught as three.
[The Jie-huan says: "The passage 'These various sentient beings' and below [explains] the intent of the *Shu-shang* regarding the Mahāyāna.

This means that although those who have escaped the three realms attain the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*) of the Hīnayāna, they still harbor a distaste for existence and an attachment to emptiness;

thus, it is not the single characteristic. They are split into two vehicles and are not of one kind. Because their attachments have not been eliminated, they are not pure. Emptiness and existence have not yet been harmonized."

It is not excellent. Therefore, [the Buddha] provides them with the various means of enjoyment found in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*) of all Buddhas—the singular characteristic and single kind of pure, wondrous bliss—just as that great carriage is fully equipped with every excellence. "Śāriputra, below" concludes the preceding text.
"They cannot receive it all" is because their spiritual capacities (*indriya*) are not uniform.
Chapter Four: The Chapter on Faith and Understanding (*Adhimukti-parivarta*).
Regarding "faith and understanding": this has been explained in detail in the preceding sections. It refers to entering by means of faith and awakening to the essential principles of the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana...
Then, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma— the World-Honored One’s bestowing of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon Śāriputra—
he gave rise to a mind of rare wonder and leaped for joy with exultation.

Furthermore, it is said: Subhūti was foremost among those who understood emptiness; yet as a śrāvaka, he merely contemplated partial emptiness and his mind took no delight in the Dharma of the bodhisattvas.
Now, having abandoned the dharma of emptiness and realized the true path, he is cited here as an example of one who understands emptiness.
Jie-huan said: "Subhūti’s years and virtue were superior to those of the assembly; therefore he was called 'Elder' (sthavira).
He was also called 'Endowed with Longevity' (āyuṣmat) or 'Life of Wisdom' (prajñājīvita). As a sutra says: 'This person is one who can obtain the life of wisdom within the Buddha-dharma.
This is precisely what is meant. Although Mahākāśyapa should have been listed first, Subhūti is placed first because he was the primary recipient of the teaching."

In the past, when the World-Honored One had been preaching the Dharma for a long time, I was seated among the assembly; my body grew weary and exhausted, and I thought only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Regarding the Bodhisattva teachings—playing with supernatural powers, purifying Buddha-lands, and bringing sentient beings to maturity—I felt no joy in my heart.
The wise are said to contemplate all phenomena based on the Four Noble Truths. The absence of self and what belongs to self is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Because of this emptiness, the characteristics of all phenomena—such as unity or difference—are in reality unattainable; this is called signlessness (*animitta*).

Knowing that all phenomena are signless and unattainable, one has no further aspirations or cravings within the triple world and no longer performs the karma that leads to birth and death within the three realms of existence; this is called [wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)].
"Non-action" (also called "wishlessness").

The *Jie-huan* says: "Since the teaching has been given for a long time"—referring to the forty-year period when he preached the Small Vehicle teachings—because of weariness and indolence, they merely contemplate the emptiness of the Small Vehicle and no longer seek further progress.
Emptiness, signlessness, and non-action constitute the Small [Vehicle].

They ride upon the three gates of liberation; this is the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, which is the Mahāyāna. Their sporting with supernormal powers and so forth constitutes the practice of the Mahāyāna.
Because they delight only in the Lesser Vehicle, sinking into emptiness and pursuing quiescence, they [remain distant] from the Great Dharma and the Great Practice.
Our hearts find no joy. Why is this?
The World-Honored One has caused us to emerge from the triple world and attain the realization of nirvana;
yet he has also caused us to reach old age while the Buddha is still teaching bodhisattvas the path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Not a single thought of delight arose [in us].
(Jie-huan said: This explains the error of the above [passage], which was due to being stalled in the Lesser Vehicle.
Now, before the Buddha, we have heard the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the śrāvakas.
His heart was filled with great joy. Having attained what he had never heard before, he thought: "I did not expect that today I would suddenly hear this rare Dharma.
I am deeply fortunate to have obtained such great and wholesome benefit, like immeasurable treasures, which I could not have sought for myself."
(And Nan said: "This indeed celebrates what has now been attained.
World-Honored One, we would now like to employ a parable to clarify this meaning.
Suppose there were a man who, while still young, abandoned his father and fled, dwelling in another land for a long time—perhaps ten, twenty, or even fifty years.
(Xing Jianzi said: "The *Nanhua* [Zhuangzi] also speaks of 'losing one's way in youth'; this is precisely what is being described here. Jiehuan said:
"Being young and immature is a metaphor for being exclusively deluded and ignorant. 'Leaving one's father' is a metaphor for abandoning fundamental enlightenment (*mūlabodhi*).

'Another country' is a metaphor for being mired and stagnant within the five destinies (*pañcagati*). Therefore, it says: 'up to fifty years,' or ten or twenty; these are metaphors for the successive stages."
Thus it was.

As he grew older, his poverty and distress increased further; he traveled in all directions in search of food and clothing, and after wandering for some time, he happened to encounter his own native land.
[And Nan said: "When one encounters a direction and heads straight toward it, yet is unable to reach the destination. Jiehuan said:
"To be old and impoverished, seeking food in all four directions, is like being trapped in the five realms of existence and passing through the four modes of birth while sustaining one's life.
To gradually head back toward one’s native land is like encountering the Buddha’s teachings, whereby one is finally able to reflect upon oneself."
His father had previously come seeking his son but was unable to find him, so he stayed in a certain city. His family was immensely wealthy, possessing immeasurable riches and treasures:
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, crystal, pearls, and the like; all their granaries and treasuries were overflowing.
He has many servants, ministers, officials, and subjects; countless elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, and sheep;
his income and interest extend throughout other countries; and his merchants and traders are also exceedingly numerous.

Furthermore, [the Master] said: "The granaries are filled with the food of *dharmaprīti*; the treasuries overflow with the wealth of all *dharmas*. The servants and attendants are those by whom one serves oneself;

the ministers and aides are those by whom one governs the people—this is analogous to the matters of benefiting oneself and benefiting others. Elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep serve as metaphors for the teachings of the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*).

The merchant (*śreṣṭhin*) represents the transfer of the existent to provide for the non-existent; the trader (*vaṇij*) represents concealing [goods] while awaiting their price. 'Shang-gu' is synonymous with 'shang'."
[He was] a human being).
Jiehuan said: "His father is like the Buddha, the Sovereign of Awakening. 'First seeking but not finding' is like having been taught and transformed in the past, yet later falling back into decline.
'Stopping at a city along the way' is like the Flower Ornament Dharma and the Bodhimanda. His family is immensely wealthy."
The various treasures and jewels are like the dharmas obtained at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), which are endowed with immeasurable merit.

The granaries, treasuries, servants, and so forth are like the flourishing and spreading [of these dharmas] throughout the great trichiliocosm; therefore, it is said that "the income and expenditure, as well as the profits and interests, extend even to other countries."
Because all living beings thereby seek the benefit of the Dharma, it is said that "the merchants are numerous. This collectively serves as a metaphor for the emergence of beneficial grace.
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and passed through kingdoms and cities until he eventually reached the city where his father resided.
(Nan-yueh further said: "The meaning of this section is that those who were formerly lost in delusion were gradually led by means of the teachings and thus entered the Right Path.

Jiehuan said: "The 'poor son' is a metaphor for one who is distressed within the five realms of existence. 'From the wealth of merit' refers to the collection [of merit]. 'The village is desolate and shallow' is a metaphor for the provisional teachings of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).

'The state city is magnificent and flourishing' is a metaphor for the gradual teachings of the Middle Vehicle (*Madhyamika*). 'The place where his father resides' is a metaphor for the Great [Vehicle]."
He followed the True Teaching.
The father constantly thought of his son; though they had been separated for over fifty years, he had never spoken of this matter to anyone.
He merely reflected within himself, harboring regret and remorse. Thinking to himself that he was aged and infirm, yet possessed of much wealth—gold, silver, and precious treasures—
His treasuries were overflowing with jewels, yet he had no offspring. Once he passed away, his wealth would be dissipated, as there was no one to whom it could be entrusted.
For this reason, he constantly remembered his son with deep longing and further thought: "If I were to obtain a son, I could entrust my wealth and property to him;
I would then be at ease and happy, free from further anxiety."

[The commentary on the Precept Ring states: "The father constantly thinks of his children" is a metaphor for the Buddha thinking of the children of the two vehicles who have long been submerged in the five realms of existence;
their natures and habits are dull and shallow, and they are not yet fit to be taught the Mahāyāna. "Reflecting with regret" means he regrets that his past teachings were not profound enough.
"I regret that my faculties have now declined. As for his reflection on his own old age and infirmity, it was because he feared there would be no one to continue the Buddha's life-span.
"World-Honored One, at that time the impoverished son, wandering about in search of employment, happened upon his father’s house and stood by the side of the gate."
(An added note states: To work for others is called *yōng* (hireling); to take advantage of one's labor is called *chèn* (rent). The city is likened to the initial entry;
the house is likened to deep penetration. This refers to relying on resources and expedient vehicles to advance gradually toward profound realization.)
The Precept Ring says: To work for hire is to seek only meager profit; the merit does not belong to oneself.

This is like relying on provisional teachings as one's primary resource—one will ultimately lack actual realization. Arriving at the house and standing by the side of the gate is like encountering the Buddha-way but being unable to enter it correctly;
one remains instead within partial emptiness because of a delight in the small.
From afar he saw his father seated upon a lion throne with a jeweled footstool supporting his feet.
He was surrounded by all the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and householders, who paid him respectful homage. His body was adorned with pearl necklaces worth ten million pieces of gold.

Officials, citizens, and servants stood in attendance at his left and right, holding white fly-whisks. A precious canopy was spread above him, from which hung various flowered banners and fragrant waters.
He sprinkled the ground, scattered various kinds of famous flowers, and arranged precious objects; he brought things out and put them away, performing such diverse acts of adornment.
His majestic power was exceptionally sublime. When the impoverished son saw that his father possessed such great authority and influence, he immediately felt terror and regretted having come here.
He thought to himself in secret: "This is either a king or someone like a king; it is not a place where I can earn wealth through hired labor."
"It would be better to go to a poor neighborhood where there is ample scope for exertion and food and clothing are easily obtained.
If I remain here for long, I may be coerced and forced to work against my will. Having thought this, he ran away quickly.

(Xiang Mai said: "This is an analogy for the two vehicles who, upon first hearing of the Buddha-fruit—the myriad virtues and the wisdom of all seeds—become confused and terrified by the Lesser Vehicle.
(Ji Nan said: "'Jin' [inner] is pronounced 'na'; it means either emitting or receiving. (Ji Nan said:

"From 'His majestic virtue is uniquely honored' upward, all refers to the matter of the myriad virtues and the wisdom of all seeds; from 'The impoverished son sees his father' downward, it refers to being confused by the Lesser Vehicle.")

(Fearing great matters). (Master Xingjian said: "If one cultivates the Mahāyāna, one must enter into birth and death; because one extensively studies the myriad practices, it is said that one is 'pressed' [by them].
Supplemental Note: "The *bǐ* (fly-whisk) can remove dust; 'white' signifies being unstained.
The left and right represent the removal of the dust of emptiness and the provisional, thereby returning to the Middle Way.)"
Jie-huan said: "To see one's father from afar is like being unable yet to realize him through direct personal witness. His sitting upon a lion throne symbolizes the virtue of fearlessness.
The jeweled footstool supporting his feet signifies that he honors the foundation of the myriad practices. These myriad practices are rooted in the ultimate truth."
Because he is able to engage with the mundane world, he is surrounded by kṣatriyas and householders; the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot so engage with the mundane world.
Because he accomplishes the myriad virtues through the myriad practices, his body is adorned with pearl necklaces;
the followers of the Two Vehicles lack such adornments. Officials govern, and the people are subject to their service; the *tóng* performs light tasks, while the *pú* performs [heavy] tasks.
This is profound. For example, within the Dharma of the One Vehicle, there is nothing—whether the methods for what is to be remedied or what is to be employed—that is not fully prepared.
That which is called "worldly speech" and "the occupations for sustaining life," and so forth, all accord with the True Dharma;

it is simply that non-attachment and impartiality are held as supreme. Therefore, he holds a white fly-whisk while attending at the left and right. The jeweled canopy is a metaphor for compassion being widely extended; therefore...

Regarding the term "covering" (*āvṛti*): the flowers and banners symbolize the manifold virtues that transform those below; thus, they are said to "hang down. Water symbolizes wisdom (*jñāna*), and flowers symbolize causes (*hetu*).
As for sprinkling fragrant water upon the ground: it represents purifying the mental ground (*citta-bhūmi*) of sentient beings through sublime wisdom.

As for scattering various named flowers: it represents adorning the mental ground of sentient beings with sublime causes. The arrangement of precious objects is intended to display their exquisite delights. Thus it is said.

"Taking and giving within" refers to acting according to their desires and inclinations; it is like leading those who have achieved great roots toward the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). "King" refers to a sovereign;
"kings and their like" refers to the king’s kin, which is analogous to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

"Living in poverty among the lanes and alleys" is analogous to the narrow path of the Two Vehicles. "Exerting one's strength with a place to do so" is analogous to having a method for progress and cultivation; it does not mean obtaining material objects.
The dwelling place is like the Great Dharma, which is difficult to mount; food and clothing are easy to obtain, like the small fruits, which are easy to seek.
Or one may see oppression, like contemplating that the Buddha-way is long and distant, requiring one to undergo diligent suffering for a long time.
At that time, the wealthy elder, sitting upon his lion throne, recognized his son as soon as he saw him. His heart was filled with great joy, and he thought to himself:
"Now there is someone to whom my wealth and storehouses may be entrusted. I have constantly longed for this son, yet had no means of seeing him;
that he has come here of his own accord fulfills my deepest wish. Although I am advanced in years, I still cherish these things. He then immediately dispatched his attendants to act with haste.

He pursued and brought him back. (Seeing his son, he recognized him immediately; this is like past conditions having already matured. He entrusted him with wealth and goods; this is like the transmission of the Dharma. Though he was old in years, he still clung to it with greed and attachment;
this is like that which has been cultivated over kalpas of vast duration not being given away recklessly. He dispatched men to pursue him urgently; this is like causing the Bodhisattvas [to act].)

[He] preached the sudden Dharma). At that time, the messenger ran swiftly to seize him. The impoverished son was startled and alarmed; crying out in grievance, he shouted, "I have committed no offense against you!
Why do you seize me? The messenger held him even more tightly and forcibly dragged him back. At that moment, the impoverished son thought to himself:
Though innocent, he was imprisoned; realizing that his death was certain, he became even more terrified. He cried out for help and fell prostrate upon the ground.
(Supplementary note: The father’s command to pursue his son was truly intended to embrace him, yet the son, seized by panic and exhaustion, abandoned himself in despair.)
It is like the followers of the Two Vehicles who, upon first hearing the *Avataṃsaka*, were intimidated by its sudden teaching.

This is because the Sudden Teaching holds that afflictions are identical to bodhi, whereas the Two Vehicles regard afflictions as enemies and thieves; thus, they speak of them as "enemies. The Sudden Teaching likewise holds that birth-and-death is identical to nirvāṇa.
Yet the followers of the Two Vehicles regard birth and death as the bondage of suffering; thus they sigh deeply.
Jie-huan said: "To be seized despite not having transgressed is like being forcibly restrained when one does not seek it, or being violently dragged away by sudden grasping."

It is like being forcibly dragged along against one's will. Although the Bodhisattva manifests birth within the three realms, according to the One Vehicle, these three realms are regarded as a prison;

thus it is said that he is imprisoned without having committed a crime. Although the Bodhisattva enters and exits the toils of worldly existence, according to the One Vehicle, there is fear of losing the fruit of meditative concentration;
thus it is said that he is certain to die here. For this reason, he appears as if deaf and mute, remaining in a state of profound bewilderment and failing to understand.
Therefore it is said that he became even more terrified, fainted, and fell to the ground.
His father saw him from afar and said to his attendants, "There is no need for this man; do not force him to come here.
Sprinkle cold water on his face to bring him back to consciousness, and do not speak to him further."
(Jie-huan said: "Seeing him in a state of alarm, urgency, and fainting, one should allow him to rest and recover. This is analogous to setting aside the sudden [teaching] to open up the provisional.
Just as cold water can revive one who has fainted, so too can the provisional teaching cure afflictions.")
Why is this? Because the father knew that his son’s disposition was inferior, and he himself was aware that his own noble and wealthy status would be difficult for the son to accept.
Although he recognized him as his son with certainty, he employed skillful means and did not tell others, "This is my son. Thus spoke the messenger.

"I now release you; go wherever you please. The impoverished son, filled with joy at having obtained what he had never experienced before, rose from the ground and went to the poor official to seek food and clothing.
(Xiangmai said: "This analogy indicates that his resolve was inferior and he could not endure the Mahāyāna; therefore, [the Buddha] provisionally ceased [teaching it to him].
It does not say 'my son' because the reality had not yet been revealed.")
The Precept Ring says: "The messenger releases him" is like abandoning the stage of stagnation (*dun*). "Proceeding wherever he wishes" is like opening up the provisional means (*upāya*).
"Rising from the ground" is precisely awakening from delusion.
"Going to the poor quarters to seek food and clothing" is relying on the impoverished dharmas favored by the Two Vehicles as provisions for entering the Path.
At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his son, devised a skillful means. He secretly dispatched two men who were haggard in appearance and lacked majesty, saying:
"You should go to that place and speak slowly to the impoverished son, saying: 'There is work here; we will pay you double wages.
If the impoverished son agrees, bring him here and set him to work. If he asks, 'What kind of work is there? you may simply say to him:"
"We hire you to remove the filth; the two of us will also work together with you. At that time, the two messengers immediately sought out the impoverished son.
Having found him, they fully explained the aforementioned matter.
(Xiang Mai says: "This first section describes the establishment of provisional means. (Ji Nan says: "Sweeping away filth is a metaphor for severing afflictions (*kleśa*).

The filth of afflictions, delusions, and karma defiles the ground of the mind. The followers of the Two Vehicles employ various contemplations to remove it. For a Bodhisattva, however, the very characteristics of both affliction and nirvāṇa act as mutual obstructions;
yet he says, 'I shall also work together with you,' because he employs the means of gathering through common purpose (*samānārthatā*"). (Xingjian)
The Master said: "Simply cease all that people ought to seek; this is called 'removing filth.
Seeking the Buddha and seeking bodhi right now is called 'carrying filth in'; it is not called 'carrying filth out.'"
The Precept Ring said: "The secret dispatching of two persons was to cause them to keep secret the practice of the Bodhisattva while manifesting the Dharma of the Two Vehicles.
His appearance being haggard and emaciated is what is meant by 'concealing his power of mastery.

Giving you double the wage is an analogy for showing a proximate fruit because one delights in the small. Your being made to remove dung is what is meant by 'using the Dharma that the poor delight in.'"
He delivered him. He related the aforementioned matters in detail, comparing them to following the Buddha and propagating his transformation.
At that time, the impoverished son first took the wages and immediately began clearing away the filth. When the father saw his son, he felt pity for him and marveled at this.
On another day, looking from within a window, he saw from afar that his son’s body was emaciated and haggard, defiled and impure with filth, dust, and dirt.
He immediately cast off his necklaces, fine soft garments, and ornaments of adornment;
instead, he put on coarse, tattered, and soiled clothes, covered his body in dust, and took a dung-removal tool in his right hand, appearing as if filled with dread.
He said to the laborers, "Work diligently; do not be indolent. By means of this expedient, you shall be able to approach his son. (The supplementary note states:

Being emaciated and covered in dust is a metaphor for the Two Vehicles suppressing and severing afflictions yet failing to grasp the essential point, thereby remaining disturbed by those very afflictions.
Moving leftward against the current while moving rightward with the flow, and holding a vessel in the right hand, is a metaphor for following the path of skillful means to entice [the son].)
The Precept Ring said:
"First take its price; this is like desiring the small fruit while yearning for it, and only then cultivating the cause.

Therefore, within the Dharma of the Four Truths, the fruit comes first and the cause follows. His father felt pity and wonder at his preference for the small and his abandonment of the great. Furthermore—
On another day, while [the child] was at the window and so forth, he employed many skillful means;
following the child's lead, he secretly applied subtle transformation to cause him to aspire toward the Great [Vehicle].
Later, he spoke to him again, saying: "Ho there, man! You shall always work here; do not go elsewhere. I shall increase your wages.
Whatever you require—such as vessels, rice, flour, salt, or vinegar—do not hesitate or feel any doubt.
I also have old and worn-out servants who will provide whatever you need. Set your mind at ease; I am like a father to you, so do not worry."
(Nan-yueh further said: "This is a skillful means to reprimand and examine him, yet to treat him with intimacy, so that he may remain at ease and free from fear.
Jiehuan said: "I shall increase your price. This is like progressing from the stage of Stream-enterer through to the four fruits of Arhatship.

The basin and vessel are metaphors for the dharmas that assist the Path; the rice and flour are metaphors for the dharmas of the provisions; and the salt and vinegar are for harmonizing the flavor, so as to [render] all..."
The Dharma is balanced, harmonious, and moderate. An aged and decrepit servant is like the exhausted teachings of the Two Vehicles, such as the so-called "worn-out straw dogs. Why is this?
I am old and advanced in years, while you are young and vigorous; when you work, you never show deceit or indolence.
"Your anger, resentment, and complaints—I have not seen these evils in you at all, as one might find in other laborers.
From this day forward, I shall treat you like my own son. Thereupon, the elder gave him a new name, calling him "Son."
(Xiangmai said: "To deprecate one's own senility while praising the mental and physical efforts of one's son is like disparaging the large to extol the small;
it is a provisional way of advancing his merit. 'Er' is a term of endearment.")
Jie-huan said: "To say 'from now on, you shall be like my children' is to treat them with increasing intimacy and to advance them.

To further bestow names upon them is like transforming those in the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) so they may advance toward subsequent fruits. All that precedes is established as a provisional expedient."
At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, he still considered himself a lowly hired laborer;
for this reason, for twenty years he was constantly made to remove dung.
(Nan Yue added: "This is precisely a metaphor for being stalled in provisional means.
Jiehuan said: "It means that although one rejoices in the Buddha’s transformation, one's aspirations remain base and inferior;
for now, one is made to eliminate the filth of the ten latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) within the teachings of the Two Vehicles."

After this period had passed, their hearts accorded with one another and they trusted each other; there was no difficulty in their coming and going. Nevertheless, the place where he resided remained his original location.

(This is like the impoverished son who, after twenty years have passed, gradually becomes more intimate with his father, yet still dwells by the side of the gate—this is an analogy for those who, after severing the fetters according to the teachings of the Two Vehicles, hear the Vaipulya teachings.)
Jie Huan said: "To exalt the great without slandering it, and to rectify the small without harboring doubt—this is called 'mutually trusting the essence of the mind.
To advance so as to be able to speak of the great, yet to retreat without being hindered by the small—this is called 'having no difficulty in entering or exiting.
That one still remains in their original place is, for example, like being unable to enter all at once."
“World-Honored One, at that time the elder was ill. Knowing that he would soon die, he said to the impoverished son:
‘I now possess much gold, silver, and rare treasures; my storehouses are overflowing. You should know the quantity of what is to be given and taken from among them.
Such is my heart’s intent; you should embody this meaning.’”
(And the Southern text says: "This is an analogy for the transmission of the teaching to bodhisattvas. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* tells Subhūti:
"You should preach the Prajñā to the bodhisattvas. The subsequent passage states: "We, moreover, by means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, expound it for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
This refers precisely to the matter of the transmission of the teaching.)
Jie-huan said: "For example, the teaching of Prajñā is like gradually leading one into the ultimate reality.

When the Elder was ill, it was like the period following the Vaipulya sutras; because people still possessed the disease of attachment to names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), the Buddha was likewise 'ill.
On the verge of passing away, he spoke of the Treasure Store, which is like the conclusion of his transformative mission; thus he taught Prajñā as the precursor to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*."
This treasury of the local dialect has not yet been entrusted [to you]. Within the Prajñā teachings, the six perfections and myriad practices are fully present;
thus, it is likened to a granary overflowing with wealth. However, as they do not yet constitute the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the treasures therein vary in quantity.
One may take them for one's own benefit, or bestow them for the benefit of others. Such was the intention of the Sage. It is fitting [that you understand this].
You should realize the Dharma as it truly is.
Why is this? Now, I and you are no different from one another; you should apply yourself with diligence so that there is no loss.
(And Nan said: "To harmonize the feelings between father and son, ensuring there is no doubt, and joyfully receiving the precious treasury.")
The Precept Ring says: "I and you are not different," and so forth. This is an analogy for the principle of Prajñā, wherein all things are thus, without duality or distinction.
This is the gateway to the Perfect and Sudden teaching; therefore, one should apply oneself with diligent care.

At that time, the impoverished son immediately accepted the instructions and took charge of the various goods—the gold, silver, precious jewels, and all the storehouses—yet he had no desire to take even a single meal for himself.
However, his dwelling remained as it was in its original place, for his mind was still base and inferior.
Nor has he yet been able to relinquish it.
(Nan said: "Having received the treasury of jewels, yet he hardly hopes to take anything from it;
this is like receiving an imperial decree to propagate the Mahāyāna teachings while having no personal aspiration for them oneself.")
The Precept Ring says: "Even the inferior mind has not yet been relinquished; it is like merely contemplating emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
This generally summarizes the former errors."
After a short time had passed, the father perceived that his son’s mind had gradually become open and serene, that he had achieved great resolve, and that he now despised his former thoughts.
As death approached, he summoned his son and assembled his kinsmen, the king, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders.
When they had all assembled, he made this proclamation: "Gentlemen, you should know that this is my son, born of me.
Having abandoned me and fled from such-and-such a city, he has wandered about in hardship for more than fifty years. His original name was so-and-so."
"My name is [Name]. Formerly, while in my native city, I was filled with anxiety and searched for him everywhere. Suddenly, in this very place, I have encountered and found him.
He is truly my son, and I am truly his father. Now, all the wealth and property I possess shall belong entirely to my son."
"What was previously brought forth and internalized is what this son knows.
(Xiang Mai said: "From my own pursuit of the awakening of the primordial beginning, it is the functioning of the true father-son nature. This true treasure-trove is innate and inherent;
who alone would not possess it? Alas, how can one lose oneself through running counter to it, and delude oneself in that which should not be so?")

Therefore, the Buddha, out of compassionate concern, urgently caused them to withdraw and return. Had they been able to contemplate the nature of the mind and its essence, they could have encountered and attained it without any difficulty.
Yet they were struck with alarm and lost their composure; they voiced grievances and harbored doubts.

Although the Buddha established true compassion and employed manifold skillful means to guide them well, in the end they will wander aimlessly and suffer in the four modes of birth and five realms of existence for a long time. This is truly lamentable.
(Sighing). He said to Jiehuan:
"Since your resolve is so great, your father has gathered the clan and, for the first time, established the father-son relationship by fully entrusting you with the family estate.
After another short time had passed—this is like the period following Prajñāpāramitā, when the great capacity [for awakening] has already matured and can be transformed in a single stroke.
This is the ultimate Way. It is like casting aside one's former, inferior mind to pursue the Great; it is like abandoning a small city for a great one.

When he was about to pass away, he summoned his son and assembled his kinsmen, as described in the *Parable of the Phantom City*. Thus, when the Tathāgata knew that the time for his *nirvāṇa* had arrived, he gathered together the bodhisattvas and the śrāvakas.
When this sutra is preached, the śrāvakas are the sons and the bodhisattvas are the kinsmen.

Gathering the kin together, he declares, "This is my son," speaking thus among the assembly of devas and humans. This is an analogy for how I previously transformed him and brought him into my Dharma.
Having abandoned me in such-and-such a city, from that time until now, you have completely forgotten him.
This is an analogy. At that time, their spiritual capacities were not yet fixed; later, they fell back into decline and wandered through the five realms of existence.

Hence it is said: "For fifty-odd years, they have wandered aimlessly in hardship. Regarding the phrase "those whose original names were so-and-so," this refers to their original names to verify the certainty of the father-son relationship.
Their original names were such-and-such, which refers to the "transformed city" (the *nirmita-nagara*). This was what was manifested at that time.
This multitude refers to you, monks, who are my śrāvaka disciples. "I am named So-and-so" refers to me, Śākyamuni, the sixteenth [Tathāgata].
Seeking him in the original city, we have now encountered one another here;

this is like the ancient reliance on the fundamental nature to manifest transformation, reaching this gate of suddenness where there is a spontaneous and perfect accord. "These are truly my sons" concludes the preceding section.
Bestowing the entire family estate upon him as proof [of his status] is like the prediction of Buddhahood and the succession to the throne of the Dharma King.
"Whatever wealth I possess is all yours"—this great matter is inherently possessed by every person; it is not obtained from without.
"That which was previously accounted for as known by this son" refers to the ordinary methods of conduct and perception;
it is not that there is anything else distinct from this.
World-Honored One, at that time, when the impoverished son heard these words of his father, he was filled with great joy, having attained what he had never experienced before, and he said:
He thought: "Originally, I had no intention of seeking anything; yet now this treasure-trove has arrived spontaneously.
(Jiehuan says: This is a metaphor for what has been attained now.)
“World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder is the Tathāgata; we are all like sons of the Buddha. The Tathāgata has always said that we are his sons.
(Jie-huan said: Subhūti is a true son of the Buddha; he says they are "like" [sons] for the sake of conforming to the analogy.)
“World-Honored One, because of the three kinds of suffering, we have experienced various torments within saṃsāra; deluded and ignorant, we took pleasure in and were attached to inferior dharmas.
Today, World-Honored One, you have caused us to reflect and cleanse away the filth of conceptual proliferation regarding all dharmas.
We shall apply ourselves with diligent vigor therein to attain nirvāṇa. Having now obtained this price for a single day’s labor, we are fulfilled.”
Having done so, their hearts were filled with great joy and they considered themselves sufficient. They then said to themselves:

"Because of our diligent application within the Buddha-dharma, what we have obtained is vast and abundant. Yet, the World-Honored One previously knew that our minds were attached to base desires and that we delighted in inferior teachings.
He then immediately let them go, not making distinctions such as, "You shall have a share in the treasure-trove of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.

(And in the *Nan* [Southern] edition it says: Regarding the three types of suffering: first, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), which refers to the various manifest aspects of present suffering—such as the discordance and oppression of the sense faculties and their objects, and birth, aging, sickness, and death.

Second, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), which arises from the transformation of pleasure and produces various anxieties and afflictions; that is to say, while pleasure has not yet...)

Suffering culminates in sorrow, which follows upon it—namely, the suffering of separation from the beloved and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. The suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) consists in the characteristic of momentary flux and transformation.
The suffering of the aggregates within the five realms of existence is entirely subsumed under the suffering of conditioned formations (1).

Jie-huan said: "The 'narrative of stagnation' refers to provisional means. To say 'today' is in contrast to 'many lifetimes,' meaning that although many lifetimes have been spent delighting in the Lesser Vehicle, one still remains mired in stagnation.
Regarding all phenomena, one falsely gives rise to delusive defilements and inverted discrimination."

The various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) that defile the ground of the mind are called "the filth of proliferation. The "price of a single day" is a metaphor for the meager profit gained from small fruits; it is not much.
By the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), the World-Honored One has taught the wisdom of the Tathāgata; we have obtained the Nirvāṇa of a single day from the Buddha.
They consider this price a great gain, yet they have no aspiration to seek after this Mahāyāna.
(Jiehuan says: "To speak of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is precisely the teaching of Prajñā.")
