Furthermore, because of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, we have been instructed and expounded upon for the sake of the bodhisattvas; yet, regarding this [Mahāyāna], we ourselves have had no aspiration for it.
Why is this? The Buddha knew that our minds delighted in the Lesser Dharma, and thus he taught us according to our capacities through skillful means.
We did not know that we were truly the sons of the Buddha.
(Śikṣānanda said: "This was to transform and instruct the bodhisattvas through Prajñāpāramitā, while [the Buddha] himself did not hope for water.
Now we have finally come to know that the World-Honored One has no stinginess regarding the Buddha’s wisdom. Why is this?
Although we have from of old truly been sons of the Buddha, we took pleasure only in the Lesser Dharma. Had we possessed a mind that delighted in the Great [Dharma],...
The Buddha then preached the Mahāyāna Dharma for me.

Now that I have obtained the Lotus Sūtra, I finally understand that at the time of the Prajñāpāramitā, he already intended to entrust [the Dharma] to me in its entirety; it was only because I delighted in the Lesser Vehicle that I was deluded.
If I had delighted in the Great [Vehicle], I would have entrusted [the teaching] to them in its entirety long ago.
In this sutra, only the One Vehicle is taught; yet previously, in the presence of bodhisattvas, the Buddha disparaged those śrāvakas who delight in the Lesser Dharma.
Nevertheless, in reality, the Buddha has always taught and transformed beings through the Mahāyāna.
(Contemplating what is said now, one sees that in the past he criticized partiality; it is sufficient to know that the Buddha’s mind has always intended a great transformation.
Therefore, we say that originally there was no mind with which to harbor expectations. Now the great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously;

By means of the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, I perceive that remote past as if it were today.
(The verse says: "The Tathāgata, being unimpeded, knows the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas, as well as their śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as if seeing their parinirvāṇa occurring right now.
This verse praises the great supernatural power of Śākyamuni.)

Jie-huan said: "By means of the knowledge and vision of sentient beings, one is deluded and transmigrates through false conceptualizations; thus, for a Buddha of supreme wisdom, eons as vast as dust and ink are separated by time.
By means of the knowledge and vision of the Tathāgata, however, past and present are simultaneous; thus, observing that which is remote and long ago is as if it were this very day.
This, moreover, is the great penetration of Śākyamuni."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “The lifespan of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was five hundred and forty million *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas.
After that Buddha had originally sat at the site of enlightenment and defeated the armies of Māra, he was on the verge of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Yet the Buddhas remained before him for one such minor kalpa, and so on up to ten minor kalpas, sitting cross-legged.”
Sitting with body and mind unmoving, yet the teachings of all Buddhas still do not appear before him.

(Jiehuan said: "The Dharma-body and the life of wisdom have no beginning; even a hundred million billion kalpas of heaven are but a lifespan that responds to conditions—it is not something to be overly prized.
(Xiangmai said: "Because faculties are either sharp or dull, people have sudden [awakening]...")
"Gradually. (This refers to the fact that kalpas have varying durations. (The Prince praised him, saying:
"For the sake of delivering sentient beings, you attained Buddhahood only after immeasurable billions of years. Such is your response to the capacities of beings.")
Jie-huan said: "That which is called the Buddha-dharma is the true wisdom of the One Vehicle, the knowledge and vision of the Buddhas.
Those of superior faculties awaken suddenly and immediately attain the Way of the Buddha; those of inferior faculties have heavy obstructions and must rely on gradual cultivation.

Even after ten minor kalpas of the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, it still does not manifest before them; this is merely a manifestation for the sake of those with inferior faculties. For those of inferior faculties, the cause lies in the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*)."
The afflictions and delusive hindrances cause one to lose and extinguish supreme wisdom. This supreme wisdom is exceedingly vast and has existed for a long time;

its power must be attained through the gradual accumulation of practice and the successive elimination of these hindrances. Therefore, it is said that from one minor kalpa up to ten minor kalpas, one exhaustively eliminates the hindrances of affliction, and only then does wisdom manifest before one.
This is why the Great Penetration (Mahābhijñā) responds to conditions in such a manner.
At that time, the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven first prepared for that Buddha, beneath the Bodhi tree, a lion throne one yojana high;
there the Buddha sat, and was about to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
(Xingjian says: "A *yojana* is equivalent to one postal station (*yi*) in this region, which is forty *li*. Others say it is sixteen *li*.

[Nanji says: "This passage describes the Great Pervader (*Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū*) about to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and how the various devas made offerings and invited the Buddha.")

Jie-huan said: Some claim that while he was originally seated at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), the Buddha-dharma did not manifest; only by moving his seat to this location did he attain bodhi.

This is intended to show that one must eliminate traces and forget conditions before attaining accord with the Way. However, the text below states that he sat upon this very seat for a full ten minor kalpas;
it is therefore unlikely that he attained it merely by moving his seat.
Just as he sat upon this seat, the Brahma Kings rained down various celestial flowers over an area of one hundred *yojanas*.

Fragrant breezes blew at intervals, sweeping away the withered blossoms and raining down fresh ones in their place. In this manner, they offered worship to the Buddha without ceasing for ten minor *kalpas*, continuing even until his parinirvāṇa, constantly raining down these flowers.
Furthermore, the gods of the Four Great Kings, in order to make offerings to the Buddha, constantly struck celestial [drums].
The drums [resounded], and the other devas performed celestial music for ten minor kalpas until his parinirvāṇa; it was likewise so [for each of the others].
(Jiehuan says:
"Just as he sat" means at the very moment he first sat. Flowers rained down and music was played when he first sat, and it continued thus until his parinirvāṇa.)
It was likewise so. (The gods all looked toward his birth with reverence).
At this mountain retreat, after ten intermediate kalpas had passed, the Dharma of all Buddhas appeared before the Greatly Penetrating Wisdom-Conquering Buddha.
He attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
(The precept-ring states: "This symbolizes the exhaustion of the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*) and the perfect manifestation of supreme wisdom, thereby achieving the most correct enlightenment.")
Before that Buddha left the household life, he had sixteen sons. The eldest was named Zhijī (Jñānakūṭa).
[According to the Southern edition, he was the son of Xīnmíng; his first name was Yǒuyì, which also carries the meaning of "accumulation" (*kūṭa*).]
Jie-huan said: "The manifested traces of the Buddhas are fundamentally intended to symbolize the Dharma. Before Dīpaṃkara left home, he had eight sons;

before Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū left home, he had sixteen sons. These all symbolize the eight consciousnesses remaining within the bonds of saṃsāra. The former [teachings] were directed toward those of superior faculties."
Being correct and not deviant, there are only eight; this refers to those of inferior capacity. When the deviant and the correct are mixed together, there are sixteen.
That which is called "Accumulated Wisdom" (Jizhi) is so named because wisdom has something accumulated within it; thus, it constitutes consciousness still bound in the fetters.
If it functions without accumulation, this is the Great Penetration of Supreme Wisdom.
Each of the sons possessed various rare and wonderful objects of pleasure;

hearing that their father had attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they all abandoned what was precious to them and went to where the Buddha was. Their mothers followed and saw them off with tears and lamentations.
(Xiangmai said: "The son of Dīpaṃkara spoke only of governing the four continents, signifying that those of superior faculties have only the four great elements as their burden.
The son of Jñānavijaya spoke of each having various objects of pleasure, signifying that those of inferior faculties have various desires and deep-seated attachments [as their legacy].")
Jie-huan said: "The reason Prince Zhen went to the Buddha was that because he possessed accumulated wealth, he had not yet attained universal penetration.
Only by being able to renounce desire can one realize penetrating wisdom. As for the 'various mothers,' it is because the prince had many foster mothers;
they followed him weeping and wailing because love is difficult to abandon suddenly."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "When the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, five million billion buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions shook in six ways.
Even those regions within those lands that were dark and gloomy, where the majestic light of the sun and moon could not reach, became brilliantly illuminated. The sentient beings therein—"
Each was able to see the others, and they all spoke these words: "How is it that sentient beings have suddenly arisen here?
(Xiang Mai said: "Generally, human beings are born from the conjunction of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and their various characteristics.

Yet, being shrouded by the ignorance (*avidyā*) of delusion, they truly cannot be illuminated by the majestic light of the sun and moon. Only when superior wisdom (*viśeṣajñāna*) opens and clarifies does one realize the nature of sentient beings.")
[The Master] said: "Phenomena arise suddenly as illusory existences from within the state of indistinctness; it is just like this.
Jiehuan asked: "Sentient beings are firmly bound by ignorance, which causes them to perceive the earth-element as obstructive and impenetrable, thereby veiling their wondrous luminosity.

Therefore, when all Buddhas attain the Way, they cause the earth to tremble and emit light to demonstrate the overturning and shattering of ignorance, thereby revealing and manifesting [the true nature]."
This is the Light of Wisdom. In the midst of that land, in the places of profound darkness, is what is called the dark space between the two Iron Ring Mountains.
The sentient beings therein formerly dwelt in this profound darkness, unable to see one another;
it was only through light that they could see, and thus doubt suddenly arose.
Furthermore, the celestial palaces throughout his realm, up to the Brahma heavens, shook in six ways;
a great light shone everywhere, pervading the world and surpassing the radiance of all the devas.
(Śikṣānanda said: "Although the devas possess constant radiance, it does not equal the radiance of the Buddha.
At that time, within five hundred myriads of koṭis of lands in the eastern direction, the palaces of the Brahmā heavens were brilliantly illuminated.
The radiance was twice as bright as usual. Each of the Brahma Kings had this thought: "The light of our palaces now is such as has never existed before.
By what cause and condition does this sign appear? At that time, the Brahma Kings each went to one another.

They deliberated upon this matter together. At that time, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Savior of All (Sarvatrāṇa), who spoke these verses for the sake of the host of Brahmās:

(Jie-huan said: "Those among the devas who possess great majesty and virtue experience a sign of auspicious light before they are to be born; these are called the 'Devas of Great Virtue' [Mahāpuṇya-deva].
The verse says: "In all our palaces, there is a radiance such as has never been seen before. What is the cause and condition for this? We should each..."
They sought it together, wondering: "Is this for the sake of a Great Virtuous One being born? Or is it because a Buddha has appeared in the world?
And so this great radiance shone everywhere throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Brahma Kings of five million billion lands, together with their palaces, each took a fold of their robes.
Carrying various celestial flowers, they went together toward the western direction to investigate this sign.

There they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded with reverence by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others; and they also saw the sixteen princes requesting [him].
The Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma.
(Xiang Mai said: "This means seeking the light to approach the Buddha. Jie Huan said: "The various devas possess palaces that move with them.")
Thus it is said that they were together with their palaces.
At that moment, the Brahma kings prostrated themselves before the Buddha, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha;
the flowers so scattered were like Mount Sumeru, and they also used them to make offerings to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree. That Bodhi...
The *tṛ* trees were ten *yojanas* high. Having made offerings of flowers, each offered their own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words:
"May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us; we pray that you will graciously accept and dwell in the palaces we have presented."
Jie-huan said: "The scattering of flowers upon the Buddha is for the purpose of seeking a teacher; the offering of them to the tree is for the purpose of honoring the Way.
The flowers were as vast as Mount Sumeru and the tree was ten *yojanas* high—these were transformations manifested according to the scale of the Buddha’s fundamental body (*mūlakāya*).

It is like a dragon king sending down rain that pours forth in all ten directions; how could it be that the water itself is so abundant? It is simply that the transformation resides within the dragon."
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, each of them spoke these words:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the wheel of Dharma, deliver sentient beings, and open the path to Nirvana."
(Jie-huan said: "The Path of Nirvana is the wondrous path that brings liberation from the cycle of birth and death.

At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, having accepted the invitation of the Brahma Kings of the ten directions and the sixteen princes, immediately turned the Wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects through three revolutions.
Furthermore, [the Master] said: "To show the signs" means to demonstrate the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Four Noble Truths so that one may know the direction to follow;
this is the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). "To encourage practice" means to demonstrate the benefits and efficacy of the Four Noble Truths so that one may know how to cultivate them;

this is the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). "To provide realization" means to demonstrate, 'I have already realized it; you too should realize it'; this is the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*)."
Jie-huan said: "The three turnings are: the turning that demonstrates the characteristics, the turning that exhorts practice, and the turning that realizes the fruit.

These cause one to enter the three stages of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning. Furthermore, the three turnings correspond generally to the three faculties: those of inferior faculty require all three; those of middling faculty may require two; and those of superior faculty require only one.
As for those of the highest-superior faculty, the Way exists before their very eyes, leaving no room for words."
There is what is called the Wheel of Dharma of the Twelve Teachings, and there is what is called the Wheel of Dharma of the Twelve Practices. The Teaching is that which turns;
the Practice is that which is turned. Based on the three turnings—demonstration, exhortation, and realization—of the Four Noble Truths, this is the Wheel of Dharma of the Twelve Teachings.
Based on the three awakenings—through seeing, cultivation, and study—of the Four Noble Truths, this is the Wheel of Dharma of the Twelve Practices.
That which cannot be overturned by recluses, brahmins, gods, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone else in the world— namely,
that "this is suffering," "this is the origin of suffering," "this is the cessation of suffering," and "this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
(Nan said: "Regarding the four propositions of the śramaṇa—meaning that these have not yet attained correct realization—they merely revolve around and remain stuck in verbal designations.
What is indicated below as 'suffering' refers to the characteristics of what is to be transformed, namely the Dharma of the Four Truths. Xiang Mai said:)
"All are called suffering" means that the Four Noble Truths are established because of suffering, for the purpose of the path to extinguish suffering. The *Jie-huan* says:

"The eight [afflictions], such as birth, old age, sickness, and death, which manifest and oppress one, are called suffering; these are the afflictions (*kleśa*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and karma."

The summoning of the eight sufferings of the future is called "origination" (*samudaya*). This applies across the three periods of time: that is, past origination brings about present suffering, and present origination brings about future suffering.
When the bonds of karma are exhausted, such that the eight sufferings of birth and death are forever ended, it is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).
To remedy these bonds of karma, one cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; this is called the "path" (*mārga*).

And he extensively expounded the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form;
name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming.

With birth as condition, there is arising. With arising as condition, there are old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease. With the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases. With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease. With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases.
With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases. With the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases.
Cessation. When there is cessation, birth ceases. When birth ceases, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction cease. (And Nan said:

"Now, regarding the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the names are one while the meanings are manifold. There is what is called the Small Vehicle’s truth of arising and ceasing:
therein, conditioned by the birth-and-death of the segmented nature, it is named 'Suffering'; the afflictions and karma are named 'Origin'; the analytical cessation of birth..."
The category of the wisdom of emptiness is called the Path (*mārga*). Regarding what is termed the Mahāyāna, there are four truths: ignorance is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*);

the obstacles to knowledge are called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); non-abiding *nirvāṇa* is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); and the category of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena is the Truth of the Path.

Some say there are eight truths, which refers to combining the aforementioned [two sets]. Furthermore, there are immeasurable four truths, which are based upon the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of perfect and sudden realization.

It is said that the manifestation of the various sufferings and their origins clarifies the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). Seeking cessation and the path externally, one finds absolutely nothing to be attained;

this is called the Four Noble Truths. The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are likewise so. Therefore, although the teachings of the Truths and Dependent Origination belong to the Two Vehicles, they actually extend to the Mahāyāna.
Their essential purpose is to sever the root of birth and death, extinguish the cause of ignorance, and cause one to return to fundamental luminosity.
It is simply the wondrous nature. For all who practice the Way, there are teachings; one should penetrate deeply into this. Regarding the "Ring of Precepts," it says:

It extensively explains the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. From "ignorance conditions volitional formations" up to "birth conditions old age and death," etc., it demonstrates the characteristics of their arising;
this is precisely an extensive explanation of the two truths of Suffering and Accumulation. From ignorance...

From the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, this demonstrates the characteristics of cultivation and abandonment; it is an extensive exposition of the two truths of Cessation and the Path.
The Four Noble Truths are presented as a rough outline for those of inferior capacity, with their basis in the traces [of phenomena].

For those of middling capacity, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are taught, through which one minutely contemplates the Four Noble Truths; their basis lies in the mind, namely that the fundamental nature of wisdom is originally luminous, wondrously profound, and perfectly clear. By means of...

When delusory objects suddenly arise, there is an instant of obscuration and dullness; this is called ignorance (*avidyā*). Within the essence of ignorance, when the first movement of a single thought occurs, it is called formative action (*saṃskāra*).
As this dullness wavers and stirs, one loses that essential clarity; clinging to the profound stillness, cognition is emitted, and thus wisdom is transformed into consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Among the twelve links of dependent origination, these three constitute the root, while the remaining nine are the branches and leaves, forming one another through mutual dependence.
These are merely conditions of the three periods of time. Wisdom is fundamentally without knowing; it knows only by means of consciousness. Form constitutes the deluded mind, which is called "name";
it is the master of the six thieves. Nature is fundamentally without birth; it arises only by means of consciousness. Form constitutes the illusory substance.

What is called "form" (rūpa) is the basis for the other four aggregates. Thus, "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) refers to the state of the consciousness initially entering the womb as a congealing and coagulating embryo.

From this congealing and coagulation, the six sense faculties (ṣaḍāyatana) are formed. Once the faculties are complete and one is born from the womb, the interaction between the faculties and their objects is called "contact" (sparśa).
The experience of these objects is called "feeling" (vedanā). Because there is that which is felt, craving (tṛṣṇā) arises. And craving...
This is grasping (*upādāna*). Because of grasping through craving, delusion and karma bind together; the manifestation of good and evil is called existence (*bhava*).

Through these various bonds of existence, one becomes the cause for birth within the three realms; this is called birth (*jāti*). Once there is birth, old age, death, and suffering follow as a matter of course.
Such is the characteristic of the arising of this [cycle]. If one wishes to extinguish it, what is essential? One should know that...
Ignorance (avidyā) has no real substance. At the very beginning, the source of the one mind is vast, empty, wondrous, and profoundly still.

Because one establishes cognition upon the perceived objects of knowledge, delusive dust momentarily arises; thus, ignorance exists. If one realizes that there is no seeing within seeing, then the nature of wisdom is truly pure.

It returns once more to wondrous stillness, penetratingly clear and perfectly lucid; this is called the extinction of ignorance. Consequently, from the "spontaneous functioning" downward, there is nothing that does not likewise cease.
For when the root no longer exists, there is nothing for the branches to attach to. This is the characteristic of cultivation and abandonment.
When the Buddha preached this Dharma amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, six hundred trillion nayutas of people, by way of not grasping at any phenomena,
attained liberation of the mind from all outflows (*āsrava*). They all attained profound and wondrous meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and were endowed with the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Furthermore, [Nan said]: "The holy and the ordinary are of one substance; delusion and enlightenment share the same source.

If a person can truly awaken to the cause of afflictions and entanglements and comprehend the beginning of turbid confusion, and if they ultimately do not receive even the dharmas, then dhyāna-concentration, liberation, the six supernatural powers, and the three insights will [naturally follow]."
"All may attain it. Jiehuan said:
"These are those of keen faculties who obtained benefit by hearing the Dharma at the first assembly.

'Not receiving any dharma' means awakening to the truth that conditions are empty and realizing there is nothing to which one is attached. For the mind is fundamentally liberated; it is because of reception [of dharmas] that..."
The nature of the mind is fundamentally luminous and settled; it becomes obscured by attachment. Therefore, by not grasping at any phenomena, the mind attains liberation from all outflows (*āsrava*).
Furthermore, one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the three knowledges (*vidyā*), and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
During the second, third, and fourth preachings of the Dharma, hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River,
likewise attained liberation of the mind from all outflows (*āsrava*) by virtue of not grasping at any phenomena.
From that time onward, the assembly of śrāvakas became immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.

[And Nan said: "From this point onward, it was no longer taught in a single session. Furthermore, there were those of lesser faculties who obtained benefit, their number being beyond calculation. Jiehuan said:
"This refers to those of middle and lower faculties who obtained benefit by hearing the Dharma in succession. As for those of sharp faculties, [they obtain benefit] in a single [session]."

Those of superior capacity attain awakening upon hearing [the teaching] once; those of middling and inferior capacity hear much but awaken little, and thus it is only by reaching the third and fourth periods that they obtain benefit.
At that time, the sixteen princes all left home as youths and became śrāmaṇeras, their faculties being sharp and keen.
His wisdom was clear and lucid. He had already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, purely cultivated the Brahma-faring, and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[The Commentary on the Precepts says: The sixteen princes heard the Dharma and obtained benefit; thereupon they left the household life and further sought the Mahāyāna.
They all addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of great virtuous śrāvakas have all already attained accomplishment.
World-Honored One, you should also preach for us the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. I...
Having heard this together, we shall all practice and study it. World-Honored One, our aspirations are like those of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision;
may the Buddha himself bear witness to what is contemplated within our profound resolve.

(This correctly describes the request to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. However, while all previous requests were for the turning of the unsurpassed wheel, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū preached the Dharma of the Four Truths and Dependent Origination.
Furthermore, he waited for this specific request because the preaching of the Buddhas always proceeds from the gradual to the sudden, relying on provisional means to reveal the ultimate reality.
For if one were led without a gradual approach, they would be startled and fail to believe; it is not merely that the teaching must not be premature.)
[The passage concludes with] "Jie" (Section). It is also because [the disciples] wish to study without skipping levels. Jiehuan said:
"All have already achieved accomplishment," meaning they have already accomplished their great resolve; therefore, they request that the Great Dharma be preached.

"Our own aspirations are inferior"—this is their self-proclamation of their great resolve, hoping for the preaching of the Great Dharma. The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are precisely what [is required].
This refers to the one great matter.
At that time, after the Buddha had accepted the śrāmaṇera’s invitation and two thousand kalpas had passed, he preached this Mahāyāna sūtra among the fourfold assembly;
it is titled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*, the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected and remembered by the Buddhas.
Furthermore, it is said: "Śākyamuni manifested a lifespan of eighty years and taught the Prajñāpāramitā and other doctrines for forty of them;
Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū manifested a lifespan of five hundred trillion nayutas of kalpas, and thus he should have taught [the Dharma] for twenty thousand [of those]."
Jie-huan said: "Only after twenty thousand kalpas did he long remain silent regarding this essential teaching in order to await the proper opportunity.

Thus, prior to those twenty thousand kalpas, he already expounded the teachings of the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā; as the verse says: 'He taught the six pāramitās, as well as the matters of various supernatural powers.'"

The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas without ever ceasing or resting. Having finished preaching this sutra, he immediately entered a quiet chamber and dwelt in meditative concentration for eighty-four thousand kalpas.
(Jie-huan said: "That which has never been interrupted or abandoned refers to the 'uninterrupted' fervent preaching.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras, knowing that the Buddha had entered his room and was in silent meditative concentration, each ascended the Dharma seat.
Furthermore, for eighty-four thousand kalpas, he extensively expounded and analyzed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the fourfold assembly;
in each instance, he delivered, instructed, benefited, and gladdened six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
He causes them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment).
[This is an expedient teaching for the sake of the doubting multitude. The sixteen princes represent the eight consciousnesses still enmeshed in afflictions (*saṃkleśa*).

The sixteen bodhisattvas represent the eight wisdoms that have emerged from such entanglements. Furthermore, the number sixteen is used to demonstrate the subduing of the eight heterodoxies by means of the Eightfold Noble Path.

The Precept Ring says: Regarding the phrase "delivering many multitudes throughout eighty thousand kalpas," this signifies that once the Way of Great Pervasive Penetration is attained, there is nothing among the eighty thousand dharma-gates that is not understood.
Therefore, it is not only the Eightfold Noble Path that constitutes wondrous wisdom; even the Eightfold Wrong Path is wondrous wisdom as well.
It is not only through the Eightfold Noble Path that one can deliver others; even through the Eightfold Wrong Path, one can deliver them.
What is called the "sage-nature" has nothing it does not penetrate; whether moving against or with the current, all are skillful means.

It is precisely because it is thus that each is able to expound the wondrous, even unto the exhaustion of kalpas, and each is able to deliver sentient beings, even as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Were it otherwise, it would be insufficient to constitute the Way of Great Penetration.
After eighty-four thousand kalpas had passed, the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū arose from his samādhi, proceeded to the Dharma-seat, and sat down with serene composure.
He addressed the great assembly, saying: "These sixteen śrāmaṇera bodhisattvas are truly rare;
their faculties are sharp and keen, their wisdom is clear and lucid, and they have already made offerings to immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas."
In the presence of all Buddhas, they constantly cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), receive and uphold the Buddha-wisdom, and reveal it to sentient beings, leading people to abide therein.
You all should repeatedly draw near to them and make offerings to them.
(Śīlaka said: "I agree with what has been spoken and praise their virtuous conduct, so that the assembly may become closely attached.

Why is this? If any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas can believe in these sutras and dharmas spoken by the sixteen bodhisattvas, and receive, uphold, and do not disparage them, such persons shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
(Jiehuan said: "If the three vehicles attain the wondrous, they likewise return to the One Vehicle.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These sixteen bodhisattvas always delight in preaching this *Sūtra of the Wondrous Flower*. Each and every bodhisattva..."
The six hundred trillion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, whom [the Buddha] transformed, were born together with this Bodhisattva in every successive life.

Having heard the Dharma from him, they all attained faith and understanding. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they have encountered forty trillion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and even now, they have not yet reached their end.
Jiehuan said: "To inquire about those converted in the past is to meet with conditions in the present.

Those among the converted who have always been with the Master are so because their karmic conditions for conversion were profound; thus they have encountered billions of Buddhas, and as their conditions are not yet exhausted, they have now met him once again."
"O bhikṣus, I now tell you: those sixteen śrāmaṇeras who were disciples of that Buddha have all now attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
They currently reside in buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, preaching the Dharma, with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as their retinues.
Of those two śrāmaṇeras, one has become a Buddha in the eastern direction."
The first is named Akṣobhya (pronounced "Xù"), who resides in the Land of Joy (*Abhirati*). The second is named Sumerukūṭa. [Master] Xiáng Mài states:
The scripture says that one is unmoved by praise or blame, like Mount Sumeru. This Buddha appears in response to the various movements of sentient beings, yet his essence remains unmoving;
furthermore, he dwells in a land of movement to demonstrate that within movement there is stillness. These two Buddhas transform beings together, and their virtuous characteristics are thus.
Zi. Therefore, although there are two names, they may be explained as a unified whole).
Jiehuan says: "This records the names and traces of the sixteen princes of Chen who attained Buddhahood.

Heaven and earth establish their positions, and the Way operates within them. The sages model themselves after this to enlighten all things and accomplish their tasks, encompassing the Way of the world. Thus, [the eight...]"
When compared to the Buddhas, each [deity] relies on a specific direction to manifest a specific virtue; thus they open the way for beings and bring them to completion.

Examining their origins and tracing them to their ends, there is no principle in the world that they do not encompass. In the East, *Zhen* (Thunder) signifies movement, and joy is also a form of movement.
Akṣobhya means "the Immovable," and the summit of Mount Sumeru is likewise the ultimate state of immovability.
In the southeast are two Buddhas: the first is named Lion’s Voice, and the second is named Lion’s Appearance.
(And it says in the south: "These Buddhas respond to sentient beings with compassionate gentleness and preach the Dharma with fearlessness.")
Jie-huan said: "In the southeast, Xun represents flexibility and compliance. 'The Lion's Sound' refers to that which is taught without fear;
'the Lion's Form' refers to that which is manifested without fear."
In the southern direction are two Buddhas: the first is named Ākāśapratisthita (Abiding in Space), and the second is named Nityanirvṛta (Perpetually Extinct).
[The Southern Tradition further states: "He does not undergo extinction again; this is called 'perpetual extinction'."]

Jie-huan said: "In the south, Li (the trigram for fire) represents vacuity and luminosity. Those who dwell in emptiness have a substance that reaches the ultimate void, thereby responding to all realities.
'Ever-extinguished' means to fully comprehend all dharmas as being, in their very essence, empty and quiescent; this is the mark of tranquil extinction."
In the southwest are two Buddhas: the first is named Śakradevendra-lakṣaṇa (Emperor-like Appearance), and the second is named Brahmā-lakṣaṇa (Brahma-like Appearance).

[And the Southern Record says: "These Buddhas respond to things through their spiritual power; all things derive their life from them, yet their virtue remains eternally pure, never being defiled by those things. ]
The Precept Ring states: In the southwest, Kun represents the source of livelihood. As for "the Imperial Aspect" (Dixiang), it refers to the spirit emerging to respond to phenomena as an Emperor;
this is the purity of Brahma.

Regarding the two Buddhas of the West: the first is named Amitābha, and the second is named Sarvalokadhātudurgatipariśodhana (He Who Delivers All Beings from the Suffering and Afflictions of the World).
Furthermore, [Nan] said: "When this Buddha manifested at the time of destruction, he revealed the Infinite Life;
thus, there is ultimately no birth or death, by which he delivers the world from the suffering and affliction of birth and death."
Jie-huan said: "In the West, the trigram Dui signifies breaking and dispersing. Amitābha is called 'Immeasurable Life.
The sufferings and afflictions of the world are precisely the impermanence of birth and death."
In the northwest are two Buddhas: the first is named Tamālapatracaṃdanagandha-ṛddhi (Sandalwood Fragrance Supernatural Power), and the second is named Sumerukūṭa (Sumeru Appearance).
[And to the south it says: These Buddhas’ supernatural powers respond to things like the unceasing Way of Heaven; they are quiescent and unmoving, yet they are moved by resonance.

Jiehuan said: "In the northwest, Qian represents firmness and vigor; the fragrance of *tamāla* sandalwood is pure, far-reaching, and subtly pervasive, which is used as a metaphor for supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
The characteristics of Mount Sumeru likewise signify immovability."
In the north are two Buddhas: the first is named Cloud Sovereignty (*Megheśvara*), and the second is named Cloud Sovereignty King (*Megheśvararāja*).

(Furthermore, it says: These Buddhas, through their unconditioned compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*), provide shelter and benefit to sentient beings in perilous and difficult circumstances, yet they remain without thought or attachment, as sovereign as the clouds.)
Jie-huan said: "In the north, Kan represents danger and entrapment. 'Clouds Moving at Will' means benefiting sentient beings without deliberate intent.
'King of Clouds Moving at Will' signifies the ultimate state of mastery."
The Buddha of the northeast is named Destroyer of All Worldly Fears.

(This Buddha, amidst the fears of birth and death, awakens all beings through the singular, true, concentrated, and eternal [nature], causing them to enter the state of neither-dying-nor-being-born; thus, fear is destroyed.)
Jiehuan said: "In the northeast lies Gen, the place where all things begin and end their completion.
The principle of beginning and ending manifests as formation and decay in things, and as birth and death in humans; this is that which the world fears."
The sixteenth [manifestation] is I, Śākyamuni Buddha, who attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the Sahā world-realm. (Some say:
"The Eight Trigrams are a book of the Central Lands; to cite them and correlate them with the teachings of India—how could this be the Buddha's intention? To this, Nan said:)
The world under the single sky is but one; as far as its borders extend, its directions are the same. The hexagrams are the natural principles of heaven and earth—how could they alone be different?
Fuxi drew them to instruct humanity, while our Buddha used images to establish the Dharma; each silently attains the same essence.
Although the current sutras do not contain the text of the eight trigrams, they clearly manifest the imagery of the eight directions, borrowing from worldly affairs to convey the truth.
To clarify the principle: how could it be otherwise?
Jiehuan said: "Śākyamuni" means "Able One of Silent Tranquility," signifying that his virtue is benevolent and rescues all classes of beings.
His Way is silent and unconditioned; because he manifests transformation within the Enduring World (Sahā), he is titled "The Capable One" (Śākyamuni).

This title is specifically designated following the Northeastern direction because, although the Great Awakened One possesses the virtue of both initiating and completing all things, his Way is perfectly responsive and does not stagnate in any particular quarter.
Being without beginning and without end, he is the synthesis of all virtues. Indeed, from the state of non-existence...
Moving forth, he responds to the myriad movements of beings; he can be supple and he can be firm. He teaches and reveals fearlessness, emptying himself to respond to all things.

Whether manifesting long life or exercising spiritual power, even down to rescuing those in peril and extinguishing their terrors—all these are none other than Śākyamuni’s skillful actions according to circumstances.

Therefore, while the virtues of the Buddhas of the eight directions are described in detail, they are summarized by Śākyamuni. This is precisely how he encompasses heaven and earth, completing all things through his subtle and perfect transformations.
The myriad things are the ultimate virtue that is without direction or substance. Were it not for the realization of the unsurpassed Right Path, how could one be endowed with this?
Therefore, it is said that Śākyamuni attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the Sahā world.
"O bhikṣus, when we were śrāmaṇeras, each of us converted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
Having heard the Dharma from me, they set their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Among these sentient beings, there are some who now abide in the stage of the śrāvaka; I constantly teach them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, these people should enter the Buddha-way by way of gradual stages.
(Jiehuan says: This clarifies the past causes and present conditions, so that they may know their meritorious practices have already deepened and they are now brought to fulfillment.
Citing the case of those converted as śrāmaṇeras clarifies the past causes; those converted at present clarify the present conditions. One should act accordingly.)
The Dharma gradually leads one into the Buddha-way; this is its fulfillment.
Why is this so? Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
(Xiang Mai says: Regarding the previous point that although one has received instruction over vast eons, one still enters gradually—this is because the wisdom of the Tathāgata...)
"Because it is difficult to believe and understand.
The *Jie-huan* says: "There are no sentient beings who do not possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom;

yet that it is so difficult to understand is due to the self-obstruction caused by habitual defilements (*vāsanā*). Judging from people today, that they have fortunately heard the True Dharma is not without the influence of past causes. How peaceful!
I know that you and your followers are not the lingering dust of Jñānavijaya’s legacy, nor are you his disciples of the future.

Yet, as your karmic obstacles remain dense and the fruit of the Way is distant and vast, even though you have been under his instruction for kalpas as long as the void, you are still only gradually entering it.
If you can advance with diligence, there is still hope; but if you should again fall back, how can one know when the time will come to surpass those who preceded you?
Kalpas. Does it not exceed this number? Thus, that which is called "difficult to understand" is not that the Buddha's wisdom is difficult;
rather, it is the capacity [of the listeners] that is itself difficult.
O Bhikṣus, when the Tathāgata knows for himself that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, and the assembly is pure, with firm faith and understanding—
Having fully realized the dharma of emptiness and deeply entered meditative concentration, he then assembled the multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas and preached this sutra for them:
"In the world, there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction; it is only through the single Buddha-vehicle that one attains extinction."
(Nanjio says: "The former [section] clarifies the initial provisional [teachings], while this assembly [clarifies] the ultimate reality. Xiangmai says: "There are no two vehicles;
this means that there is no further vehicle beyond what was previously mentioned.")
Jie-huan said: "The time for Nirvāṇa has arrived" means that his transformative mission is nearing its end. "The assembly is pure" means that their spiritual faculties have already matured.
As for "the assembly is pure," it means they have already severed delusions and eliminated fetters through the teachings of the Tripiṭaka. "Faith is firm and solid" means—

One has already gained heartfelt conviction regarding the nature of the mind through the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). Having thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness, one may say that one has awakened to *prajñā*.

Having entered deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one may say that one has wondrously reached the profound source. When this is so, all illnesses have been eliminated, and even the medical prescriptions are discarded.
Therefore, he set aside the three provisional powers and specifically elucidated the one true reality. Those who attain *nirvāṇa* obtain the fruit of the path of true permanence.
Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata’s skillful means penetrate deeply into the nature of sentient beings; he knows that their inclinations and joys lie in the lesser Dharma.
Deeply attached to the five desires, for the sake of such people as these, he speaks of nirvana. When these people hear it, they immediately believe and accept it.
(Jiehuan says: For those who delight in the small, he provisionally speaks of the small fruit; they then believe and accept it, like being stuck in a conjured city.)
It is like a perilous and evil road five hundred *yojanas* long, desolate and uninhabited, a place of terror.
(Nan Yue says: "This is a metaphor for the long and distant perilous road of the evil paths of birth-and-death and afflictions. Xiang Mai says:)
"Vast and desolate, with no people," etc., is an analogy for the long duration of birth and death, where there is no true knowledge or vision, and one falsely gives rise to fear).
Regarding the "five hundred yojanas of the precept-ring": the ancient explanations are even more numerous;

now, we take it to mean that when those of the Two Vehicles sever the fetters and delusions of the three realms and depart from the birth-and-death of segmented existence to realize *nirvāṇa* with remainder, they have passed three hundred yojanas and reached [this point].
The illusory city. Yet, one remains constantly mired in the cycle of birth and death characterized by transformation.

If one turns the mind toward the Great Vehicle and advances to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), exhausting all residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), this is like having traveled four hundred *yojana* and being near the place of treasure.

Furthermore, advancing to the eighth stage and above, one exhausts all ignorance (*avidyā*), leaves behind the cycle of birth and death characterized by transformation, and realizes *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; this is like having traveled five hundred *yojana*.
In ten days, one reaches the place of treasure.
Suppose there is a great multitude who wishes to traverse this path and reach the site of precious jewels, and there is a guide who is wise, intelligent, and far-sighted.
He thoroughly knows the characteristics of the dangers and the passages, whether open or blocked, on the perilous path; he leads the multitude, desiring to cross over this difficulty.
(Jiehuan says: "If there are three phrases regarding 'many,' they are like those of the three vehicles seeking Buddhahood.
(He further says: "Virtue leads to openness, while evil leads to blockage; thus one may be free from difficulties.")
The Precept Ring says: "The Guide" refers to one who points out the way, such as the World-Honored One Śākyamuni. To open this path is to advance; to block it is to stop.
Opening is analogous to severing delusions; blocking is analogous to giving rise to obstacles.
The multitude they were leading grew weary and despondent along the way. They said to their guide, "We are utterly exhausted and filled with fear;
we can no longer proceed, yet the path ahead is still long. We now wish to turn back."
(Jie-huan said: "It is like those of the Two Vehicles seeking the Way, who advance with difficulty but retreat easily.
The Guide, possessing many skillful means, thinks to himself: 'These people are pitiable; why do they abandon such great treasures?')"
Yet they wished to turn back. Having formed this thought, by the power of skillful means, he created an illusory city within the perilous path after three hundred *yojanas* had been traversed.
He addressed the multitude, saying: "Do not fear; do not turn back. You may now halt here in this great city and do as you please.
If you enter this city, you will find swift peace and security. If you can proceed further..."
One may also proceed to the place of the precious treasure.

(Jie-huan said: This is a metaphor for how, after the practitioners of the Two Vehicles have severed the fetters and delusions of the three realms and rested in their minor fruits, they advance toward the ground of wisdom.
"Acting according to one's inclination" means to act according to the capacity of one's own strength, gradually attaining the principle of entering the Way).
At that time, the exhausted multitude was filled with great joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, saying,
"We have now escaped this evil path and have swiftly attained peace and security."
(Jie-huan said: "This is because they have fulfilled their aspiration for rest.
At that time, the Guide, knowing that these people had attained rest and were no longer fatigued, immediately caused the conjured city to vanish.
He spoke to the multitude, saying: "Come, all of you! The place of treasure is near. That great city you saw earlier was merely a transformation created by me for the sake of providing rest."
(What is manifested is not truly real; therefore, it perishes in an instant. Only the treasure-land is real. Expedient means are not substantially existent;
therefore, they are ultimately abandoned. Only the One Vehicle is the reality.)
"O bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is likewise. Now, acting as your great guide, he knows that the various births and deaths, afflictions, evil paths, and perilous difficulties are long and far-reaching;

those who should go forth and be delivered—if sentient beings hear only of the Single Buddha Vehicle (Ekayāna), they will not wish to see the Buddha, nor wish to draw near to him, and will instead think: 'The path of the Buddha is long and far.'"
Only by undergoing diligent toil can [enlightenment] be achieved.
(Furthermore, it says: "The former speaks of the long duration of the evil realms; this speaks of the long duration of the Buddha-way.
The former observes sentient beings through right view; this observes the Buddha-way through inverted views. (It further says: "If, indeed, there were no birth and death... )

If delusion and karma were such that the fundamental substance is eternally concentrated and pure, what would there be to treat or rectify? The vision of long-term [salvation] and the diligent application of effort to alleviate suffering would be utterly futile.

This would bring reproach upon the Buddha-way, leading inevitably to indolence and regression; it is for this reason that the Great Awakened One described these inverted views in order to guide and encourage [practitioners].
Jiehuan said: "If one hears only of the One Vehicle without the expedient means of salvation, one will grow weary of the Great and have no desire to see the Buddha;
one will be daunted by its complexity and anxious that the Way is too distant. Therefore, expedient means are necessary. From the very beginning, the Buddha-way was not far from people."

Fundamentally, there is neither cultivation nor realization. It is only because one has turned one's back on the cycle of birth and death that returning to the source is difficult, and thus it appears long and distant.
Because delusions and karma accumulate as obstructions, their remediation is difficult, and thus it appears arduous.
Therefore, this long duration and these hardships arise from inverted delusion; what connection do they have with the Way?
The Buddha, knowing that these minds were timid, weak, and inferior, employed skillful means to provide rest along the way and spoke of two types of nirvana.
If sentient beings abide in these two stages, the Tathāgata then says to them:
"What you have accomplished is not yet complete; the stage upon which you reside is close to the wisdom of the Buddha. You should observe and deliberate upon what has been attained."
Nirvāṇa is not ultimate reality; it is merely the skillful power of the Tathāgata to differentiate and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
It is like that guide who, for the sake of providing rest, conjured a great city. Once he knew they had rested, he told them:
"The place of treasure is near; this city is not real; I created it by transformation."
(Jiehuan said: "The Middle Way refers to the intermediate stage between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The two nirvāṇas refer to the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles;
it is said that this corresponds to the [first] two stages. He further said: "To abide in these two stages means to be stalled at the provisional fruits of the two vehicles.")
Yet they did not know how to advance. Therefore, he spoke to them of the Buddha-wisdom, causing them to observe and deliberate so that they might advance and attain the true fruit.
Chapter Eight: The Bestowal of Prophecies upon the Five Hundred Disciples.
Here, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra and the five hundred arhats attained realization according to their respective capacities; the Buddha then confirmed their understanding and bestowed prophecies upon them.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra heard from the Buddha this teaching of wisdom and skillful means given according to what was appropriate;
he further heard the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the great disciples;

he further heard the matters concerning their causes and conditions in past lives; and he further heard that all Buddhas possess the power of great sovereign supernatural penetrations. Having attained...

It was unprecedented; his heart was pure and leaped with joy. He immediately rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, he did not for a moment turn his eyes away.
(Jie-huan said: "I have heard that 'expedient means according to suitability' comprehensively covers the teachings of the three assemblies.

Furthermore, I have heard that 'the Great Record' comprehensively covers the accounts of Śāriputra and others receiving the prediction. Again, I have heard that 'causes and conditions' specifically covers the matter of the Great Pervasive One.")
Furthermore, having heard of the miraculous powers and the extraordinary manifestations of the Guide and Teacher—things rarely encountered—he attained that which he had never experienced before;
as his delusions were dispelled, his mind became pure, and he leaped with joy.
They then had this thought: "The World-Honored One is most extraordinary; his deeds are rare and marvelous.
In accordance with the various dispositions of the world, he employs skillful means and insight to preach the Dharma for them, pulling sentient beings out of their attachments everywhere.
We cannot fully express the Buddha’s merits in words; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know our deep-seated hearts and original vows."
(The preceding section was a narrative by the compiler. This, however, is truly Pūrṇa’s resolve:

his profound mind and original vow to diligently protect, uphold, and assist in the propagation of the Buddha-dharma, extending even to those who assist in its propagation in the past and future; it does not mean that he sought a prediction of his own enlightenment.)
The Precept Ring said: "To speak of its marvelousness and rarity, it reaches to every place of attachment;
this is a general praise of the Dharma taught during the three turnings of the wheel. We cannot fully proclaim the Buddha’s merits;

we can only offer a general praise for the bestowal of predictions, even down to the spiritual transformations of the Guide, which cannot be fully declared. From 'Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One' onwards, he extends his original vow."
This is a vow to protect and uphold [the Dharma].
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "Do you see this Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra?
I have always declared him to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma, and I have also constantly praised his various merits."
Virtuous and diligent in upholding [the Dharma], he assists in proclaiming my teaching;
he is able to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly, fully explaining the Buddha’s true Dharma and greatly benefiting his fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life.
Apart from the Tathāgata, no one is able to exhaust the eloquence of his discourse.
(And the Southern Record says: "First in expounding the Dharma" describes his correct practice; "various meritorious virtues" describes his manifold deeds;
"diligently protecting and upholding" describes his original vow; and "eloquence in discourse" describes his rhetorical skill.)
Jie-huan said: "This describes the fulfillment of his profound mind and original vow.

As for the question, 'Does the assembly see it?'—it is because the assembly merely knows the outward traces of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra and does not know his profound practice; therefore, the text opens with this question to reveal it to them."
"You should not think that Pūrṇa is merely able to protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming my Dharma;
he also protected, upheld, and assisted in proclaiming the True Dharma of ninety billion Buddhas in the past. Among those who preached the Dharma at those times, he was likewise the foremost.
Furthermore, regarding the Dharma of emptiness taught by those Buddhas, he clearly understood and mastered it, attaining the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge."
He was always able to preach the Dharma with careful discernment and purity, free from all doubt.

He was fully endowed with the supernatural powers of a bodhisattva and constantly practiced the pure conduct (brahmacarya) for the duration of his life. To the people of that Buddha’s world, he was universally regarded as being truly a śrāvaka.
Thus, Pūrṇa, by these skillful means, benefited immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings;
furthermore, he transformed immeasurable asaṃkhyeya people, causing them to establish themselves in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of purifying a buddha-field.
Constantly relying on the Buddha’s work, he transforms and educates sentient beings.

(Xiangmai says: The preceding was a general summary; this is a detailed exposition. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "A bodhisattva takes up a buddha-field according to the sentient beings he transforms.
That which is called a pure buddha-field is achieved by purifying one's own mind, thereby bringing about the purity of the buddha-field.")
Furthermore, regarding the necessity of teaching and transforming sentient beings in order to purify the Buddha-land:

this requires being able to purify while remaining within the midst of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), rather than seeking purity by detesting worldly afflictions as the followers of the Two Vehicles do. Viewed from this perspective, his fundamental nature is that of a Great Expedient Sage who manifests the propagation of the Dharma.
Therefore, the verse praises him through the theme of "inner secrecy and outer manifestation. (And the Southern Text says:)
Ratnākara secretly concealed [the profound meaning] while manifesting it outwardly to serve as a guiding principle for the masses; therefore, I have described it in full detail.
The "Ring of Precepts" states: "To cite the locations of ninety billion Buddhas" extensively sets forth the distant causes for protecting and proclaiming [the Dharma].

One who clearly understands and thoroughly penetrates the Buddha’s teaching on emptiness is not like those of the Two Vehicles who stagnate in the emptiness of annihilation. They have attained the four [unhindered knowledges]...
To obstruct those who preach the pure Dharma is to speak according to what is as it is, yet not to become mired in names and signs.

The supernormal powers of a bodhisattva are not to be compared with those of the two vehicles. "According to their lifespan" means throughout the duration of one's life. "Causing them to establish themselves in Bodhi" [is the purpose].
This ensures that the True Path is established. Those who transform sentient beings for the sake of purifying Buddha-fields do so by relying on altruistic conduct to perfect their own practice.
O Bhikṣus, Pūrṇa was also ranked first among those who expound the Dharma under the seven Buddhas; now, in this [Buddha-field]...
Among those who preach the Dharma, they shall be foremost; among those who preach the Dharma for all future Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa, they shall likewise be foremost.
They shall protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma and assist in its proclamation;

furthermore, in the future, they shall protect and uphold the teachings of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, teaching and benefiting immeasurable sentient beings, and establishing them [in the path].
For the sake of purifying the Buddha-field, they constantly apply themselves with diligent vigor, teaching and transforming sentient beings,
gradually fulfilling the path of a bodhisattva until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
(Xiang Mai said: "The preceding section describes distant causes; this section covers three lifetimes, both clarifying the profound practice of preaching the Dharma and proclaiming transformation.
(Supplementary Note: Regarding the three kalpas and the three thousand Buddhas, the first thousand attained Buddhahood during the *Vibhūṣaṇa-kalpa*.)
Those headed by Padmaprabha (Huāguāng) up to Viśvabhū; next, the thousand [Bodhisattvas] who will attain Buddhahood in the Bhadrakalpa, headed by Krakucchanda (Hóulúsūn) up to Ruci (Lóuzhì);
and finally, the thousand [Bodhisattvas] who will attain Buddhahood in the Tārakakalpa, headed by Sūryaprabha (Rìguāng) up to Merudhvaja (Xūmíxiàng).
The Precept Ring states: "The Seven Buddhas are Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni.
The first three belong to the preceding kalpa; the latter four belong to the present kalpa. Regarding the three thousand Buddhas of the three kalpas, they begin with the Buddha Prabhāsa.
During the age of the Final Dharma, one leaves the household life to practice the Way and hears of the fifty-three Buddhas."

One who hears this name will deeply admire it from the core of their heart and further transform others until they have gathered a multitude of three thousand people, all of whom pay homage with deep sincerity;
such a person shall immediately transcend the sins of birth and death accumulated over many kalpas and attain the realization of Buddhahood.
After the passing of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, you shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in this very land,
and be known as the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid.
The Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

(According to the *Huayan ji*: "A Bodhisattva who has resolved their mind shall, after passing through more than a thousand unspeakable kalpas, attain Buddhahood and be named Pure Mind (*Vimalacitta*).
The *Śāstra* states that this refers to the total purity resulting from clearly understanding such a dharma-gate regarding the measure of kalpas; this is precisely the meaning here. The rest...)
The recorded meaning regarding the number of kalpas is identical [to what precedes].
Jiánhuan said: "Since Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra planted the causes under many buddhas in the distant past, he has nevertheless still passed through asaṃkhyeya kalpas."

Thus one attains Bodhi, which is termed "Dharma-illumination" (Dharmāloka). This means that within a single moment, one clearly and thoroughly penetrates the Dharma-gates of immeasurable kalpas, thereby immediately accomplishing the Buddha-way;
it is not like the view of ordinary sentiment, which regards it as occurring after a vast number of kalpas.
That Buddha’s buddha-field consists of as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
Its ground is composed of the seven treasures and is level as the palm of a hand, without mountains, ridges, ravines, gullies, or chasms.

Within it, towers and pavilions made of the seven treasures fill the space, while the palaces of the various devas are situated nearby in the void; thus humans and devas interact and can see one another, and there are no evils.
In that land, there are no women; all sentient beings are born by transformation and are free from sexual desire.
(Jiehuan said: "These are all signs of the purity of the environmental retribution.

Because they constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) during the causal stage and extensively transformed sentient beings, causing them to establish themselves in the Right Path, there are no matters of depravity or impurity at the stage of fruition. All unions are those of supreme goodness.")
Such a person has attained great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
their body emits radiance; they travel through the air with ease; their resolve and mindfulness are firm and steadfast; and they possess diligence and wisdom.
They were entirely golden in color, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
(And the Southern Commentary states: "Examining this by worldly standards, the essence of the vital qi may transform into the arrayed stars;

if those who practice inhalation and exhalation can still achieve levitation, then it is beyond doubt that when all dross and turbidity are exhausted, the wondrous body becomes brilliant and refined, and one attains mastery over flying and traveling.")
Jie-huan said: "Since one has already been born through transformation, one is free from all defilements of desire; therefore, its original essence and appearance are pure and wondrous like this.
Such a wondrous essence is inherently possessed by all people, yet it is merely obscured by the turbid stains of coarse desires and evils."

Therefore, Ānanda said: "The energy of desire is coarse and turbid; when the stench of male and female copulates, it cannot give rise to the supreme, pure, wondrous, and luminous mass of purple-gold light.

If one were to sever the craving of desire and not undergo birth from a womb, then the fundamental essence and appearance would no longer be obscured by defilement, and the adornments of penetrating light would naturally manifest."
The sentient beings of that land constantly subsist on two kinds of food: first, the food of the joy of the Dharma; second, the food of the bliss of dhyāna.

There are immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas who have attained great supernormal powers and the four types of unimpeded wisdom, and who are well able to transform and guide all classes of sentient beings.
As for their assembly of śrāvakas, they cannot be calculated or reckoned by any numerical computation.

They were able to know this. All attained the full realization of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the three types of clear knowledge (*trividyā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
(Xingjianzi said: "The eight liberations are: first, possessing form, one perceives external forms; second, being without internal perception of form, one perceives external forms;

third, with a pure and resolute mind, one realizes the body through direct experience; fourth, transcending the perception of form, one extinguishes the perception of resistance and does not attend to the diversity of perceptions...")

One forms various perceptions. Having transcended the five [attainments], one enters the Sphere of Infinite Space. One enters the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness. Having transcended the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, this is the sixth;
one enters the Sphere of Nothingness. Having transcended the Sphere of Nothingness, this is the seventh; one enters the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
Having transcended all of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, this is the eighth; one enters the Cessation of Perception and Feeling.
The Precept Ring says: Because he does not proceed through a womb, he does not rely on solid food; he consumes only the joy of the Dharma and the liberation of dhyāna.
"Immeasurable" and below clarify the land and its inhabitants. "All bodhisattvas" and below clarify his fellow practitioners who have likewise attained the Dharma.
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is fully endowed with the power of a bodhisattva’s supernormal knowledges and has attained the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom; he speaks with thorough discernment.
The Dharma teaches and transforms sentient beings with clear understanding and thorough penetration; therefore, the assembly of the Dharma and its conditions share in these qualities.
Such are the immeasurable merits that adorn and perfect his Buddha-land.
(Śīlaka said: "This concludes the preceding section.
The eon was named Jewel Radiance, and the land was named Virtuous Purity. That Buddha’s lifespan lasted for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and his Dharma remained for a very long time.
After the Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, stupas made of the seven precious substances were erected, filling the entire land.
(Xiang Mai said: "The name of the country is 'Excellently Pure' (Śubhavimala). This is because the mind is pure; thus the Buddha-field is pure.

(Xing Jianzi said: "The seven treasures are: the wheel-treasure of gold, the white elephant treasure, the wish-fulfilling jewel treasure, the jade-woman treasure, the treasurer treasure, the military commander treasure, and the deep-blue horse treasure.")
Jie-huan said: "The kalpa possesses the true illumination of the Dharma-treasure; therefore, it is named 'Treasure Illumination' (Baoming). The land has no women and is devoid of evil realms;

therefore, it is named 'Virtuous Purity' (Shanjing). Because the Dharma is preached throughout the three periods of time, continuing the Buddha’s life-span, the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable and the Dharma abides for a very long time.
After his parinirvāṇa, stupas will arise and fill the entire country, and other virtues will further be dispersed and moisten all beings."
At that time, twelve hundred arhats who had attained mastery over their minds thought to themselves: "We are filled with joy at having obtained what we have never experienced before.
How wonderful it would be if the World-Honored One were to grant us each a prediction of our future enlightenment, just as he has done for the other great disciples!"
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in their minds, addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"These twelve hundred arhats—I shall now, in their very presence, bestow upon them the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in due order."
(Jie-huan said: "The twelve hundred arhats requested that [the Buddha] record their names.
The World-Honored One granted this request in general, yet he specifically addressed Kāśyapa because Kāśyapa was the foremost leader of the assembly; therefore, he spoke to him.")
Within this assembly, my great disciple, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya, shall make offerings to sixty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas;
thereafter, he will attain Buddhahood, known by the name of Samantaprabhāsa Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

(And in the south it says: Puming [Universal Radiance] means that by means of the radiance of wisdom, one shatters all darkness of delusion and causes all sentient beings everywhere to clearly understand the nature of phenomena.
He is the foremost among the Arhats currently dwelling in the world.)
Jie-huan said: "Kauṇḍinya was the first to receive ordination and served as the leader of the assembly; therefore, he is specifically recorded here.
As for his title 'Puming' (Universal Radiance), a verse states: 'He constantly emits great radiance, revered by all.
It further says: 'He constantly proclaims the unsurpassed path'; thus he is named Puming."
The five hundred arhats were: Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Kālodāyin, Udāyin, Aniruddha, Revata, Kapphiṇa, and Bakula.
Cunda, Śāgata, and the others shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
they will all share the same name, called Samantaprabha.
(Xiangmai said: "Uruvilvā and the others are the foremost arhats listed in the introductory section; they are mentioned here both in detail and in brief.
They share the same name 'Universal Radiance' because their virtues are identical.")
The *Jièhuán* (Circlet of Precepts) states: "Possessing the fullness of five hundred majestic virtues, he was the preeminent figure among the twelve hundred [disciples].

Therefore, he is recorded separately. At the end of the *Mùliánjì* (Record of Maudgalyāyana), it says: "Among my disciples, those who possess full majestic virtue number five hundred; this refers precisely to him."
As for the remaining seven hundred members of the assembly, they were only granted general permission and received general predictions in verse.
At that time, the five hundred arhats, having received their predictions before the Buddha, were filled with joy and exultation.
They immediately rose from their seats, approached the Buddha, and, repenting and reproaching themselves, said: "World-Honored One, we have always harbored this thought, considering ourselves..."
We have already attained ultimate nirvana, yet only now do we realize it, like those who lack wisdom. Why is this?
It is because although we ought to attain the wisdom of a Tathāgata, we instead considered ourselves satisfied with our own meager wisdom.
Jie-huan said: "To repent and reproach oneself means to regret past failures and rejoice in present attainments. The Tathāgata’s wisdom is the knowledge of all modes;
we ought to have attained it, yet we regret not having awakened to it sooner."
“World-Honored One, it is as if there were a man who went to the house of a close friend and lay down after becoming intoxicated with wine.

At that time, the friend had business to attend to at the government office; he tied a priceless jewel into the lining of the man’s garment and gave it to him before departing. The man, lying drunk, was entirely unaware of this.
Having risen, he wandered on until he reached another country, where for the sake of food and clothing, he sought and labored with great effort.”
It is a great hardship. If one obtains even a little, one considers it sufficient.
(Xing said, "Those who discard their supreme treasure and busily seek it abroad are found everywhere throughout the world.")
Is this not also deeply pitiable? (The parable of Liezi’s fondness for forgetting is similar to this).
Jie Huan said: "A close friend tying a jewel [around one's neck] is like the Buddha preaching the Lotus Sūtra when he was among the sixteen bodhisattvas."
This concludes the causes for the Mahāyāna. "Drunk with wine and lying down" is a metaphor for the time when I [the Buddha] was amidst thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings;

they all gave rise to doubt and confusion, as if in a state of drunken stupor. "Official business to be attended to" refers to the fact that the Buddha’s transformation of beings is nearing its end, yet he continues to benefit living beings in other places;

because his actions are impartial and without partiality, it is likened to official business. "Having risen and wandered about" means that their delusion has further increased. "Arriving at another place" [refers to...]
To abandon one’s homeland is to forsake the fundamental. To pursue such things as food and clothing is to delight in the trivial.
Later, when his kinsmen and friends encountered him by chance, they spoke these words: "Alas, O man! Why have you come to such a state for the sake of food and clothing?
In years past, I wished for you to attain peace and happiness, allowing you to indulge freely in the five desires on such-and-such a day."
"Son, I tied a priceless jewel inside your garment when you were born; it remains there even now, yet you did not know of it.
