You have been laboring in toil and distress to provide for your livelihood, which is truly foolish. You may now trade this jewel for whatever you require."
May you always have your wishes fulfilled and lack nothing.
(The *Jiehuan* says: "Meeting with close friends" is like now encountering the Buddha again; "reproaching and warning" is like scolding those who advance slightly toward the Great [Vehicle].
The term 'noble man' (*zhàngfū*) refers to those of the Mahāyāna lineage, and serves to exhort them forward. The remaining meaning is as follows in the subsequent correspondence.)

"Manifesting what is required for trade is a metaphor for the unfolding of one's inherent nature; thus, one shall obtain great benefit. To transport goods according to the seasonal changes of objects is called 'trade' (mào);
to exchange that which one has for that which one lacks is called 'exchange' (yì)."
The Buddha is also like this. When he was a bodhisattva, he taught and transformed us, causing us to give rise to the mind of omniscience;

yet we soon forgot it, neither knowing nor perceiving it. Once we had attained the path of an arhat, we considered ourselves to have reached nirvana, and thus the means of our livelihood became difficult to obtain.
To be content with what one has attained little of; yet the vow for omniscience remains undiminished. (Master Jiehuan said:
"This causes one to give rise to the mind of wisdom, yet to neglect and forget it without realizing it, like being intoxicated while sleeping with a jewel tied to one's garment.

Although one has attained the rank of Arhat, one is not yet free from the fetters of the Dharma; this is the hardship of sustaining one's life. That the vow for wisdom is not lost is like the jewel within one's clothing.")
Now, at this time, the World-Honored One has awakened us by speaking these words: "O bhikṣus, that which you have attained is not ultimate extinction.
For a long time I have caused you to plant roots of merit for Buddhahood; it was only through skillful means that I manifested the appearance of nirvana."
Yet you thought that you had truly attained *nirvāṇa*. [Śīharatna said: "...
"World-Honored One, it is only now that I know I am truly a bodhisattva, one who has received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
He made a record of this. For these reasons, he was filled with great joy, having attained what he had never experienced before.
(Jiehuan remarked: "This is equivalent to obtaining a precious wish-fulfilling gem.")
Chapter Nine: Bestowing Predictions upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training.

This chapter records the minor assembly of disciples. Those who investigate the truth and sever delusions are called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*); those who have exhausted the truth and eliminated all delusions are called "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).

That these individuals, though not yet having attained the state of *aśaikṣa*, were nonetheless predicted by the Buddha to attain Buddhahood, is because there is no one who hears the Dharma and does not become a Buddha.
At that time, Ānanda and Rāhula had this thought: "We have often reflected to ourselves that even if we were to receive [the prediction]..."
Recorded. Is this not indeed a joy?
(The Record of the Assembly of Learners states: "He shall serve and exhaustively honor Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust and protect the treasury of the Dharma;
thus his virtue will equal that of Ānanda and Rāhula, and for this reason, he is subsumed under these two masters.")
Jiehuan said: "Ānanda was of vast learning and upheld the treasury of the Dharma; Rāhula practiced in secret.

Both were great disciples, yet they were recorded as receiving the prediction together with the assembly of students. This was to show that they too belonged to the class of those who maintain secret practice while appearing outwardly otherwise."
They immediately rose from their seats and addressed the Buddha together, saying: "World-Honored One, we too should have a share in this;
the Tathāgata alone is our refuge. Furthermore, we are well-known and recognized by all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
Ānanda has constantly served as our attendant and protects and upholds the treasury of the Dharma. Rāhula is the son of the Buddha."
If the Buddha were to see me and bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, my own vows would be fulfilled and the hopes of the multitude satisfied.
(And it is said: "Because Bodhisattvas penetrate the Buddha-way, there is nothing they do not manifest; therefore, in the 'Chapter on the Buddha-way' of the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra...")
Taking the joy of the Dharma as his wife, compassion as his daughter, and sincerity and goodness as his son—Śākyamuni’s having an illegitimate son, Rāhula, was entirely for the sake of manifestation;
it was not like the wives and children of the mundane world.

Jie-huan said: "Ānanda and Rāhula were in close attendance upon the Buddha; since they are already known and seen by the assembly, if they do not receive their predictions, it would fail to satisfy the expectations of the multitude."

At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood, with the title Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Śāntarājāgrya, Sāgarabuddhi-vaiśāradya-vaśitā-abhijñā-rāja."
O Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, you shall make offerings to sixty-two billion Buddhas and uphold the treasury of the Dharma;
thereafter, you will attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
(Xiangmai said: "Regarding the King of Sovereign Wisdom and Supernatural Powers of the Mountains and Seas: there is nothing higher than the mountains, and nothing deeper than the seas.
Jiehuan said: "Ānanda has long maintained the treasury of the Dharma; his extensive learning and broad erudition are equal to his wisdom. Regarding all [matters]...
Within the Dharma, he attained great penetration and mastery like a king; thus, he received his name based on the cause for his fruit.
He shall serve many Buddhas and protect the treasury of the Dharma, after which he will attain Buddhahood—this is indeed his original vow.
He taught and transformed twenty quadrillion *koṭis* of *ganges*-sands of bodhisattvas, causing them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
His land was named Constantly Erected Victorious Banner; that realm was pure, with lapis lazuli for its ground, and it was filled with the pervasive sound of wondrous music.

(And the South said: "Ānanda, you shall succeed in the future. That there are so many such as this is because you have long upheld the Dharma-treasury and your conditions for transformation are profound.")
Jie-huan said: "The banner symbolizes the virtue of supreme excellence. Because Ānanda was foremost in extensive learning, the country was named 'Constantly Erecting the Supreme Banner.
Because he proclaimed the treasury of the Dharma, it was subsequently named 'The Wondrous Sound Pervading Everywhere,' due to the widespread circulation of the sound of the Dharma."
The lifespan of that Buddha shall be immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
even if one were to calculate and reckon for thousands of myriads of koṭis of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, it could not be known.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world twice as long as his lifespan, and the Semblance Dharma shall remain in the world twice as long as the True Dharma.
(Questioning the doctrine of kalpas of lifespan, it remains profound and inexhaustible, with nothing upon which to rely. Nanzi said: "The birth and death of the myriad things continue without end;
does the preservation of their lifespan ever reach its limit? The succession of antiquity and the present has never known a boundary; do the kalpas ever reach their end?
Since the Sage transcends birth and death and the Ultimate Way is without succession, then even if the kalpas were to double and double again..."
This is not yet sufficient to exhaust its spiritual longevity.

The *Jiuhuan* says: "The Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable kalpas, and the periods of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) are each doubled in succession because the power of the propagation of the Dharma-treasury is far-reaching.
○ Xing Jianzi’s Supplemental Note says: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa..."

After the [Buddha’s] passing, the bequeathed Dharma consists of three periods: the True Dharma (saddharma), the Semblance Dharma (pratirūpakadharma), and the Final Dharma (paścimadharma). The True Dharma lasts for five hundred years;
the Semblance Dharma lasts for two thousand years; and the Final Dharma lasts for two thousand years.
Ānanda, this Buddha, King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Ocean-like Wisdom, is praised together by immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas,
Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, who extol his meritorious virtues.
(Śīlamegha said: "Because he has protected and upheld the treasury of the Dharma, he has obtained such a preeminent reward that his fame reaches throughout the ten directions.
At that time, eight thousand bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds within the assembly all had this thought:
"We have not even heard that the great bodhisattvas receive such predictions. By what causes and conditions do these śrāvakas receive such [predictions]?"
Resolution.
[Jie-huan said: "The facts regarding Ānanda’s posthumous title, his realm, his teachings, his transformations, and his accomplishments are particularly distinct from the general records.
Since those with initial resolve do not know the remote causes, they wonder by what conditions he attained these things."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, addressed them, saying:
"O sons of good family, Ānanda and I simultaneously resolved our minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the presence of the Buddha Śūnyarāja.
Ānanda always delighted in much hearing (*bahuśruta*), whereas I always applied myself with diligent vigor (*vīrya*). For this reason, I have already attained [enlightenment]."
Regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi: Ānanda shall protect and uphold my Dharma, and likewise protect the Dharma-treasury of all future Buddhas;
he shall teach and bring to maturity the assembly of Bodhisattvas. Because his original vow was such, he has received this prediction.

(Jiehuan said: "This tells of his distant cause; because he resolved his mind for enlightenment together with the Buddha, his merit was profound and his vows were vast, it was fitting that he receive this prediction.
The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states that the Buddha Śūnyarāja was the Buddha whom Śākyamuni encountered during the middle of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. )
Furthermore, Nan said: "If one examines their distant causes, their merit is already equal to that of the Buddha.

However, because Ānanda vowed to protect and uphold the Dharma-treasury, he always delighted in extensive learning; whereas the Buddha vowed to attain the Way to benefit sentient beings, he was always diligent and energetic.
Consequently, while the Buddha has already attained the Way, Ānanda must still protect the Dharma and teach others before he can become a Buddha. This is indeed his original [vow]."
"May it be so! It is not due to the superiority or inferiority of their faculties or wisdom that there is a sequence of priority and posteriority.
Ānanda, having personally heard before the Buddha his own prediction of enlightenment as well as the adornments of his buddha-field, his aspirations were fully realized;
his heart was filled with great joy at such an unprecedented experience. He immediately recollected the immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas of the past.
The Dharma-treasury is thoroughly understood without obstruction, just as it is heard now; one also recognizes one’s original vows.

(Jiehuan says: "Immediately recollecting" and so forth means that because the Buddha granted him a prediction and further recounted his past causes, he attained the Samādhi of Sovereign Awareness of the Dharma-nature, whereby he was able to recollect the Dharma-treasuries of past Buddhas and recognize his own original vows from long ago, upholding them.)
[This is] the cause).
At that time, the Buddha addressed Rāhula: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood.
Your name shall be Tāp-saptaratnapuṣpa (Treading upon the Seven-Jeweled Flower) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi."
O Noble One, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, you shall make offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten worlds,
and you shall always be the eldest son of those Buddhas, just as you are now.
(Xiang Mai said: "The propagation of the Way takes virtuous conduct as its priority; thus, among the four categories of the Confucian gate, virtuous conduct is also ranked first.
Yuan Nanyue said: "He concealed the traces of his great power and manifested as a son of the Buddha;
his meritorious virtues are beyond counting, and only a Buddha can know them. This is what is called 'secret practice' [guhyacaryā])."
The Precept Ring states: "Treading upon the seven-jeweled lotus flowers is the response to the wondrous, pure, and secret practices.

To act as the eldest son is to perpetually continue the Buddha-way through secret practices. Just as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* takes Samantabhadra as its eldest son, this also symbolizes that great practice is able to establish the dharma of the Buddha-family."

The adornments of the land, the duration of the lifespan, the disciples he transforms, and the periods of the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma of this Buddha Padmottara (Isaodao Qibao Hua) will be no different from those of the Tathāgata Śikhin (Shanhai Hui Zizai Tongwang).
Furthermore, you shall become his eldest son. After this period has passed, you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

(Jie-huan said: "Because extensive learning and secret practice constantly support one another, Rāhula attained the fruits of the *kalpa* of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma just as Ānanda did;
furthermore, in the future, he shall also be the eldest son of Ānanda.")

At that time, the World-Honored One saw that two thousand individuals—both those still in training and those beyond training—were gentle in mind, tranquil and pure, and gazing at the Buddha with single-minded devotion.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Do you see these two thousand individuals, both those in training and those beyond training? "Indeed, I see them," [Ānanda replied].
"Ānanda, these people shall make offerings to as many Buddhas and Tathāgatas as there are atoms in fifty worlds."

Come! With reverence and respect, you shall protect and uphold the treasury of the Dharma. At the end of time, simultaneously, you shall each attain Buddhahood in lands throughout the ten directions, all bearing the same title:
Ratnaketu Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Your lifespan shall be one...
The kalpas, the adornments of the lands, the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, and both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma shall all be identical.
[Jiehuan said: "This person was also transformed by him in the past; therefore, he now receives a prediction. His intention is gentle, meaning his faculties have already matured.
When asked whether he had seen [the Buddha], he silently indicated his past causes. As for Ānanda, though he is widely learned and profoundly erudite, he has long remained silent. ]

[The Buddha] knows that the names of the two thousand fruits are all identical because their causes are identical. Having fully realized the state of both those still training and those beyond training, they immediately realize the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);

this is called the "Precious Mark. Regarding the phrase "a lifespan of one *kalpa*" and below, it means that the two thousand [Buddhas] will simultaneously attain Buddhahood, and their supported rewards (*niśraya-vipāka*) and Dharma-transformations will all be identical.
○ Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Master (Dharmabhāṇaka).

One who is able to uphold the True Dharma and is sufficient to serve as a teacher for others is called a Dharma-Master. This chapter provides a detailed record that encompasses and completes the preceding records;
it is titled "The Chapter on the Dharma-Master" because it extensively documents those who uphold the sutra and thereby extols their excellence.
It is for this reason.
At that time, the World-Honored One, because of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, addressed eighty thousand great beings:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, do you see within this great assembly the immeasurable devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras..."
Naras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—
those seeking the path of the śrāvaka, those seeking the path of the pratyekabuddha, and those seeking the path of the Buddha— all such beings as these,
who before the Buddha hear even a single verse or a single line of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, or even for a single moment rejoice in it; I [shall protect them].
All were granted the prediction that they would attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
(Regarding the phrase "and the Southern Record": this refers to the "Extensive Prediction" (*pratyakṣa-vyākarana*). Xiang Mai states:

"The reason for announcing the Extensive Prediction through the Medicine King Bodhisattva was because the Extensive Prediction is vast and remote, and its Dharma benefits are supreme and wondrous; it is not for those who do not deeply understand their past karmic affinities."...)

"O Great Bodhisattva, this is because it cannot be realized or known by anyone else. The Medicine King is none other than the Bodhisattva Joyful Vision (Ratnaprabhāsa), who long upheld this sutra and burned his body and arms;
one may say he deeply understood his karmic affinity from former lives."
Jie-huan said: "The eighty thousand great beings are precisely the eighty thousand bodhisattvas at the beginning of the sutra;

those among the eight classes and fourfold assembly present before him who were all granted predictions of enlightenment—this refers to the saying that 'if there are any who hear the Dharma, not one shall fail to become a Buddha.'"
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja: "Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa,

if there should be anyone who hears even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and rejoices in it for even a single moment of thought, I likewise grant them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

(And the Southern Record states: "This is the Extensive Record of Future Generations. When it says that after his parinirvāṇa there will be certain persons, it means that although the conditions for them have not yet manifested, he has nonetheless prophesied them from afar.
Thus, this 'Extensive Record' is perfectly complete and encompasses everything without exception.")
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if someone should ask, "What kind of sentient beings will attain Buddhahood in future ages?
you should show them that these people will certainly attain Buddhahood in future ages. Why is this?
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding even a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra, receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes it in various ways...

One who makes offerings of sutra scrolls, flowers, incense, garlands, powdered incense, ointment incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and music, and who joins their palms in reverent worship—such a person is one whom all the worlds should look up to and honor;
they should be honored with the same offerings as the Tathāgata. You should know that this person is a great Bodhisattva who has accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having attained *samyaksambodhi*, out of compassion for sentient beings, you vowed to be born in this world to extensively expound and analyze the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
How much more so, then, for those who are able to fully receive, uphold, and provide various offerings to it?

(Jiehuan said: "This causes Medicine King to proclaim the manifest supreme cause. (Jiehuan said: "The preceding [passage] clarifies that because the conditions are supreme and the person is honored, one shall become a Buddha.
Yet, if one can possess the merit of the six kinds of Dharma-teachers within even a single phrase, it is already sufficient to be highly esteemed, venerated, and honored, and one shall attain Bodhi;
how much more so if one is able to receive and uphold an entire sutra—then its [merit]..."
The more excellent the conditions, the more honorable the person; such a one will certainly become a Buddha.

O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such a person, having voluntarily relinquished their own pure karmic retribution, will—out of compassion for sentient beings—be born into a degenerate age after my parinirvāṇa to extensively expound this sutra.
[The Precept Ring said: "Those who have relinquished their pure retribution must be people who have attained the fruit of the Pure Land and manifest birth in this evil world.

"If, after my parinirvāṇa, any good man or good woman can secretly preach even a single phrase of the Lotus Sūtra for the sake of a single person, you should know that such a person is an envoy of the Tathāgata, one dispatched by the Tathāgata, performing the work of the Tathāgata."
How much more so when one expounds it extensively for others amidst the great assembly.
(Jiehuan says: To cause those who are about to depart this life to entrust [the teaching] to another carries the sense of a solemn commission;
thus, those who reverently uphold the sutra should be regarded as having been entrusted with their very lives by the Tathāgata. It is fitting that they be honored for extolling this great matter.)
Bhaiṣajyarāja, this sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others.
It is protected by the World-Honored Buddhas and has never been openly proclaimed since the past.
Even while the Tathāgata is currently present, there are still many who harbor resentment and jealousy toward this sutra, let alone after his parinirvāṇa.

Jiehuan said: "The essential points of the secret Dharma—if bestowed upon those who are arrogant, they will withdraw from their seats; if explained openly, the impoverished son will fear his father, and resentment, slander, and jealousy will arise.
If this was so even while the Tathāgata was present in the world, how much more so in the degenerate age after his parinirvāṇa?
One must not fail to discern the capacity of the recipient."

Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, whoever is able to write down, uphold, read, recite, and make offerings to [this sūtra], and explains it to others—the Tathāgata shall cover them with his robe.
Furthermore, they will be protected and remembered by the Buddhas currently residing in other directions.
Such a person possesses the power of great faith, the power of aspiration, and the power of all roots of goodness. You should know that this person is equal to...
When the Tathāgata dwells with them, he will personally stroke their crowns with his hand.
(He further said: "This sutra is difficult to hear; it is likewise difficult to believe, accept, uphold, and maintain.
Therefore, none can transcribe, uphold, read, or explain it unless they are protected by the Tathāgata and possess their own faith, aspiration, and roots of goodness.")
The Precept Ring said: "To be covered by the Tathāgata’s robe means to have attained the power of the Buddha’s patience.
To dwell together with the Tathāgata means to settle one's mind in accord with the Buddha. To have the Tathāgata rub the crown of one’s head means to receive the Buddha’s consolation.
Because of this, one will be able to uphold and expound this Dharma in the evil world of the future."

Bhaiṣajyarāja, wherever this may be—whether it be spoken, read, recited, written, or wherever a scroll of this sūtra may reside—one should erect a stupa made of the seven precious substances, making it exceedingly high, wide, and magnificently adorned. It is unnecessary to enshrine relics therein. Why is this?
Because within this very place resides the entire body of the Tathāgata.
(Jie-huan said: "These three cycles of exposition and all other auxiliary manifestations are none other than the Tathāgata’s entire body.
This stūpa should be honored, revered, respected, and praised with all manner of flowers, incense, necklaces, silk canopies, banners, pennants, music, and hymns.
If anyone should behold this stūpa, prostrate before it, and make offerings, one should know that...
All such [beings] are close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
(Jiehuan says: Those who attain Buddhahood through making offerings do so because their primary cause is correct and their conditions are superior.)
Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many people, both householders and renunciants, who practice the bodhisattva path;
yet if they are unable to see, hear, read, recite, copy, uphold, or make offerings to this Lotus Sūtra, you should know that these persons have not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path.
If there are those who hear this sutra, they will then be able to practice the bodhisattva path well.
(Jiehuan says: To practice the bodhisattva path without hearing this sutra is like wishing to quench one's thirst while not knowing that water is required.)
If there are sentient beings who seek the path of the Buddha, and they either see or hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and having heard it,
believe, understand, accept, and uphold it— then you should know that such persons have drawn near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
(Jie-huan said: "This is like a person digging a well who has already drawn near to the source of the spring.
Medicine King, it is as if there were a person, parched with thirst and in need of water, who dug into a high plateau in search of it.
Seeing only dry earth, he knew the water was still far off; yet, without ceasing his exertion, he saw moist soil appear, and eventually reached the mud. His mind—
One knows with certainty that water must be near.
(Furthermore, it is said: "If one gradually reaches mud, then one is already close to water. If one can transcendently reach its true source, [one attains liberation].)
Then the wondrous clarity will manifest perfectly and spontaneously, without the need for effort; compared to what was previously practiced, all such efforts appear as turbid dregs.

That the sutras do not speak of this is what is meant by "drawing the bowstring without releasing the arrow," causing one to advance on one's own. Indeed, in the state of non-effort (*anābhoga*), there is no room for verbal discourse.
Jie-huan said: "Digging for water on high ground is like cultivating the Bodhisattva path. If one does not grasp its essential method, it is like seeing only dry soil;
yet if one exerts effort without ceasing, it is like progressing gradually from the Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi).

As one continues to see moist soil, this is a metaphor for having successively heard the Prajñāpāramitā and thus gradually reaching the mud, which symbolizes first hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. However, as long as one still lags behind in cultivation, then—"
Regarding the water of the Buddha’s wisdom, one merely draws near to it.

It is the same for a bodhisattva: if one has not yet heard, understood, or been able to practice this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should know that such a person is still far from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. However, if they do hear, understand, and contemplate it...
If one practices it, one will certainly know that one is drawing near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Because all the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all bodhisattvas is contained within this sutra.
(Jiehuan said: "Buddhahood and Bodhi both belong to this sutra; if one has neither heard nor understood it, how can one attain the Way?
This sutra opens the gate of expedient means and reveals the mark of reality. The Dharma-treasury of the Lotus Sutra is profound, firm, remote, and deep, such that no one could reach it;
now the Buddha teaches and transforms beings to bring bodhisattvas to fulfillment, and thus reveals it for them.
(Nan said: "Opening the gate of expedient means is like digging a well; revealing the true reality is like seeing the water. Jiehuan said:
"The Dharma-treasury of the Lotus Sutra is the Tathāgatagarbha of sentient beings. Within sentient beings, it is hidden amidst worldly afflictions;
within Bodhisattvas, it is hidden within the myriad practices; and at the place of treasure, it lies beyond the five hundred [yojanas]."
A *yojana* may be described as deep, firm, remote, and far-reaching; no human being is able to reach it. Therefore, it can only be revealed and shown by a Bodhisattva.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there is a Bodhisattva who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, becomes startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that such a person is a newcomer.
If bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, or śrāvakas, hear this sutra and become startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
(Jie Huan says: Those with newly resolved minds, those of small faculties, and those with overweening pride are all not suitable vessels.)

Bhaiṣajyarāja, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, those who wish to preach this Lotus Sūtra for the sake of the fourfold assembly must enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat; only then should they extensively expound this sūtra for the fourfold assembly.
The Tathāgata’s chamber is the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings. The Tathāgata’s robe is gentleness and patience.
The seat of the Tathāgata is the mind of shame. That which is the emptiness of all phenomena is the seat upon which one dwells;
having thus established oneself therein, one should then, with a mind free from indolence, extensively expound this Lotus Sūtra for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
Furthermore, [the Master] said: "Take great compassion as your chamber; take gentleness and patience as your robe; and take the emptiness of all phenomena as your seat.
Resolve your doubts within the intervals of sound and enter into wisdom. This is comparable to digging a well until the spring is reached; only then is it ultimate."
Xiangmai said: "That all phenomena are empty does not mean a void of annihilation; it refers to the state where all phenomena are vast and clearly realized.
Jiehuan said: "In the way of preaching the Dharma and transforming others through teaching, one must first have a firm foundation before being able to bring peace."
A person must first have something they wear before they can subdue others; they must first have something they rely upon before they can reach others.
The Tathāgata takes compassion as his chamber, gentle forbearance as his garment, and the emptiness of phenomena as his seat. He enters the chamber of compassion.
Thus, one has already found a place to dwell. By donning the robe of gentle forbearance, one has already found what to wear.

By sitting upon the seat of the emptiness of dharmas, one has already found a basis to rely upon. In this way, one is fully endowed with the body of a Buddha and may then extensively expound this sutra.
If one has not yet realized this, one lacks a master for rectification; how then can one serve as a guide for others? Therefore it is said: "Abide securely in this."

In the midst [of this], one should then expound this Dharma extensively with tireless diligence. Now, those who occupy the precious flower seat and engage in the practice of both the sacred and the mundane should deeply reflect upon this.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, in other lands I shall dispatch emanated persons to assemble for them a congregation to hear the Dharma;

I shall also dispatch emanated bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to listen to their preaching of the Dharma. These emanated persons will hear it with faith, accept it, follow it, and not oppose it.
If the preacher of the Dharma is in a secluded place, I will at that time extensively dispatch devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas.
The gandharvas, asuras, and others listened to his preaching of the Dharma.
(Jiehuan said: "This is the Buddha’s miraculous transformation to extol this great matter; 'other lands' refers to worlds in other directions.")
Although I am in a foreign land, I shall from time to time enable the preachers of the Dharma to behold my body.
If they should forget or lose any phrases or clauses of this sutra, I will speak them for them once more so that they may be complete.
(Jie-huan said: "To cause them to see [the Buddha] while in a foreign land—this is what is meant by 'manifesting or remaining hidden to transform sentient beings'").
*The Exquisite Commentary and Critical Forest on the Lotus Sutra*, Volume I;
*The Exquisite Commentary and Critical Forest on the Lotus Sutra*, Volume II.
Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa.
The Dharma has been fully prepared through three cycles; the fourfold assembly has received their predictions of enlightenment; the Dharma-body is complete, and the original vows are fulfilled.
Therefore, the Many Treasures Stūpa is manifested to reveal the path of cultivation and realization of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—past, present, and future.
At that time, there was a stupa made of the seven treasures before the Buddha. It was five hundred yojanas high and two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
It emerged from the earth and remained suspended in mid-air. It was adorned with various precious objects, featuring five thousand railings and ten million gabled chambers.
It was further embellished with countless banners and streamers, and hung with precious necklaces and ten thousand jeweled bells.
A hundred million [banners] were suspended above it. From all four sides, the fragrance of *tamālapatra* sandalwood issued forth, pervading the entire world.

Those various banners and canopies were composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, pearl, and ruby—and reached as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
There, the gods rained down *mandārava* flowers as an offering.
The precious stupa was honored, revered, respected, and praised by the remaining hosts of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others— countless thousands of myriads of koṭis— who offered all kinds of flowers,
incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and musical performances.

Jie Huan said: "The precious stupa is preeminent; it is the environmental retribution resulting from [the Buddha's] fruitive practice. The various ornaments manifest the functional virtue of that fruitive practice.
The manifold decorations are the image of the myriad virtues. The five thousand railings represent the power of *dhāraṇī*.
The thousands of millions of chambers correspond to immeasurable compassion. The countless banners and streamers correspond to the subduing of the heterodox and the manifestation of the orthodox."
The hanging jeweled necklaces signify the descent of manifold virtues to transform beings below. The ten billion jeweled bells signify the widespread resonance of the Dharma-sound.

Fragrance emanating from the four sides represents the universal reach of spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) and their omnipresence. The canopies and banners of the seven jewels reaching as high as the celestial palaces represent the supreme majesty of all virtues.
Regarding the thirty-three heavens below, it is said that the various devas make offerings to the stupa because it contains the complete body of the Tathāgata.
At that time, from within the jeweled stupa, a great voice issued forth, exclaiming: "Excellent, excellent!

Śākyamuni, World-Honored One, you are able to teach the Bodhisattva-dharma through the great wisdom of equality, and to proclaim for the great assembly the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which is protected by the Buddhas.
It is so, it is so! Śākyamuni, World-Honored One, all that you have spoken is indeed the truth."
"Indeed.
(Jie-huan said: "The Great Wisdom of Equality is precisely the precious wisdom of the One Vehicle.
At that time, there was a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva named Mahāpratibhāna who addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, by what cause..."
“Because of this, this precious stūpa has emerged from the earth, and within it this sound has been uttered.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāratnakūṭa: “Within this precious stūpa is the entire body of a Tathāgata.
In the past, in the east, beyond immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, there was a land named Ratnaviśuddha. In that place, there was a Buddha named...”
He is named Prabhūtaratna. When that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made this great vow:

"If, after I have attained buddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa, there should be any place in the lands of the ten directions where the Lotus Sūtra is being preached, may my stupa emerge before them for the sake of hearing this sūtra, appearing as a witness to provide testimony."

Jie-huan said: "The entire body of Prabhūtaratna remains undispersed after his parinirvāṇa, as if he had entered a state of meditative concentration; yet he is able to manifest and certify the sutra wherever he wishes.
This demonstrates the sovereign power of the Dharmakāya, which is neither subject to extinction nor birth, enabling those who hear the wondrous Dharma [to attain realization]."
Having realized that there is neither extinction nor birth, he attained sudden enlightenment into the true nature of reality; thus he manifested such a demonstration of realization.
After that Buddha had attained the Way and was approaching his parinirvāṇa, amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"After my parinirvāṇa, those who wish to make offerings to my entire body should erect a single great stūpa."
(Jie-huan says: This narrates the origins of the stūpa.

By the power of his supernatural faculties and vows, wherever in the worlds of the ten directions there may be those who preach the Lotus Sūtra, this precious stūpa shall emerge before them; the entire body of the Buddha remains within the stūpa, not only here.
"O Mahāpratibhāna, because they have heard the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has now emerged from the earth.
(Jie-huan says: This indicates the present circumstances.)
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna, through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we wish to behold this body of the Buddha."

Jiehuan said: "To manifest the realization of perfection, one must appear in the full body; this is no small matter, and thus it is necessary to invoke the supernatural power of the Tathāgata to initiate it."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna: "This Buddha Prabhūtaratna has made a profound and solemn vow:

'When my jeweled stupa emerges before the Buddhas for the sake of hearing the Lotus Sutra, and there are those who wish to show my body to the fourfold assembly, all the emanated bodies of that Buddha who are currently preaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions shall return.'"
Only after they have gathered in one place will my body appear.
(Jiehuan said: "That one must wait until all the Buddhas preaching the Dharma throughout the ten directions have assembled before appearing signifies perfect realization.
These emanated Buddhas are the hundreds of thousands of millions of transformations—like reflections of the moon in water—that respond to sentient beings.")
"Mahāpratibhāna, those Buddhas who are my emanations and who are currently preaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions should now assemble.
(Jie-huan said: "This is likely to fulfill the vow of Prabhūtaratna.")

Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, we also wish to see the Buddhas who are the emanations of the World-Honored One, so that we may pay them homage and make offerings to them.

At that time, the Buddha emitted a single ray of light from the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows, and immediately all the Buddhas in worlds as numerous as the sands of ten million billion nayutas of Ganges Rivers in the eastern direction became visible. In all those lands, the ground was made entirely of crystal.
It was adorned with precious trees and precious garments. Countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas filled its midst.
Precious canopies were spread everywhere, and precious nets covered them above. In that land, the various Buddhas preached all dharmas with great and wondrous voices.
Furthermore, one saw immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas filling all those lands, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
(Jiehuan said: "These are all manifestations of Śākyamuni preaching the Dharma throughout the ten directions.
It is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—wherever the light from the ūrṇā-kośa illuminates.
(The Precept Ring said: "Illuminating the ten directions, summon all to assemble.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of good family, we shall now proceed to the world of Sahā to visit Śākyamuni Buddha and also to make offerings to the precious stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna. At that time, Sahā...
The Sahā world was immediately transformed into purity: its ground became of lapis lazuli, adorned with jeweled trees, and demarcated by golden cords into eight paths.
It was devoid of villages, hamlets, camps, cities, and towns, as well as great oceans, rivers, mountains, streams, forests, and marshes.
Great precious incense was burned, and *mandārava* flowers were strewn everywhere across the ground. Canopies of jeweled nets were spread over it, suspended from above.
[He removed] all the jeweled bells, leaving only those for this assembly, and moved the devas and humans to other lands.
(Jie-huan says: "Transforming the land" means preparing it to accommodate the multitude of emanations. "With lapis lazuli as the ground," etc., manifests the pure characteristics of the Buddha-land;
"without villages," etc., eliminates the defiled conditions of sentient beings. Moving the devas and humans to other [lands]...)
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "A Bodhisattva can seize a great trichiliocosm and hurl it beyond sands of worlds, yet the sentient beings therein neither perceive nor know [this].
At that time, each of the Buddhas, taking a great Bodhisattva as his attendant, arrived at the Sahā world and reached their respective locations.

Beneath the jewel trees—each individual jewel tree being five hundred yojanas high, adorned in succession with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits—there were lion thrones beneath every tree, five yojanas high and likewise embellished with great jewels.
At that time, the Buddhas each sat cross-legged upon these thrones; in this manner, they extended and filled [the space].
Throughout the trichiliocosm, the emanated bodies of Śākyamuni Buddha in a single direction have still not been exhausted.
[Jièhuán says:
"A single direction" refers to the eastern direction. The emanations of Śākyamuni are like a single lamp lighting hundreds of thousands.]
The lamps would truly be inexhaustible, yet because the vessel-world has its limits, even a great trichiliocosm could not contain them.

Therefore, Śākyamuni Buddha, in order to serve as the precursor for all future Buddhas, further transformed two hundred trillion nayutas of lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure.
He then moved the devas and humans from those places and established them in other lands.
The land of those to be converted is likewise made of lapis lazuli and adorned with precious trees.
The trees are five hundred yojanas high, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arranged in successive tiers of adornment. Beneath each tree is a precious lion throne, five yojanas in height.

It was also adorned with great jewels. There were no great oceans, rivers, or mountains such as Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, or Sumeru—the king of all mountains.
The entire area constituted a single buddha-field, where the ground of jewels was level and even, covered above by canopies of interlaced jewels, from which various [ornaments] hung down.
Banners and canopies were displayed; great precious incense was burned, and celestial jewel-flowers were strewn across the ground.
(Furthermore, it was said: "The chamber of Vimalakīrti could broadly accommodate many seats; Śākyamuni’s transformed land is like the palace of the Sovereign Heaven (*Īśvara*).
The multitude who emerged there was as vast as the sands of immeasurable rivers, yet each arrived at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa without hearing of any crowding. And this—")
"It must be that the pure land undergoes three transformations before it can accommodate the emanated bodies; this is merely a case of manifesting the Dharma through specific events.
(Nan says: "Mucilinda" means "stone. (Xiangmai says: "In the *Vimalakīrti*, the inconceivable realm is demonstrated, and thus the chamber of one zhang is made vast enough to contain all.
In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the intent is to lead those of provisional capacity into the ultimate reality, and thus [it proceeds] from a defiled land..."

Yet, as there are three transformations, the fundamental tenets differ; thus, their establishments are not the same. (If one attains the ultimate meaning and returns to the root, how could they be different? Jiehuan said:
"The wondrous realm of the Pure Land is fundamentally shared by both sentient beings and Buddhas; the Dharma-body and its manifested forms leave neither things nor self deficient."

It is solely because the consciousness-mind of sentient beings is self-defiled and self-limiting that the Sage, taking this as his cause, divided his body to constrain them and specifically revealed this teaching to them.
First, the single transformation within Sahā world-system was to extinguish the defiled conditions of sentient beings.

Next, the second transformation throughout the eight directions was to dispel the limitations of the consciousness-mind. Finally, the subsequent transformation throughout the eight directions was to expand [the realization] to encompass the entire Dharma-realm.
This is the true realm. After the three transformations, the emanated bodies have all assembled and the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna appears in its entirety.

This demonstrates that once defiled conditions have been extinguished, obstructive thoughts have been dispelled, and the true realm has been expanded, then the transformation-body of the Dharmakāya manifests right before one.
The perfect interfusion of the one and the many, and mastery over recollection according to one's thought—this alone clarifies the sublime purport of the Great Dharma.
Therefore, on account of these events, I have specifically provided this instruction.
At that time, the Buddhas who were emanations of Śākyamuni in the eastern direction— numbering as many as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Ganges Rivers—
in each of their respective lands where they were preaching the Dharma, all came together and assembled here. At that time,
Śākyamuni Buddha saw that the Buddhas who were his emanations had all arrived and were each seated upon lion thrones.
All heard that the Buddhas had granted their consent to open the precious stūpa together. They immediately rose from their seats and remained suspended in mid-air.
The entire assembly of the fourfold community stood up with palms joined, gazing at the Buddha with single-minded devotion.

Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha opened the door of the seven-jeweled stūpa with his right finger, producing a great sound like that of a massive city gate being flung open after its bolt and lock have been removed.

(Jie-huan said: "This symbolizes the unfolding of development in accordance with the Way. With a single finger raised as a mere illustration, the pivotal gate is suddenly released, and the entire body of the Tathāgata can thus be seen.)
At that time, within the jeweled stupa, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna offered half of his seat to Śākyamuni Buddha and spoke these words:
"Śākyamuni Buddha, please take this seat. Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha entered the stupa and sat upon that half-seat, assuming the full lotus posture.
Jiehuan said: "The wondrous Dharma truly eliminates all distinctions and is perfectly interfused; subject and object are not divided, and past and present are of one accord.
Therefore, the past Prabhūtaratna and the present Śākyamuni sit together upon two seats within the jeweled stupa."
Jie-huan said: "The fact that Prabhūtaratna shares his seat is intended to demonstrate the nature of the triple world:

there is neither birth-and-death nor passing away, neither emerging nor departing; there is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa. It is neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different."
This is the ultimate pinnacle of this sublime Dharma.

Therefore, he has manifested such a realization and, with a great voice, universally proclaimed to the fourfold assembly: "Who among you is able to extensively expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in this Sahā world-system?
Now is the very time; before long, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa. The Buddha wishes to use this sublime Dharma..."
The *Huayan jing* (Avataṃsaka Sūtra) has its entrustment.

(Nan said: "When the teaching and realization are complete, the entrustment takes place at Ling. To say that there is a specific locus for this entrustment means that the propagation of the Dharma's benefits depends upon finding the right person.")
Jie-huan said: "After the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had preached this sutra, he immediately proclaimed his parinirvāṇa amidst the assembly, bestowing predictions and entrustments.
Now that the present Buddha has arrived here, he likewise says that before long he will enter nirvana and that the entrustment rests with others.

It is clear from this that the threefold exposition has reached its conclusion. What follows—revealing the subtle and exhorting to uphold it—is a separate matter. Therefore, although [the Buddha] proclaims..."
The *Mie-jie jing* (Sūtra on the Extinction of Bonds) further contains a later teaching (a general discussion).

The *Jiehuan* (The Ring of Precepts) states: "Initially, within the discourse on the Dharma, he extols the two wisdoms and clarifies the ten suchnesses, fully presenting the wondrous Dharma and revealing the Buddha."
Wisdom and vision. Next, through parables: rejecting the sheep and the deer, and pointing out the white ox.

It clarifies that delusion regarding this leads to falling into the burning house, while awakening to it leads to the attainment of the Buddha-ground. Subsequently, through the discourse on causes and conditions:

revealing the universal wisdom of what was deluded about, showing the distant cause of instruction, destroying the illusory city, and pointing to the treasure place—all for the purpose of opening and demonstrating [the truth], so that one may see it within oneself.
The Buddha-nature is primordial; by seeing this nature, there is none who does not become a Buddha.

Therefore, after their realization, each was granted a prediction of Buddhahood, culminating in the matter of the perfect inclusion and perfect realization. This marks the conclusion of the threefold exposition.
Chapter Twelve: Devadatta.
Devadatta—herein translated as Tiānshòu (Heaven-Bestowed)—was the son of King Droṇodana. He was born through prayers offered to the heavens.
This chapter is titled after his name to clarify what has been bestowed upon him and to manifest the wondrous benefits of the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, as well as the fourfold assembly of devas and humans:

"Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, I sought the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* without ever succumbing to weariness or indolence. During many kalpas, I constantly served as a king, making vows to seek unexcelled bodhi with a mind that never regressed."
(Jie-huan said: "This was likely intended to excel over the world through the Right Path.
Desiring to fulfill the six pāramitās, he diligently practiced giving, his heart free from stinginess regarding elephants, horses, and the seven treasures.
One does not spare kingdom, city, wife, children, slaves, servants, attendants, head, eyes, marrow, brain, body, flesh, hands, or feet, nor does one cherish one's own life or body.
(Jiehuan says: This is intended to lead those who are deluded by greed through right practice.)
Xing Jianzi said: "The six pāramitās are: first, giving; second, ethical discipline; third, patience; fourth, diligence;
fifth, meditative concentration; and sixth, wisdom. They are also called the six perfections."
At that time, the lifespan of the people of the world was immeasurable. For the sake of the Dharma, he renounced his royal throne and entrusted the administration to his crown prince.
He beat the drum to proclaim a decree throughout the four quarters, seeking the Dharma: "Whoever can preach the Mahāyāna for me, I shall serve as their attendant for the rest of my life.
At that time, there was a rishi who came and said to the king, "I possess the Mahāyāna, called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
"If you do not oppose me, I shall preach it for you. Upon hearing the words of the seer, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness;
he immediately followed the seer, providing all that was required—gathering fruit, drawing water, collecting firewood, and preparing food—even using his own body as a seat and bed.
His body and mind were free from weariness. He served [the Buddha] for a thousand years; for the sake of the Dharma, he attended to him with diligent devotion, ensuring that nothing was lacking.
(Jiehuan said: "Because the Way excels the secular, you have thus attained non-action. (Jiehuan said: "This vision encompasses both...")
"Forget the world; follow only the Way. (Jie Huan said: "This is lifelong provision:
to take the body as one's seat demonstrates forgetting the self as the Dharma, free from fatigue—fatigue meaning weariness.")
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The king at that time was none other than myself. The rishi at that time was Devadatta.
It was because of Devadatta as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) that I was enabled to fulfill the six pāramitās."
The [Buddha’s] qualities of compassion, joy, and equanimity; the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; the purple-golden hue; the ten powers;
the four fearlessnesses; the four means of integration; the eighteen unique attributes; the power of the superknowledges; the attainment of perfect enlightenment;
and the vast deliverance of sentient beings—all these were due to the spiritual friend Devadatta. He addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta, in the past..."
After the passing of immeasurable kalpas, he shall attain Buddhahood, to be known as the Tathāgata Devendra,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
His world shall be named Devamārga.
(Nan Yue states: "The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus," and so forth, concludes the causal practice. "He addressed the fourfold assembly," and so forth, records the transmission to Deva.
(Jie Huan states: "As for the one titled 'King of Heaven,' Śākyamuni relied upon him to achieve the Way;
he is thus the Dharma King, the God among Gods.")
At that time, the Buddha Devendra remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, extensively expounding the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the fruit of Arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds on the path of Pratyekabuddha;
and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges resolved their minds on the unsurpassed path, attaining the patience of non-arising and reaching the stage of non-retrogression.
(Śīlaka said: "Record that he shall dwell in the world in the future to benefit those of the three vehicles.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Devendra, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, and his bodily relics shall remain.
A stūpa made of the seven precious gems was erected, sixty yojanas in height and forty yojanas in length and breadth.

All the devas and human beings offered worship and veneration to this wondrous stūpa of the seven jewels with various flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, ointment incense, robes, necklaces, banners, pennants, precious parasols, musical instruments, and songs of praise.
Through this, immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of arhatship. Immeasurable...
Sentient beings awaken as pratyekabuddhas; inconceivable sentient beings resolve their minds on bodhi and reach the stage of non-retrogression.
(Jiehuan says: This refers to the True Dharma after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, which is also accessible to those of the three vehicles.)

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In future ages, if there are those who, regarding the 'Devadatta Chapter' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, give rise to a pure heart of faith and reverence without harboring doubt, they shall be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions. In whatever place they are born, they will always hear this sūtra.
If they are born among humans or devas, they will experience supreme and wondrous bliss. If they are before a Buddha, they will be born by transformation upon a lotus flower."

(Furthermore, the preceding section clarifies the causal conditions for Śākyamuni Buddha’s attainment of Buddhahood, while the following section clarifies the dragon girl’s attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood;
both manifest the wondrous benefits of the One Vehicle.)
Jie-huan said: "This chapter clarifies how Śākyamuni sought the Dharma through his causal practices and thereby attained Buddhahood.
Thus, those who hear it will develop pure faith and be free from doubt; this enables them to distance themselves from evil realms and be born into the family of the Buddhas."

At that time, the bodhisattva named Zhijī (Jñānakośa), who had come from the world-system below with the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna, addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, saying, "I shall now return to my own land.
Śākyamuni Buddha said to Jñānakośa, "Good son, wait but a moment."
"There is a bodhisattva here named Mañjuśrī with whom you may meet; he will discourse on the sublime Dharma. You may now return to your own land.
At that time, Mañjuśrī sat upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel, together with the bodhisattvas who had come with him.
Sitting upon a precious lotus flower, he emerged spontaneously from the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King in the great ocean. Remaining suspended in mid-air, he proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain.

Descending from the lotus, he arrived at the place where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones, and having completed his respectful salutations, went to the place of Prajñākūṭa.
They exchanged greetings and polite inquiries, after which he withdrew to sit to one side.
(The matter of the realization was concluded. Thereupon, he announced his departure and initiated the subsequent conditions.

Jiehuan said: "At the beginning of this assembly, Mañjuśrī was present; now, he has again emerged from the ocean. This is because the essence of wisdom is all-pervasive, manifesting before us throughout the ten directions like an echo responding to a sound, without the characteristics of coming or going.
It merely manifests the Dharma according to the capacities of beings. Now, it has manifested that which was transformed within the Dragon Palace."
[This was done] for this reason; thus he manifested as emerging from the ocean).
The Bodhisattva Zhijie asked Mañjuśrī: "Virtuous One, how many sentient beings did you transform while in the Dragon Palace?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Their number is immeasurable, beyond calculation, not to be proclaimed by words, nor conceived by the mind."

"What you have measured, wait but a moment and you shall know for yourself. Before he had finished speaking, countless bodhisattvas emerged from the sea, seated upon precious lotus flowers, and proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain, where they remained suspended in the air.
All these bodhisattvas were those who had been transformed and delivered by Mañjuśrī; they were fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva and were all together discussing the six pāramitās.
Those who were originally śrāvakas were in the midst of the void expounding the practices of the śrāvakas; now they all practice the meaning of emptiness of the Mahāyāna.
Mañjuśrī said to Jñatikūṭa: "The manner in which he teaches and transforms beings in the ocean is such as this."
[The Jie-huan says: "This Mañjuśrī was in the Dragon Palace, which is not a dwelling for humans; thus, the sentient beings he transformed were all of the dragon class.

Yet, upon hearing the wondrous Dharma just once, they immediately became Bodhisattvas. This is sufficient proof that all sentient beings are without exception endowed with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
they simply lack awakening. As for the statement regarding those who were originally Śrāvakas and so forth, it clarifies that the capacities of those to be transformed were likewise [limited]."
[They] possess the three vehicles, yet [by means of] inference they enter into reality.
Mañjuśrī said: "In the midst of the ocean, I have always preached only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*."
(Jie-huan said: "This answers the preceding verse.
Zhijī asked Mañjuśrī, saying: "This sutra is exceedingly profound and subtle; it is a treasure among all sutras, rare in the world.
Are there perhaps sentient beings who, by applying themselves with diligent vigor, practice this sutra and quickly attain Buddhahood? Mañjuśrī—
Mañjuśrī said, "There is the daughter of the Dragon King Sāgara, who is only eight years of age. She possesses sharp faculties and wisdom;

she well understands the faculties, karmas, and activities of all sentient beings. She has attained dhāraṇīs and is able to receive and uphold all the profound secret treasuries spoken by the Buddhas.
She has deeply entered meditative concentration and thoroughly comprehends all phenomena. In a single kṣaṇa, she has resolved her mind upon Bodhi and attained [it]."
They do not regress; their eloquence is unimpeded; they regard all sentient beings with compassion as if they were their own infants; they are fully endowed with merit;

what they contemplate in mind they express in speech, which is subtle, wondrous, and vast; they are compassionate, kind, and yielding; their will is harmonious and refined; and they are able to reach Bodhi.
Jiehuan said: "This scripture teaches that by practicing it, one may swiftly attain the realization of Buddhahood.

Although there are countless bodhisattvas in the Dragon Palace, all of whom were transformed and delivered by Mañjuśrī, the text specifically mentions the eight-year-old dragon girl attaining Buddhahood to clarify that the Buddha-nature does not depend on whether one is male or female, nor on being aged or mature, nor does it exclude different species;
it depends solely on the sharpness of one's faculties and wisdom, and the depth of one's cultivation."
If one turns the light back in a single instant, then Bodhi can be attained; this also breaks the long fetters of the Three Vehicles and advances beyond their lingering stagnation.
Bodhisattva Zhijie said: "I have seen Śākyamuni Tathāgata, throughout immeasurable kalpas, performing difficult practices and ascetic austerities."
Accumulating merit and virtue, he sought the path to Bodhi without ever ceasing.
He observed the trichiliocosm and found that there was not even a space the size of a mustard seed where he had not sacrificed his body and life for the sake of sentient beings;
only after this did he attain the path to Bodhi. One cannot believe that this woman could have attained perfect enlightenment in a mere instant.
(Jie-huan remarked: "This clings to the traces of the Separate Teaching and doubts the principle of the Perfect and Sudden.
Before he had finished speaking, the Dragon Girl suddenly appeared before them. Then Śāriputra addressed the Dragon Girl, saying:
"You claim that you will attain the unsurpassed path before long; this matter is difficult to believe. Why is this? The female body is defiled and impure; it is not a vessel for the Dharma.
How could one obtain unsurpassed bodhi? The Buddha-way is vast and remote, requiring immeasurable kalpas."
One must diligently accumulate practices and fully cultivate all the perfections before finally achieving success. Furthermore, the female body is subject to five obstacles:
first, one cannot become a Brahmā King; second, Śakra; third, a Māra King;
fourth, a Cakravartin Sage-King; and fifth, the body of a Buddha. How, then, can a woman’s body quickly attain Buddhahood?
[The Precept-Ring said: "Śāriputra’s analysis of the difficulty based on the traces of the Hīnayāna teachings was intended to resolve doubts for those of limited wisdom;
thus, his statements that 'the Buddha-way is vast and remote' and 'the female body has many obstacles' are all traces of the Hīnayāna.
[He cites] Brahmā’s pure conduct, Śakra’s few desires, Māra’s firmness, the Cakravartin’s great benevolence, and the Buddha’s possession of myriad virtues, yet notes that women have much defilement."
They are full of desire, weak-willed, and envious; being possessed of such afflictions, they act in opposition to the aforementioned qualities, and thus bring about the five obstacles).
At that time, the dragon girl had a precious jewel worth as much as a trichiliocosm, which she took and offered to the Buddha.
The Buddha accepted it immediately. The dragon girl said to the Bodhisattva Zhijī (Jñānākūṭa) and the Venerable Śāriputra, "I offered this precious jewel and the World-Honored One accepted it;
was this matter not swift? They replied, "It was exceedingly swift. The girl said, "By means of your supernatural powers, observe me as I attain Buddhahood;
it shall be even swifter than this. At that moment, the entire assembly saw the dragon girl suddenly transform—
Having become a man and perfected the practices of a bodhisattva, he immediately proceeded to the stainless world in the southern direction.

There, seated upon a precious lotus flower, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. For the sake of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, he extensively expounded the sublime Dharma.
Furthermore, Nan said: "The Sūtra states that the Dharma-nature is like a great ocean; it does not speak of right or wrong. Whether ordinary person or sage, all are equal without high or low.
It depends solely on the extinction of mental defilements; to realize the fruit is as easy as turning over one's palm.
This is why the Dragon Girl, upon merely relinquishing attachment to the Dharma, immediately and swiftly attained Buddhahood."
The Precept Ring said: "The pearl symbolizes the wondrously perfect true mind. To offer it to the Buddha represents the relinquishing of attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
When attachment to dharmas no longer exists, the wondrous mind is free from defilement. There is nothing more swift than this for the essential path to Buddhahood;
therefore, one immediately proceeds to the Southern World of No Defilement (*Vimalā*) to attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment."
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa, Śāriputra, and the entire assembly accepted this in silence with faith.
(Ji Huan remarked: "The wondrous Dharma is so manifest; who would not believe it?")
Chapter Thirteen: On Upholding.
Regarding "upholding," because the preceding entrustment has manifested the contemplation, the assembly vows to uphold and expound it in order to broaden the transformation through the Way.
First, Bhaiṣajyarāja and others vow to uphold it in this world; next, the assembly of Śrāvakas vows to uphold it in other worlds; finally, the great Bodhisattvas...
"Sa. May the ten directions uphold it.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna, together with a retinue of twenty thousand bodhisattvas, all made this vow before the Buddha: "We only pray, World-Honored One, do not..."
"We shall, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, uphold, recite, and expound this sutra. (Jiehuan says:
This passage at the end of the "Chapter on the White Jewel Stupa" clearly reveals the difficulty of encouraging its preservation;
therefore, Bhaiṣajyarāja and the others exerted the power of their great vows, undaunted by such hardship, and expressed their wish that the Buddha need have no concern.)

In the evil world of the future, sentient beings will have even fewer roots of goodness; they will mostly be full of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), coveting profit and offerings, and increasing their unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
Thus, they will remain far removed from liberation and will be difficult to teach and transform.

Nevertheless, we shall arouse the power of great patience (*mahākṣānti*) to read and recite this sutra, uphold it, explain it, copy it, and provide all manner of offerings, not begrudging even our own bodies or lives.
(Nan-yueh further stated: "This refers to the meaning of the parable of entering the kalpa-conflagration and reaching Mount Sumeru, which expresses the intent of making a vow.

Jing-huan said: "Though the evils and violence of the末法 (mofa) age may be like the kalpa-conflagration, and though the arrogance of those with superior pride may be as high as Mount Sumeru—making them difficult to transform—I vow not to avoid anything;
therefore it is said: 'One should give rise to great patience and not begrudge one's own body.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One gazed upon eighty trillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from this world and other worlds—
looking back with the blue lotus gaze because his vision was not limited or restricted to any single direction, but intended to encompass the ten directions.
Śīhaka said: "Eighty million billion is the number of the assembly gathered from one direction.
These bodhisattvas are all *avaivartika*, turning the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma and having attained various *dhāraṇīs*."
They immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, and had this thought:

"If the World-Honored One were to command us to uphold and preach this sutra, we would propagate this Dharma extensively in accordance with the Buddha's teaching. They further thought: "The Buddha now remains silent and does not issue a command;
what should we do? At that time, the bodhisattvas, wishing to respect and comply with the Buddha’s intention while also fulfilling their own aspirations, [remained there].
Having made this original vow, they then uttered a lion’s roar before the Buddha and made this solemn declaration:

"World-Honored One, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we shall travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions, enabling sentient beings to copy, uphold, read, recite, explain the meaning of,
and practice according to the Dharma while maintaining right mindfulness of this sutra— all of which is through the majestic power of the Buddha."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, while remaining in another realm, will behold us from afar and protect us.
(Jiehuan said: "If even this single Sahā world is so fearful and plagued by evil, then the ten directions must indeed be difficult;
therefore, I ascribe this merit to the Buddha's power and further seek his added protection.")
Chapter Fourteen: On Peaceful and Joyful Conduct.
The myriad practices depend upon the three karmas; they are rooted in wisdom and compassion. If one desires in general not to lose their correctness, then there will be peace and joy.
If they are incorrect, then there will be peril and sorrow. Therefore, one relies upon Mañjuśrī’s correct wisdom, correct body, correct mind, and great compassion.
The Four Dharmas, titled "The Chapter on Peaceful Conduct.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these bodhisattvas are truly rare;
out of reverence and compliance with the Buddha, they have made great vows to protect [the Dharma] in the evil world of the future."
To uphold, read, and preach this Lotus Sūtra— World-Honored One, how can a bodhisattva-mahāsattva preach this sūtra in the evil world of the future?
(And as for the phrase "with Mañjuśrī’s request," it shows that one relies on correct wisdom to initiate correct practice.)
Jie-huan said: "I ask: how must one practice in order to be able to preach this sutra and encounter no difficulties?
This is the teaching on the Dharma of the Practice of Peaceful Conduct."
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to expound this sutra in the future evil age, they should abide securely in four dharmas."
(To follow the three karmas with great compassion: once the three karmas are correct, right wisdom will be truly pure.

Having attained one's own benefit, one must give rise to great compassion and extensively practice altruism. Only when wisdom and compassion support each other can one expound this sutra and be free from all obstacles.)
The Precept Ring states: "These are the four practices of peaceful dwelling: first, right conduct of body; second, right conduct of speech; third, right conduct of mind;
and fourth, the practice of great compassion."
First, one dwells securely in the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice (*caryā-vihāra*) and sphere of intimacy (*upaniṣad*), being able to expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.
(And as for "intimacy," it refers to approaching with focused conduct. Second, not to deviate from the Path—this is called the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice and sphere of intimacy;
this is the essential requirement for bodily conduct.)
Jie-huan said: "In both cases, there are practices of phenomena (shi) and practices of principle (li). Without phenomena, one cannot engage with the mundane;

without principle, one cannot accord with the ultimate truth. Only when one is proficient in both principle and phenomena, and when the ultimate and the mundane do not obstruct each other, can one benefit sentient beings and propagate the Dharma, finding peace and joy everywhere."
Mañjuśrī, what is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the ground of patience, being gentle, compliant, and well-disposed, without sudden outbursts of violence, and with a mind that is not startled.
(Nan Yue said: "This refers to the practice of deeds. (Xiang Mai said: "One who dwells in the place of practice must necessarily abide in patience (*kṣānti*).

Among the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), each has its application according to the occasion; yet, when encountering difficulties, nothing is superior to patience. For when one moves toward affairs with haste, regret and blame arise;
therefore, one must employ patience to govern them.)
The Precept Ring says: "In one's sphere of practice, one must abide in patience. This is because by being able to endure, one can be supple amidst the rigid so that things cannot crush them;
one can be compliant amidst adversity so that things cannot harm them; one can exercise discernment in affairs so that what is enacted is not violent;
and one can observe the subtle so that one is not startled by what is encountered. Through this, one successfully accomplishes the Practice of Peaceful Abiding.
Furthermore, he does not engage with any phenomena, yet he contemplates all phenomena as they truly are; neither engaging nor discriminating—
this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
(Ji Nan said: "This refers to principle and practice. (Ji Nan said: "Although one practices this Dharma, not dwelling upon its marks is called 'non-practice.
For where there is an object, there is a subject; when subject and object stand in opposition, self and other become adversaries, and thus suffering arises while peace and joy are lost.)
Jie-huan said: "Dharma" refers to all dharmas of practice. One contemplates the dharmas one practices oneself, and thereby contemplates all dharmas.
"As it truly is" means there is nothing to be contemplated, nor is there any practice; this means there is also no practice whatsoever.
"Without discrimination" means that emotional consciousness is entirely forgotten and both right and wrong are simultaneously extinguished. Such is the conduct and aspiration of a Bodhisattva.
What is called the "proximity" of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not associate with kings, princes, ministers, or high officials;
nor does he associate with various non-Buddhist practitioners such as brahmins or nirgranthas;
nor does he compose secular writings, praise foreign scriptures, or engage with the Lokāyatas or the Prati-Lokāyatas.

Furthermore, [Nan] says: "This refers to the practice of affairs, which takes precept and meditative concentration as its essence. 'Not associating with kings and the like' means that the precept avoids proximity to those with political power.
'Not associating with various [nearby] paths and the like' means that the precept avoids proximity to non-Buddhist paths."
Jie-huan said: "Though external protection may be honored, I fear that relying on such power will obstruct the Way.

If one is truly intent upon this [path], yet dwells in mountain forests while the heart remains fixed upon the imperial palace, can one ever find even temporary peace? Do not associate with non-Buddhists, so as to cease heterodox views.
Do not compose secular writings, so as to sever extremist doctrines. Stay far from malicious criticism and debate, so as to distance oneself from crooked sophistry."
Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as empty, according to their true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), without inversion, immovable, non-retrogressive, and non-reversing.
(And the southern tradition says: combining the subsequent words and principles of practice constitutes the second stage of proximity; the first stage of proximity is through ethical discipline.)
