Concentration (*samādhi*) constitutes its essence. The second stage, the "near-attainment" (*upasthāna*), takes contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) as its essence.

Thus, it integrates the preceding stages of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and concentration, enabling them to perfectly accord with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), thereby constituting sublime practice. Furthermore, Nan said: "The mind and dharmas are one.

When viewed through a perverted mind, illusory objects proliferate in confusion; when viewed through the true mark, the genuine mechanism is naturally quiescent. Therefore, one cultivates tranquility."
Delightful Practice (valuing *yathābhūta-parīkṣā*).
The Precept Ring says: All phenomena (*dharmas*) are, in their very essence, truly pure. Not receiving a single speck of dust is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*);
being unmoving and indestructible, free from all illusions and delusions, is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as empty, in accordance with reality.
Since the marks (lakṣaṇa) are neither augmented nor diminished, one’s vision is non-perverted and the mind is without fluctuation.
That the vision is non-perverted corresponds to what the verse calls "not discriminating whether dharmas exist or do not exist, or whether they are right or wrong.
That the mind is without fluctuation corresponds to what the verse calls "gathering the mind so it is unmoving, like Mount Sumeru. For the nature of the mind-dharmas is fundamentally...
Quiescence: Relative dependence gives rise to agitation. Because of inverted views, one regards phenomena as having birth and arising;
thus, the mind undergoes movement and fluctuation, like the moon appearing to move because the clouds are racing.
If one can contemplate according to reality, the mind will neither move nor regress, and one will realize that phenomena are neither born nor arise, like waves becoming still when the wind ceases.
It is like space: its nature is non-existence; all paths of language are cut off; it is unarisen, unproduced, and unoriginated;
it is nameless and signless; in reality, nothing exists; it is immeasurable, boundless, unimpeded, and unobstructed, existing only through causes and conditions.
Because it arises from inversion, one should always joyfully contemplate such characteristics of phenomena. This is called the second station of intimacy for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
(The verse says: "Contemplate all phenomena as being entirely non-existent, like space, lacking solidity, and unarisen.")
It does not emerge; it is neither moving nor retreating, eternally abiding in a single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*). This is called the "near station. (Furthermore, the Southern Text says:

"The nature of space is non-existence, up to being unimpeded and unobstructed, eternally abiding in a single mark—namely, that there is no arising, production, movement, or retreat—and thus it is not different.")
Jie-huan said: "That which has the nature of non-existence means that the natures of arising, ceasing, and the characteristics of names and forms are all absent.
Since names and forms are all absent, they cannot be reached by verbal expression; thus, the path of language is severed.
'Immeasurable and boundless' means that words are like space, which can never be exhausted. 'Unobstructed and unimpeded' means that [the nature] is like space, which cannot be divided."
This is eloquence. Such is the true mark (*dharmatā*); how could words ever reach it? Thus, whatever can be spoken exists only through conditions and is a phenomenon of inversion.
One should know that what does not arise from conditions and does not arise from inversion is ultimately inexpressible.
By constantly observing in this way, one is able to harmonize previous matters and practices to achieve the sublime.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when the Dharma is about to perish in the final age at the end of time, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who receive,
uphold, read, and recite this sutra must not harbor thoughts of envy, flattery, or deceit.
(Xiangmai said: "From envy, flattery, and deception down to frivolous discourse regarding all phenomena, these are all subtle perverse conducts of the mental ground;
therefore, they must be rectified.")
Jie-huan said: "When the Dharma is about to perish, the ways of the world fall into ruin, and wicked violence prevails everywhere.

As people become full of envy and flattery, those who study the Buddha’s teachings are easily subjected to contempt and abuse, with others seeking out their faults. Therefore, those who uphold the precepts and recite the sutras should harbor no envy or flattery;
rather, they should regulate their conduct according to the times, thereby bringing their karmic activities to rest."

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—whether they seek the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the bodhisattva path—you must not trouble them or cause them doubt and regret by saying to them:
"You are very far from the Path; you will never be able to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Why is that? Because you are negligent."
Such a person is indolent regarding the Path.
(And the Southern Text says: "If there are members of the fourfold assembly who seek the three vehicles, one should encourage their progress according to their capacities.
To suddenly disturb them and cause them to lose the benefits of goodness—this refers to the act of disturbing them immediately upon hearing someone's words.")
Furthermore, one should not engage in frivolous speculation regarding phenomena nor contend with others.
One should give rise to the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings, the thought of a loving father toward all Tathāgatas, and the thought of a great teacher toward all Bodhisattvas.
Toward the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, one should always pay deep homage and prostrations with a sincere heart, maintaining equanimity toward all sentient beings.
He teaches the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, neither too much nor too little; even for those who deeply love the Dharma, he does not speak excessively.
(And it is said:
To engage in inverted discrimination regarding the existence or non-existence of phenomena is called frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) and contention; all of these constitute mental karma.)
Therefore, one should cease [such thoughts].
Regarding the "Precept Ring" (Jie-huan), it says: To conceive of them with compassion is to pity their wandering in delusion and to think of rescuing them.

To conceive of them as a father is to rely upon their Dharma-transformation and to seek their protection. To conceive of them as a teacher is to admire their conduct and to think of following them. In this regard, at the Great...
A bodhisattva practices the Way out of compassion for sentient beings and, with a profound resolve, benefits others; therefore, one should respect them with a profound mind.

One’s speech should be impartial and free from partiality, and it should accord with the Dharma and conform to reason. Although one may feel deep affection later on, one must weigh what can be endured;
one values not failing the person, nor failing in one's words.
Mañjuśrī, when the Dharma is about to perish in the final age at the end of time, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished this third practice of peace and happiness will,
while preaching this Dharma, be unable to be disturbed or distracted, and they will obtain good companions in the study of the Dharma.
By reciting this sutra together, one will also cause a great assembly to come and listen to its teachings.
(Jiehuan says: From "Mañjuśrī descended" onwards, it speaks of the efficacy of ensuring there are no obstacles.
From "obtaining good companions for study" onwards, it means that by practicing these deeds, one finds friends through joy and gains a multitude through magnanimity.)

Having heard it, they are able to retain it; having retained it, they are able to recite it; having recited it, they are able to explain it; having explained it, they are able to write it down, or cause others to write it, and then make offerings to the scripture, honoring, respecting, and praising it.

Jiehuan said: "If this propagation of the Dharma's benefits continues to spread and expand, then although the Dharma may be on the verge of extinction, it will nonetheless achieve fulfillment through this third practice."
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, in the future final age when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Among those who are householders and those who have left the home life, they shall give rise to a mind of great loving-kindness;
toward those who are not bodhisattvas, they shall give rise to a mind of great compassion.
Furthermore, it is said: "In the practice of the Mahāyāna, one always begins with right conduct through wisdom and concludes with compassion that perfects wisdom.
Therefore, in the four modes of peaceful practice (*catur-śukla-vihāra*), one first relies on right wisdom and right action, and subsequently benefits sentient beings through great compassion."
The Precept Ring says: "Regarding the statement that 'this may give rise to great kindness (maitrī) or great compassion (karuṇā)':

kindness is able to bestow happiness, while compassion is able to pity and rescue the fourfold assembly. Those who have faith and understanding in the Buddha-dharma are called lay bodhisattvas or monastic bodhisattvas;
those who are icchantikas and lack faith are called non-bodhisattvas. Because they are able to have faith and understanding, they give rise to great kindness and bestow the Dharma upon them."
Out of compassion for those who have abandoned all aspiration (*icchantika*), one gives rise to great pity, grieving for their delusion and loss of direction.
One should reflect: "Such persons suffer a great loss. The Tathāgata employs skillful means to preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate."
They have not heard it, do not know it, and are not aware of it; they have not inquired about it, do not believe it, and do not understand it.

Although such persons do not inquire, believe, or understand this sutra, when I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, wherever they may be, I shall draw them in by means of my supernatural powers and the power of wisdom, causing them to abide within this Dharma.
(All of this is out of compassion for those who have lost their way. Teaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate is precisely the method of opening up the three to reveal the one.

"Not hearing, not knowing, and not awakening" refers to being deluded and obstructed by oneself. "Not inquiring, not believing, and not understanding" refers to falling into ignorance through one's own stupidity.
Yet, even though they do not inquire or understand, the Bodhisattva’s great compassion vows to deliver them all at last.)
Mañjuśrī, in immeasurable lands, even the name of this Lotus Sūtra cannot be heard,
let alone being seen, received, upheld, read, or recited.
(Jie-huan said: "This praises the difficulty of such an encounter. It is for this reason that one pities those who do not believe or understand, considering it a great loss.
Mañjuśrī, it is like a powerful Wheel-turning Sage King who, wishing to subdue various kingdoms by his majestic power, [proceeds to do so]."
Yet the various minor kings did not obey his commands. At that time, the Wheel-Turning King raised various armies and went forth to subdue them.
(Furthermore, it is said: "The meaning of this metaphor clarifies why this sutra is so difficult to hear and difficult to see:
because the Māra of the aggregates is rampant, there are many enemies, and it is difficult to believe; therefore, it is not spoken falsely.)"
Jie-huan said: "The wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) is a metaphor for the nirmāṇakāya Buddha. The various kingdoms are metaphors for the objects of the five aggregates (skandhas).
The minor kings are metaphors for the demons of the five aggregates and so forth. Their failure to obey his commands is a metaphor for ignorance and afflictions not yet being subdued.

Because he cannot prevail through mere majesty, he raises an army to campaign and conquer; this is a metaphor for how the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, and the dharmas of fearlessness alone, are insufficient."
To subdue all subtle afflictions, he establishes the methods of severance and remedy for the three vehicles; this is called "raising various armies.
When the king sees that his troops have performed meritorious service in battle, he is greatly delighted and bestows rewards according to their merit, such as granting them fields and houses.
Villages and cities; or he gives garments and articles for adorning the body; or he gives various kinds of precious treasures:
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, *musāragalva*, agate, coral, amber, elephants, horses, carriages, and vehicles, as well as male and female slaves and subjects.

(Jie-huan said: "This parable refers to the assembly of the Three Vehicles, who are able to subdue the Māra of the aggregates. According to the depth or shallowness of their merit, they obtain various benefits of the Dharma;
however, it has not yet been taught to them that there is but the One Vehicle Dharma.")
Only the bright jewel from within the topknot shall not be given to him. Why is this? This single jewel exists only upon the king’s own head;
if it were given to him, the king’s entire retinue would surely be greatly shocked and amazed.
(A bright pearl is used to stabilize the throne; to give it away recklessly would cause the king’s subjects to be struck with alarm. In the Lotus Sūtra, Buddha hands over to Buddha;
to speak recklessly would cause the hearts of the multitude to be filled with shock and doubt.)
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is also like this. By the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, he has acquired the lands of the directions and reigns as king over the three realms;
yet the various Māra kings refuse to submit. The Tathāgata’s noble and holy generals engage them in battle.
[And Nan said: "It is like a Wheel-Turning King who, when minor kings do not submit, subsequently raises various military strategies.
Jiehuan said: "The 'kingdom' is the true realm of the Dharma-dhātu; 'sages and worthies' refers to the assembly of the Three Vehicles."
Those who have performed meritorious deeds also rejoice in their hearts.

Among the fourfold assembly, he preaches various sutras for them to gladden their minds, bestowing upon them the wealth of dharmas such as dhyāna, samādhi, liberation, and the faculties and powers free from outflows.

Furthermore, he grants them the city of nirvāṇa, declaring that they have attained extinction (parinirvāṇa), thereby guiding their minds and causing them all to be joyful; yet, he does not preach this [ultimate truth] to them.
The Lotus Sutra.
[Jiehuan said: "It is like bestowing rewards according to merit, yet not giving the crest-jewel. The 'untainted faculties and powers' refer to the five faculties and five powers.
'The wealth of all dharmas' generally indicates the methods for utilizing the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma). The 'city of nirvana' refers to the Middle [Way]."
This is the provisional fruit of the cessation of the Path).
Mañjuśrī, it is like a wheel-turning monarch who, seeing among his troops those who have achieved great merit, feels profound joy in his heart.
"This pearl, so difficult to believe in, has long remained within my topknot; I did not give it to others recklessly, yet now I bestow it upon you.
(Jiehuan said: "To speak of a pearl so difficult to believe in—had it been bestowed upon one for whom it was unsuitable, there would have been great alarm and wonder.")
The Tathāgata is also like this. Within the triple world, he is the Great Dharma King who teaches and transforms all sentient beings through the Dharma.

Seeing the army of the noble ones battle against the Māra of the five aggregates, the Māra of afflictions, and the Māra of death, and achieving great merit—extinguishing the three poisons, escaping the triple world, and shattering the net of Māra—the Tathāgata likewise experiences great joy at this Dharma.

The Flower Garland Sutra can cause sentient beings to reach all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*). Though it is full of enmity and difficult to believe in throughout all worlds, that which was not previously taught is now being taught.
(Jie-huan said: *Māra* is here translated as "the Killer," meaning that which can inflict suffering and hardship, slaying the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*).
The *kleśa-māra* (affliction-demon) is the cause of birth and death; the *skandha-māra* (aggregate-demon) and *mṛtyu-māra* (death-demon) are the effects of birth and death.

Therefore, to extinguish and destroy them is to transcend the three realms. [The text notes: "Many enemies" refers to the various *māras* not yet being subdued; "difficult to believe in" refers to the capacities of sentient beings not yet being matured).
Mañjuśrī, this Lotus Sūtra is the foremost teaching of all Tathāgatas; among all teachings, it is the most profound.
It is bestowed at the very end, just as a powerful king who has long guarded a bright jewel finally grants it to someone.
Jiehuan said: "The first teaching is like a single jewel atop one's head; the final gift is like the great merit earned through long-term cultivation."
Mañjuśrī, this Lotus Sūtra is the secret treasury of all the Tathāgatas;
it stands supreme among all sūtras. Having guarded it through the long night, I have not proclaimed it recklessly.
Only today do I expound it for you.
Jie-huan said: "The secret is like [the hair] within a topknot; it is most supreme, like [a jewel] upon a king's crown.
For over forty years, throughout the long night of birth and death, I have guarded this, awaiting the opportune moment. Hence it is called 'guarding through the long night.'"
Chapter Fifteen: The Emergence from the Earth.
In this Sahā world, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers who have cultivated the Buddha’s wisdom for incalculable kalpas.
They were transformed by Śākyamuni Tathāgata; always delighting in quietude and practicing with diligent vigor, they do not rely upon the realms of humans or devas, but abide [in the Dharma].
In the space below, he manifested eternal bliss to demonstrate that there is no obstruction whatsoever;
thus, he fully revealed the traces of transformation through the wondrous Dharma, and for this reason, the chapter is titled "Emergence."
At that time, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from other lands, numbering more than the sands of eight Ganges Rivers,
rose from within the great assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if you would permit us to remain in this Sahā world after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
to apply ourselves with diligent effort to protect, uphold, read, recite, copy, and make offerings to this sutra, we shall do so."
I shall explain it extensively in this land.
(Jiehuan said: "The assembly of this Dharma-collection wishes to come from other directions to this place to uphold the sutra.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: "Cease! There is no need for you all to protect and uphold this sutra."
Why is this? In my Sahā world, there are naturally sixty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
Each of these bodhisattvas has a retinue of sixty thousand followers, likewise as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
These individuals will be able, after my parinirvāṇa, to protect, uphold, recite, and extensively expound this sutra.
Jiehuan said: "The Buddha’s refusal was not due to any opposition or rejection; rather, it was for the purpose of manifesting his traces and manifesting the Dharma.

To manifest his traces means to reveal the manner of his arrival as a transformation of the Buddha to those present. To manifest the Dharma means that this [teaching] is inherently perfect and complete, requiring nothing external."
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the earth throughout the Sahā world—the great trichiliocosm—trembled and split asunder.
From within it, immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas simultaneously surged forth.
(Jie-huan said: "Profound wisdom manifests before him; the great trichiliocosm is not an obstruction.
These bodhisattvas all have golden bodies, possess the thirty-two marks, and emit immeasurable light.
Previously, they were all beneath this Sahā world, dwelling in the space of this realm.
(Jie-huan said: "They dwell in the space below this Sahā world in order to demonstrate their constant joy and profound wisdom, which are free from all obstacles.
These bodhisattvas, having heard the sound of the voice spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, ascended from below and arrived.
Jiehuan said: "This is what Mañjuśrī meant by 'the hearing of the mind penetrating the ten directions.
This [text] speaks of the Real; that [Mañjuśrī] spoke of the hearing of the mind."

Once these bodhisattvas had emerged from the earth, they each proceeded through the air to the exquisite stupa made of the seven treasures where the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha were located.
Having arrived, they paid homage toward the two World-Honored Ones, and likewise prostrated before all the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jeweled trees;
with palms joined in reverence, they offered various kinds of bodhisattva praises.
Having offered praise, they stood to one side, joyfully gazing up at the two World-Honored Ones.
From the moment these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first leaped forth, they praised the Buddha with various bodhisattva methods of eulogy for a period of fifty intermediate kalpas.
During that time, Śākyamuni Buddha remained seated in silence. And...
The fourfold assembly likewise remained silent for fifty intermediate kalpas; through the Buddha’s spiritual power, he caused the great multitude to perceive this duration as being like half a day.
(As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus one understands.")
One knows the affairs of the three periods of time and transcends all expedient means to achieve the ten powers.
For one who can, in a single thought-moment, universally observe that there is no going, coming, or abiding, then realizes that this extension and brevity are both merely expedient means.
Jie-huan said: "The sage’s divine wisdom and skillful means constitute a dharma-gate by which he can extend a single day to become an eon, or contract an eon to become a single day.
For the Way undergoes no transition or change; it is only that purity has its measure of brevity and duration.
It is like a person in a dream who, without moving for even a moment, dreams through many years; thus, the perception of brevity and duration has no fixed reality from the outset."
Therefore, the Sage, responding to the capacities of beings, manifests both extension and brevity, yet fundamentally there is neither extension nor brevity.

When it is said that Bodhisattvas praise the Buddha for kalpas, this is merely manifesting extension within brevity; when he causes the great assembly to perceive it as being like half a day, this is manifesting brevity within extension.
The reason for doing so is that he intends to reveal and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas.
This is because the power of sovereign spiritual penetrations causes one to forget the sentiments of extension and brevity, thereby deeply realizing the true mark (*dharmatā*).
At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the fourfold assembly also saw all the bodhisattvas filling the voids of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands.

Furthermore, [Nan said]: "The physical eyes of the fourfold assembly are obstructed and not supernormal; yet that they can see immeasurable lands is due to the power of the Buddha's supernormal faculties."

The Precept Ring says: Regarding the manifestation of the many and one within the multitude, the appearance of time as extended or brief, and the function of seeing as unobstructed or impeded—these clarify that the measure of things is infinite, time has no cessation, and divisions are impermanent.
Thus, they awaken the ordinary mind, causing one to abandon inverted thoughts and limited intentions, and to rely upon unimpeded wisdom for perfect, harmonious, and subtle penetration. From this...
It proceeds to the secret teaching on the duration of the life-span, whereby one enters the Buddha’s wisdom and accomplishes the Buddha-body.
Therefore, although the matters and dharmas of this chapter are intended to manifest the traces [of the Buddha] and encourage their upholding, they also serve to elicit the teaching on the life-span.
Within this assembly of bodhisattvas, there were four guiding teachers: the first was named Upariṣṭacārin, the second Anantacārin, the third Viśuddhacārin, and the fourth Supratiṣṭhitacārin.
These four bodhisattvas were the foremost leaders and preceptors within that multitude.
Standing before the great assembly, they each gazed upon Śākyamuni Buddha and inquired after his well-being, saying: "World-Honored One..."
"Venerable One, are you free from illness and affliction, and are you dwelling in peace? Are those who are to be delivered easy to instruct?
Do they not cause the World-Honored One weariness?
(Jiehuan said: "This question concerns dwelling in endurance and sharing the sufferings of the people.")
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "It is so, it is so.
The Tathāgata is at ease, with little illness and little affliction. These sentient beings are easily transformed and delivered, and I feel no fatigue.
Why is this? Because throughout successive lifetimes, these sentient beings have constantly received my transformation, as well as that of the Buddhas of the past."

Having made offerings and shown respect, and having planted various roots of goodness, these sentient beings, upon first seeing my body and hearing what I have taught, immediately believe and accept it, entering into the wisdom of the Tathāgata—except for those who previously practiced and studied the Lesser Vehicle. Such persons as these [are excluded].
I now also cause them to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
(Jiehuan said: The statement that they receive transformation life after life specifically clarifies those transformed by the Original Chapter on the Lifespan;

the statement that they also planted roots of goodness in the past concurrently clarifies those transformed during the Assembly of the Wise and Holy, because the conditions for their transformation were profound. Thus, they are seen for the first time...)
Upon hearing this, they all believed and accepted it.

At that time, the various Buddhas who were emanations of Śākyamuni and had come from immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of other lands sat cross-legged upon lion thrones beneath the jeweled trees in the eight directions. Those Buddhas—
The attendants each saw this great assembly of bodhisattvas emerging from the earth in the four directions throughout the trichiliocosm and remaining in the air.
Each addressed his own Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, from where have these immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable multitudes of bodhisattvas come?
At that time, the various Buddhas each told their attendants: "For now..."
Wait a moment. There is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Maitreya, who has been prophesied by Śākyamuni Buddha to become a buddha next after him;
he has already inquired about this matter, and the Buddha is now answering it. You yourselves shall hear it through him.
(Jie-huan said: "This is a question from another assembly. (Ji-nan said: "Each addresses their own Buddha; this refers to the emanated bodies.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Ajita!"
That you are able to ask the Buddha about such a great matter as this— you all should now be of one mind, don the armor of diligence, and resolve with firm intent.
The Tathāgata now wishes to reveal and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas,
the sovereign power of the supernatural penetrations of all Buddhas, the lion-like valorous power of all Buddhas, and the majestic, mighty power of all Buddhas.
(And as for "Nan," it is the surname of Maitreya. His title is Ajita, which means "Invincible.

"Great Matters" refers to the deeds of converting vast multitudes through the vigorous and majestic power of his wisdom and spiritual penetrations. (This proclaims the transformative traces of Śākyamuni;
yet he speaks of "all Buddhas" because the Way of every Buddha is the same.)

The Precept Ring says: "Regarding the statement, 'Before intending to proclaim and reveal [the teaching], one first causes them to don the armor of diligence,' etc., the Precept-Envoy urges you to listen with courageous acuity;
do not give rise to doubt or retreat because the path is profound. Below it says:

'After I have attained Bodhi in this Sahā world, I shall teach and bring such a multitude of beings to fulfillment. This is the general proclamation, which is explained in detail in the subsequent text."
It proclaims the wisdom of all Buddhas, as stated in the verse on the lifespan: "Such is my power of wisdom; the light of my insight shines immeasurably.
It refers to the sovereign supernatural powers of all Buddhas, as in: "They manifest nirvana through skillful means, yet in reality they do not pass into extinction.
It refers to the power of the lion’s vigorous stride, as in: "Constantly preaching the Dharma to teach and transform countless billions."
This refers to sentient beings. By the power of his majestic and great might, he causes those sentient beings who are inverted to fail to see him, even though they are close to him.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "I now declare to you all within this great assembly: A..."
Ānanda, these great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas— immeasurable, incalculable, and asaṃkhyeya—
who have emerged from the earth and whom you have never seen before, were taught, guided, and instructed by me after I attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this Sahā world;
I have tamed their minds and caused them to resolve [for enlightenment].
[He asked about] the aspiration for the Way. [Jie-huan said: "To whom did this answer refer? Who was preaching the Dharma and providing instruction?
From whom did they first resolve their minds? These bodhisattvas all dwell in the space beneath this Sahā world.
(Jie-huan said: "This answers the request; please state the name of the land from which you come.
Regarding all the sūtras, he has read and recited them until they are mastered, contemplating and discerning them with right mindfulness.
(Nan Yue added: "This refers to the praise of one's virtue.

Jiehuan said: "Regarding the various scriptures, if one can read them to grasp their principles, recite them to master their meanings, contemplate them to refine them, and maintain them through right mindfulness, then one's virtue is truly worthy of praise."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva and countless other bodhisattvas felt doubt and wonder at this unprecedented occurrence,
thinking to themselves: "How is it that in such a short time, the World-Honored One has taught and transformed such immeasurable,
boundless, and incalculable numbers of great bodhisattvas, causing them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"

Bodhi then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata was a prince, he departed from the palace of the Śākyas and, not far from the city of Gayā, sat at the site of enlightenment and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
From that time until now, only forty-odd years have passed. World-Honored One, how is it that in such a short time, you have performed such great deeds as a Buddha?"
By the power of the Buddha and by the merit of the Buddha, he teaches and transforms such an immeasurable multitude of great bodhisattvas so that they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

World-Honored One, even if someone were to count this great assembly of bodhisattvas for thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, they could not exhaustively enumerate them nor reach their limit; these beings have come from such a vast antiquity.
"In the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, he has planted various roots of goodness, accomplished the path of a bodhisattva, and constantly cultivated the holy life.
World-Honored One, such a matter is difficult for the world to believe."
(Ji Nan said: "This is to harbor doubt by clinging to the superficial traces. (Ji Nan said: "This is because one is deluded regarding the distant cause of the lifespan;
hence this doubt arises. (Jie Huan said: "Because one clings to the proximate trace of Gayā, this objection arises.")
For example, suppose there were a person with a handsome appearance and black hair, twenty-five years of age, who pointed to a hundred-year-old man and said, "This is my son.
And suppose that hundred-year-old man also pointed to the youth and said, "This is my father; he begot and raised me. Such a thing would be difficult to believe.

(As for the Southern [tradition] stating "twenty-five" and "one hundred years," this is because taking the former refers to one who is still young and not yet mature, while the latter refers to one already past the age of senility;
thus, they are seen to be even more contradictory).

Jiehuan said: "The father is young, which is comparable to the recent period since Śākyamuni began his propagation of the teachings; the son is old, which is comparable to the long duration since [the Buddha] emerged and perfected his virtue.
That the power of a recent propagation and the duration of long-established virtue are not logically consistent."

The Buddha is also like this. Although it has not been long since he attained the Way, this great assembly of bodhisattvas has already, for the sake of the Buddha-way, practiced with diligent vigor for immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.
They have skillfully entered, emerged from, and dwelt in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of samādhis;
they have attained great supernormal powers and have long cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya), being well-able to proceed through the stages in succession.
He has practiced all wholesome dharmas and is skillful in answering questions; he is a jewel among men, exceedingly rare in all the worlds.

Today, the World-Honored One says that when he first attained the Way of the Buddha, he was the one who first inspired him to resolve his mind, teaching and guiding him toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Not long after the World-Honored One attained Buddhahood, he was already able to perform such great [deeds].
[This concerns] matters of merit.
[Jie-huan said: "That the Buddha has attained enlightenment not long ago corresponds to the father being young; yet that this great assembly is so exceedingly rare corresponds to the son being old.
That today the World-Honored One is able to perform such a great deed corresponds to their being in opposition. He enters and emerges with skill."
"Abiding" refers to entering, emerging from, or dwelling within immeasurable samādhis with sovereign mastery of wondrous functions).
○ Chapter Sixteen: The Lifespan of the Tathāgata.

Previously, because sentient beings harbored doubts regarding the duration [of the Buddha's life] and perceived arising and ceasing, they were unable to accord with the reality-limit (*tattvārtha*) of the fundamental state. This is the explanation thereof.

To resolve their doubts and obstructions, [the Buddha] causes them to know that the Tathāgata is fundamentally without birth or extinction. The transformation at Gayā was specifically for the sake of the capacities of those to be taught.
Because the *Lotus Sūtra* accords with the nature of reality and is immeasurable, it is titled the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly: "You all should have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s words of truth.
He further addressed the great assembly: "You all should have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s words of truth."
Furthermore, he addressed the great assembly: "You all should have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s words of truth and reality.
(Jie-huan [戒環] said: Because the fundamental nature of the lifespan is profound and difficult to believe, he proclaims it repeatedly. 'Sincerity' (*cheng*) refers to the reality of the mind;
'truth' (*di*) refers to the accuracy of the words.)
All the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras, all say that the present Śākyamuni Buddha left the palace of the Śākya clan and,
not far from the city of Gayā, sat at the site of enlightenment and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Yet, in reality, it has been immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas since I truly attained Buddhahood.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] said: "The world perceives only their traces, yet does not know that their fundamental reality is immeasurable.
For example, suppose there were five hundred thousand million billion nayuta asaṃkhyeya trichiliocosms, and someone were to grind them into fine dust.
Suppose one were to pass beyond five hundred thousand million billion nayuta asaṃkhyeya [worlds] to the east...
"In the *Saṃghāṭa* world-system, one places a single mote of dust. Continuing thus toward the east until all these motes of dust are exhausted—O sons of good family, what do you think?
Is it possible to conceive of, calculate, or know the number of those world-systems?"
(Keihan said: "This is like the analogy of surpassing dust and ink with wisdom.
Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others all addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these worlds are immeasurable and boundless;
they cannot be known by calculation, nor can they be reached by the power of the mind. All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, by means of their outflow-free [wisdom]..."
"O Wisdom! One cannot contemplate or know their limit or number. Even we, who dwell on the stage of *avaivartika*, do not penetrate this matter.
World-Honored One, such worlds are immeasurable and boundless. At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of Bodhisattvas:
"I shall now clearly declare to you: suppose these worlds were filled with atoms of dust."

And even those who do not cling to them, I consider all to be like motes of dust. If one mote of dust represents one kalpa, the time since I attained Buddhahood has already exceeded this by hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
(Jie-huan said: "This clearly demonstrates that the Buddha's lifespan is immeasurable. The lifespans of all Buddhas are entirely immeasurable, and the lifespans of sentient beings are likewise so.
It is only because they are deluded regarding their own wisdom that they falsely pursue birth and death;

for instance, once one falls into hell and remains there for countless kalpas, is this not an immeasurable lifespan? If one were simply not deluded and did not fall [into such states], then one would be no different from a Buddha.")
Since that time, I have constantly remained in this Sahā world, preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings;
I have also guided and benefited living beings in hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya lands in other places.
Furthermore, it is said: "The Sahā world and its ten billion lands are none other than pure lands. Because they are based upon the single Dharma-realm, they have never been destroyed or extinguished.
Any instances of destruction or extinction are merely false perceptions resulting from individual karmic conditions."

Jiehuan said: "From that time onward—meaning from the attainment of Buddhahood throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust—it has been said that [the Buddha] is always here, yet is also in other places.
Thus, it is not only the physical form that is eternally abiding, but it also reveals that the land is eternally abiding."
"Sons of good family, all the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata are for the purpose of liberating sentient beings. He may speak of his own person or speak of the persons of others;
he may manifest his own person or manifest the persons of others; he may manifest his own affairs or manifest the affairs of others."
"Whatever has been spoken is all true and not false.
(And the Southern tradition says: "The scriptures expounded herein, though their expressions differ, are in principle entirely without falsehood.")
Jie-huan said: "Self" refers to Śākyamuni; "others" refers to all Buddhas. To speak of seeing is to see through words; to demonstrate seeing is to see through practice. Why is this so?
Because the Tathāgata knows and sees the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are: there is no birth-and-death, neither retreating nor emerging;
there is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa. It is neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different; it is not as [it appears].
The Tathāgata clearly perceives the three realms as they appear within the three realms; such matters he sees with perfect clarity, free from error.

Because sentient beings possess various natures, various inclinations, various conducts, and various thoughts and discriminations, [the Tathāgata] employs various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions to preach the Dharma in manifold ways, in order to cause them to give rise to roots of goodness. This is what he does.
The Buddha’s work has never been suspended for even a moment.
(Jiannan says: The principles explained above are without exception true, yet there are differences in their expositions. (Jiannan says:
"The Buddha’s work" refers to the various different matters that are pointed out and demonstrated.)

Jie-huan said: "The myriad dharmas of the three realms do not admit of the application of the conceptual mind. From the deluded vision of sentient beings, they appear as various and chaotic phenomena;
from the true vision of the Tathāgata, they are fundamentally quiescent and still, wherein there is neither birth-and-death nor even extinction.
One does not perceive them through the marks of arising and ceasing. Those who do not view the three realms as the three realms [do not see them at all]."
This is because they come and go to meet one another. Since their clear vision is unhindered, there should be no divergent teachings;
it is only because the desires, natures, practices, and thoughts of sentient beings differ in myriad ways that the traces of teaching and transformation are likewise shown in myriad different ways.
"Sons of good family, the lifespan I have accomplished while originally practicing the bodhisattva path is still not yet exhausted;
it is even twice as long as the number mentioned above. Yet, although I am not actually entering parinirvāṇa now, I proclaim that I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
It is by such skillful means that the Tathāgata teaches and transforms sentient beings."
(And the Southern text says: "This describes the intent behind the teaching of extinction.
Why is this so? If the Buddha were to remain long in the world, those of meager virtue would fail to plant roots of goodness;
being poor, lowly, and base, they would be greedily attached to the five desires and fall into the net of discursive thoughts and false views. If they were to see the Tathāgata as always present...

Not perishing, they then give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, harboring weariness and indolence; they are unable to conceive the thought that [the Dharma] is difficult to encounter, nor do they possess a heart of reverence.
For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks by means of skillful expedients.
(Jie-huan says: "The Buddha's proclamation refers to the intent of cessation. 'Poverty and lowliness' refer to the wealth of merit;
'recollections and false views' constitute the net of birth and death—namely, the delusions of view and the delusions of thought.)
"Monks, you should know that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is difficult to encounter. Why is this?
Because those of meager merit may or may not see a Buddha even after passing through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas. For this reason, [it is rare]."
I speak these words: "O Bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is difficult to encounter. When these sentient beings hear such words, they will certainly conceive the thought that he is hard to meet;
their hearts will be filled with longing and they will thirst for the Buddha, thereby planting roots of goodness.
For this reason, although the Tathāgata does not truly pass away, he speaks of his parinirvāṇa.
(Furthermore, Nan said: "To say they are difficult to encounter is to awaken them and cause them to thirst for the Dharma so that they may plant roots of goodness.
Moreover, son of good family, the dharmas of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are thus; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they are entirely real and not false.
(Jie-huan said: "The Buddha’s skillful means for benefiting sentient beings through the [precious] pearl are all like this.
It is, for example, like a skilled physician who is wise and discerning, proficient in medical formulas and prescriptions, and adept at treating all manner of illnesses.
(Xing Jianzi said: "The various parables in the Lotus Sūtra all enter into the subtle; the other [teachings] that open up worldly expedients are clearly evident.
This [Lotus Sūtra] shares the same underlying mechanism as the parable of the burning house.")
Jie-huan said: "The Buddha is like a physician; the teaching is like a medical prescription; and the principle is like a potent medicine.

The various dispositions, desires, conducts, and conceptualizations are what are called 'various illnesses. The Buddha is able to employ numerous causes and analogies to dispense medicine according to what is appropriate for each case and thereby eliminate them.
This is what is meant by a skilled physician who treats effectively."
That man has many sons—perhaps ten, twenty, or even a hundred in number. On account of some business matter, he travels far away to another country.
Later, his sons drink a poisonous drug; the poison takes effect, causing them to become dazed and disoriented as they writhe upon the ground.
Furthermore, [Nan said]: "The children of the burning house are spoken of in relation to the Three Vehicles; therefore, their number stops at thirty.
The children of the skilled physician are spoken of in relation to all sentient beings; therefore, the number extends to one hundred."
The Precept Ring says: "The physician has gone far away while his sons have drunk poison; it is like a householder who has recently departed while his home catches fire.
Drinking other toxic medicines is a metaphor for following false teachings; wallowing on the ground is a metaphor for transmigrating through the various realms of existence."
At that time, their father returned home. Among his sons who had drunk the poison, some had lost their original minds while others had not;
seeing their father from afar, they all rejoiced greatly, prostrating themselves and greeting him, saying: "We have returned safely and in good health. We were foolish."
"By mistake we have consumed poison. We pray for your rescue and treatment, that you may grant us further life.

Seeing his sons suffering in such a manner, the father, following various medical treatises, sought out excellent medicinal herbs complete in color, fragrance, and flavor; he then pounded, sifted, and blended them together.
He gave them this medicine and spoke these words: "This is a great and excellent medicine; its color, fragrance, and flavor are all perfectly complete.
You should take it; it will swiftly eliminate your suffering and affliction, so that you shall no longer have any further ailments."
(Nan said: "The Sage shares the illness of humanity; he grieves over the grief of others. The virtue of the Tamer is indeed seen herein. Jiehuan said:
"The household of the three realms is that which the Buddha has long transformed; thus it is called 'returning home. Within it lies the poison of heterodoxy."

Those who are deeply [immersed in delusion] have lost their innate goodness; those who are shallowly [immersed], though they may not yet have lost it, are nonetheless obstructed by evil habits and are unable to personally realize the essence of awakening;
hence it is said they "see from afar. "Granting them longevity" means hoping they will not meet with untimely death through perverse calamities.
"Administering medicine to remove suffering" means causing them to sever their delusions and realize the Truth. Relying upon all Buddhas...

The method for the economy is to seek the medicine of the sages’ governance and judgment, to manifest the true color of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), and to display the five fragrances of precept and meditative concentration (*śīla-samādhi*).
It possesses all the five flavors of milk and curd without exception. "Pounding" means to break the rigid into the supple;
"sifting" means to transform the coarse into the fine. When these are blended and administered, there will be no fault of distorting the Buddha’s teachings. As for the color...
If the flavor and fragrance are exquisite, there will be no toxic effects such as dizziness or nausea.
Among his sons, those who have not lost their wits see that this excellent medicine is both fine in color and fragrant, and they immediately take it.

The illness was completely cured. As for those who had lost their minds, although they were joyful to see their father arrive and inquired after him while seeking treatment for their ailment, even when he gave them medicine, they refused to take it.
Why was this? Because the toxic vapors had penetrated deeply and they had lost their original minds;
thus, they regarded these excellent colors, fragrances, and medicines as unpleasant.
(Śīlaka said: "This is a metaphor for the transformation of existence...").
The father thought to himself: "This son is pitiable; he has been struck by poison and his mind is completely deranged.
Although he sees me and seeks relief with joy, he refuses to take such excellent medicine as this. I must now employ skillful means to cause him to take it."
This physician then spoke these words: "You should know that I am now old and decrepit, and the time of my death has arrived.
This excellent medicine remains here; you may take it and drink it. Do not worry that you will not be cured.
Having given this instruction, he departed for another country and sent a messenger back to announce: "Your father is already dead."
(Jiehuan said: "This metaphor provisionally indicates extinction. [The verse says: "I am called the Father of the World, rescuing all who suffer;
for the sake of ordinary beings who are deluded, I say that I truly enter extinction. This refers to it. (Jiannan said: "Leaving behind medicine is a metaphor for the Bequeathed Teaching;
departing from the kingdom is a metaphor for indicating extinction.")
At that time, when the sons heard of their father’s death, their hearts were filled with great sorrow and distress, and they thought to themselves:

"If our father had been alive, he would have felt compassion for us and been able to protect and save us. Now he has abandoned us and passed away far away in another land; we find ourselves orphaned and exposed, with no one left to rely upon.
Constantly harboring this grief, their minds finally became clear, and they realized that the medicine was indeed beautiful in color, flavor, and fragrance.
He immediately took it and consumed it; his toxic illness was entirely cured. (Jiehuan said:
"This is a metaphor for being moved by a question and responding through transformation. (Xing Jianzi said:
"In human nature, one often neglects that which one relies upon, yet is always moved by the thought of what has departed; such is frequently the case.")
When the father heard that his son had fully recovered, he immediately returned and allowed him to see him all at once.
(Jie-huan said: "This is a metaphor for the exhaustion of hindrances and the seeing of the Buddha.")
And Nan said: "When the water is clear, the moon appears; how could it have come or gone?
Sons of good family, what do you think? Is there anyone who could say that this skilled physician has committed the sin of falsehood?"
"No, World-Honored One.
(Jiehuan says: This is a further inquiry to confirm his faith.
The Buddha said: "I am also like this. Since I attained Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, nayutas [of eons] have passed."
Throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, for the sake of sentient beings, he has used the power of skillful means to say that he shall enter parinirvāṇa;
yet, there is no one capable of rightfully accusing him of the fault of falsehood.
(Jie-huan said: "Guiding the deluded through skillful means is precious; there is no fault in this regarding the Dharma.
Chapter Seventeen: Discerning Merit.
The realization of the Way and the verification of its nature vary in depth; the Buddha accordingly extols them according to their faculties. Therefore, it is called "Discerning."

[This is] the merit. At that time, when the great assembly heard the Buddha speak of the lifespan being so long and vast— extending through immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons—
an infinite number of sentient beings attained great benefit.
(Regarding this, Jie-huan said: "One shall obtain great benefit, as described below.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya:
"Ajita, when I spoke of the long duration of the Tathāgata’s lifespan, six hundred and eighty million *nayuta* of beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained [enlightenment]."
The patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
[Jie-huan says: Because one hears of the lifespan, one realizes there is neither arising nor ceasing; by means of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, one can perfect the practice.
There being neither realization nor patience, it is called "patience regarding dharmas" (*dharma-kṣānti*). "Patience" refers to the perfection of the name through practice.]
Furthermore, there are a thousand times as many bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining.
(Master Xianzi said: "The word 'door' in this context refers to what is called the 'dhāraṇī-door' in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*;
it means attaining all things.")
The Precept Ring said: "Upon hearing it once, one awakens to a thousand truths and attains the Great Dharani. All other dharanis emerge from this;
therefore, it is called a 'gate.
When the Buddha spoke of these Bodhisattvas Mahasattvas attaining the great benefit of the Dharma, a rain of *manis* fell from the void."
With *tāra* flowers and great *mandārava* flowers, they scattered them over the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of jeweled trees;
they also scattered them over Śākyamuni Buddha seated upon the lion throne within the stupa made of the seven treasures,
as well as over the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna who has long since entered parinirvāṇa, and over all the great bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
Furthermore, a rain of finely powdered sandalwood, aloeswood, and other incenses fell. In the midst of the void, celestial drums resounded spontaneously with profound and wondrous sounds.
Moreover, a thousand kinds of celestial garments rained down, along with hanging necklaces:

necklaces of pearls, necklaces of *maṇi* jewels, and necklaces of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*), pervading the nine directions. Countless precious incense burners burned priceless incense of their own accord.
Furthermore, throughout the great assembly of offerings, above each and every Buddha, there were bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies,
ascending one after another as far as the Brahma Heaven. These bodhisattvas, with wondrous voices, sang immeasurable verses in praise of all the Buddhas.
[The Master] Jiéhuán said: "All these auspicious signs rained down from the void, pervading the nine directions.
This serves to manifest that the lifespan and the benefits of the Dharma are as boundless as space, beyond the reach of thought or calculation. Thus Maitreya praised it, saying:

'The World-Honored One has spoken of the lifespan, an inconceivable Dharma that brings manifold benefit, like the boundlessness of [empty] space. As for the mention of the 'nine directions,' this excludes—"

Below [the assembly], at a place that was not a site for the Dharma-gathering, the Bodhisattva held up a banner that reached as far as the Brahma-heaven, declaring that it filled the void as an offering and praise.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Ajita, there are sentient beings who hear of the Buddha..."
The span of his life is thus long and far-reaching. Even the merit obtained by one who can give rise to a single thought of faith and understanding is without limit.

(Jiehuan says: "By explaining the measure of the lifespan, one immediately attains the indestructible essence; because one realizes the constant function of the Truth, the merit is therefore limitless.")
Furthermore, Ajita, if there are those who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching and understand the meaning of these words, the merit they obtain will be immeasurable;
they will be able to give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata. How much more so for those who hear this sutra extensively!
Whether one causes others to hear it, or upholds it oneself, or causes others to uphold it;

whether one writes it out oneself, or makes offerings to the scripture with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, flags, silk canopies, fragrant oils, and ghee lamps—the merit of such a person shall be immeasurable and boundless.
It is able to give rise to all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
(Furthermore, as for the discourse on the lifespan, its intent lies in severing views of arising and ceasing to reveal the eternally true essence.
If one can clearly understand this, then the unsurpassed wisdom will arise, making one equal to the Tathāgata; therefore, its merit is immeasurable.)
Jiehuan said: "Hearing of the Buddha’s lifespan severs the view of arising and ceasing and reveals the true, eternal essence; it merely enables the arousal of superior wisdom.
Hearing this sutra extensively, however, provides the four types of knowledge and vision, exhausting the path of the One Vehicle, and thus enables the birth of the seed of omniscience (*sarvajñā*).
Yet, though worldly people do not calculate such hearing and upholding, they are nonetheless able to arouse superior wisdom and give birth to the seed of omniscience."
Who is this person? It is one who encounters the royal banquet yet does not eat, or who finds a pearl in their garment yet falls asleep in intoxication.

How lamentable! Ajita, if anyone hears me speak of my long lifespan and, with a profound heart, believes and understands it, they shall see the Buddha always present on Vulture Peak Mountain, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, preaching the Dharma.
(Jie-huan said: "When the views of arising and ceasing are exhausted, the mark of true permanence is manifest at every turn.
Furthermore, he saw this Sahā world, its ground of lapis lazuli, level and even.
The eight paths were demarcated by Jambūnada gold, with rows of jewel trees and all the terraces and towers made entirely of jewels. All the assembly of Bodhisattvas...
Abiding therein, if there is one who can contemplate in this way, it should be known that this is the mark of profound faith and understanding.
(Jiehuan said: "When the notions of filth and purity are forgotten, then every step taken is within the realm of supreme excellence.")
Jie-huan said: "The true reality (*dharmatā*) of body and land is fundamentally and originally of one suchness (*eka-tathatā*). Birth-and-death, defilement, and purity all arise from emotional views.
Therefore, when views are exhausted and emotions forgotten, the marks of true permanence and the realm of supreme wondrousness manifest before one at every touch.
None may participate herein without profound faith and understanding of the secret teaching on the lifespan."
Chapter Eighteen: Rejoicing in Merit.

As for "rejoicing," it refers to those who are unable to listen to, read, or practice according to the teachings with single-minded devotion, but merely rejoice in accordance with what they have heard.

He delights in preaching it to others. Following his instructions, he delights in hearing it even for a brief moment; by hearing it, he attains supreme merit. Therefore, this is designated as the "Chapter on Life.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if there is anyone who hears this Dharma..."
"How much merit does one who rejoices in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* obtain? At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:

"Ajita, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or other wise persons—whether old or young—who, having heard this sūtra and rejoiced in it, depart from the dharma assembly and go elsewhere..."

Whether in a monastic dwelling, in a secluded place, in the streets and lanes of a city, or in the villages and fields, they shall expound the Dharma according to their strength for their parents, kinsmen, good friends, and spiritual mentors.
Having heard it, these people will rejoice and in turn teach others; others, having heard it, will likewise rejoice and teach others. In this way, it shall be passed on from one to another.
Upon reaching the fiftieth person, [Jiehuan said:

"When one first hears the Dharma assembly, receiving it directly from the teacher, the merit is most supreme. As one rejoices in it and transmits the teaching further, one gradually moves further away from the teacher.
By the time one reaches the fiftieth person, the words have become very distant, yet the merit remains immeasurable—as described below."
[The third and final collation]. (The fifth merit).
Ānanda, I shall now describe the merit of rejoicing of the fiftieth son or daughter of good family;
you should listen attentively. Suppose there were four hundred million *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, filled with beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth.
Those born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; those with form or without form;

those with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception; those without feet, with two feet, four feet, or many feet—all such beings included within the category of sentient beings.
There are those who seek merit; whatever articles of enjoyment they desire, he provides them all.

To each and every sentient being, he gives gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, and various exquisite treasures sufficient to fill Jambudvīpa, as well as elephants, horses, and carriages, and palaces and towers made of the seven precious gems.
[The Precept Ring said: "In the *Saṃghāṭa* world-system, sentient beings are inexhaustible, yet one can bestow gifts such as precious objects; thus, their merit is vast.

Devas, humans, ghosts, and animals constitute the six destinies (*ṣadgati*). Embryonic, oviparous, moisture-born, and transformational births comprise the four modes of birth (*caturyoni*), encompassing all categories of form and perception.

It is established upon the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). Because consciousness falsely constitutes the boundaries, there are the four directions.

Chapter Twenty: The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging.
"Never Disparaging" was a previous incarnation of Śākyamuni. During the time of King Awesome Sound, he diligently upheld the wondrous Dharma and extensively bestowed its benefits.

This is the trace of his guidance. By means of the principle of Buddha-nature, he universally addressed the fourfold assembly: he would bow when encountering the good and feel no anger upon meeting the wicked;
thus everyone respected him, and for this reason he was called "Never-Disparaging" (Adhimātra).
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta: "You should now know this:
if anyone slanders one who upholds the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, they will incur the retribution for great sin as previously described;
whereas the merit they shall obtain is as previously described—namely, the purification of their eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind."

(The Southern Text further states: "The reason for manifesting the power of diligent upholding at the outset is to warn the assembly, so that they may know the retribution for upholding or violating [the precepts] is unfailing, and thus develop deep faith in the extensive benefits of diligent upholding. The Precept Ring says: As for the sin of slandering and disparaging [the Dharma], it is as explained at the end of the "Simile" chapter and in the "Dharma Master" chapter;

The kalpa was named 'Free from Decline' [離衰], meaning that worldly ways flourished together. The country was named 'Great Achievement' [大成], signifying correct transformation."
There was no deficiency.
That Buddha Prabhūtaratna, within that world, preached the Dharma for devas, humans, and asuras.

For those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths, delivering them from birth, old age, sickness, and death, so they might ultimately attain nirvāṇa. For those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha...
The Buddha teaches the Dharma corresponding to the twelve links of dependent origination for the sake of all bodhisattvas;
and based on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the six *pāramitās* to bring the wisdom of a Buddha to ultimate completion.
(Jie-huan said: "This passage also describes how Vīradhvaja taught the Three Vehicles.

He attained Great Power. This Buddha King of Majestic Voice had a lifespan of four hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand eons.

The duration that his True Dharma remained in the world was equal to the number of dust motes in one Jambudvīpa; the duration that his Semblance Dharma remained in the world was equal to the number of dust motes in the four continents.
After that Buddha had extensively benefited sentient beings, he then entered parinirvāṇa, followed by the periods of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma.
After their parinirvāṇa, another Buddha appeared in this land, also named Vimalacandra-rāja Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām,
Buddha, Bhagavān. In this manner, there were twenty-two thousand koṭis of Buddhas, all bearing the same name.

After the Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound had first entered parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma had ceased, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there were bhikṣus of overweening pride who possessed great power.

"One shall surely attain Buddhahood.

"All you bodhisattvas on the path shall become buddhas.
Because he constantly spoke these words, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas,
and upāsikās who were arrogant toward him called him "Never-Disparaging."

Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think? Was that Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging at that time anyone else? It was none other than myself.

Chapter Twenty-one: The Supernatural Powers of the Tathāgata.
Herein, this Bodhisattva makes a formal request, and the Tathāgata immediately manifests supernatural powers and praises the virtue of the sutra in order to inspire faith.
To cause it to spread widely, it is therefore called the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a thousand worlds, who had emerged from the earth, all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, after the extinction of the Buddha, wherever the World-Honored One’s divided bodies reside in various lands and pass into parinirvāṇa..."

"Venerable One, you should expound this sutra in detail. Why is this? We ourselves also desire to attain this truly pure Great Dharma, to receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, transcribe, and make offerings to it."
(Jie-huan said: "The 'Chapter on the Spontaneous Emergence' describes how the assembly manifested before the Buddha to encourage him to uphold [the Dharma];
here, the request is extended for the sake of universal penetration. The extensive exposition concerns benefiting others, while the act of receiving and upholding concerns one's own benefit.")

At that time, the World-Honored One [addressed] Mañjuśrī and countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had long resided in the Sahā world, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Before the entire assembly of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, he manifested great supernormal power and extended his broad and long tongue, reaching up as far as the Brahma world.
From every pore, he emits immeasurable and innumerable rays of light of various colors, which completely illuminate the worlds of the ten directions.
(Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* states: "The illusory arts of a magician can manifest all manner of things:

an asura may transform his body to be equal in size to Mount Sumeru; a dragon may send down rain in an instant, its refreshing moisture pervading the world beneath. Yet such beings are possessed of greed and hatred.")
If even the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of one who is still deluded is such as this, how much more so the wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-prajñā*), which possesses complete mastery!
Thus, while the tongue may reach the Brahma-world and its light pervades the ten directions, these are merely the function of a single atom within the wisdom of the Dharma-realm.
As for the "long-resident bodhisattvas," they are those dwelling here in the lower regions of this Sahā world (the Brahma-world being the first dhyāna heaven).
Jie-huan said: "The extending of the broad and long tongue up to the Brahma-world manifests the divine power of eloquent exposition.
The emission of immeasurable light that shines throughout the ten directions manifests the divine power of wisdom-illumination.

Before praising the merit of the sutra, he first manifests these divine powers; beginning from the extension of the tongue and the emission of light, up to the shaking of all the heavens, they demonstrate thorough penetration."

Regarding the Buddha-fields, the text concludes by stating: "If one were to use such supernatural power to describe the virtues of this sutra for billions of kalpas, one would still be unable to exhaust them.
This most clearly demonstrates its supreme excellence. The supernatural power of the Tathāgata is the effortless, wondrous function within the essence of the Dharma-realm.
The Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jeweled trees were likewise;
they too extended their broad and long tongues and emitted immeasurable light (these Buddhas who are emanations of Śākyamuni also assist by following this same path).
When Śākyamuni Buddha and the Buddhas beneath the jewel trees manifested their supernatural powers, they did so for a full hundred thousand years.
Thereafter, they withdrew their tongue-marks and simultaneously cleared their throats and snapped their fingers.
These two sounds reached all the Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions, causing the earth everywhere to quake in six ways.
Jiehuan said: "Upon a tongue only a few inches long, he manifests [himself] as far as the Brahma-world; in the space of a single assembly, he manifests [a lifespan of] hundreds of thousands of years.

Furthermore, with a single cough or the snap of a finger, his voice can pervade the ten directions and shake the great earth—all of which clearly demonstrates the excellence of his supernatural powers."
In brief, all the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata, all the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgata,
all the secret and essential treasuries of the Tathāgata, and all the most profound matters of the Tathāgata are all contained within this sutra.
He proclaimed and expounded [this]:
"The 'dharmas that exist' refers to what is attained within the *bodhimaṇḍa*. 'Sovereign spiritual power' refers to that which manifests in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*).
'The secret treasury' refers to the dharma that cannot be pointed out. 'The profoundly deep matter' refers to the mind."
All that cannot be transmitted [is contained] within this sutra.
Therefore, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, you should single-mindedly receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe it.
As it has been taught, in whatever land one practices accordingly— wherever this sutra is upheld, recited, read, explained, written down, or practiced as taught;
wherever the scroll of the sutra may reside, whether in a garden, a grove, beneath a tree, in a monastery,
in a layperson’s house, in a hall, or in mountain valleys and wildernesses— in those places...

he has attained such samādhis as these, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, characterized by mutual penetration, harmonious integration, and inexhaustible layering—all of which are possessed by Wondrous Sound.
Because he possesses these, he is able to accomplish sublime practices and circulate the sublime Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña addressed the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara: "Do not disparage that land, nor conceive a notion of it as inferior.
Good son, that Sahā world is uneven with highs and lows; it is filled with mountains of earth and stone and is replete with filth and impurity.
The Buddha’s body is short and small, and the forms of the assembly of bodhisattvas are likewise small. Yet your body is forty-two..."
"It is one thousand yojanas away. My body is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas tall.
Your body is foremost in its beauty, possessing hundreds of thousands of millions of merits and a most exquisite radiance; therefore, go. Do not hold that land in low esteem.

If you should conceive thoughts of inferiority toward the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or their lands," the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara said to his Buddha, "World-Honored One, I shall now proceed to the Sahā world."
The world is entirely through the power of the Tathāgata, the playful manifestation of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers, and the adornment of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom.
(And as for the homage: the reason all three virtues are called "Tathāgata" is that the power and function of that which I am now proceeding toward...)

Therefore, while manifesting various forms and preaching various dharmas, there is no diminution in his supernormal powers or wisdom, for he remains as he truly is.
The Precept Ring said: "The Buddha-body in this Sahā world conceals its excellence and manifests inferiority.

Then, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, without rising from his seat and without moving his body, entered into samādhi. By the power of this samādhi,
not far from the Dharma-seat on Vulture Peak, he manifested eighty-four thousand multitudes of various precious jewels.
A lotus flower with a stem of Jāmbūnada gold, leaves of white silver, filaments of diamond, and a pericarp made of karketana jewel.

"I shall manifest my form for you. Then, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed those bodhisattvas: "Come, noble sons!

(Jiehuan said: "Mañjuśrī, I pray that the World-Honored One will, by means of his supernormal powers, manifest the Sublime Sound.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land and set out together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas (and it is said:
"This is Gadgadasvara coming to pay his respects").

The Precept Ring said: "Those who came together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas demonstrate that wondrous conduct transforms the afflictions of sentient beings extensively according to their needs.
As they passed through various lands, the earth shook in six ways, and everywhere there rained down seven-jeweled lotus flowers and hundreds of thousands of celestial melodies."
Without being struck, it resounds of itself.

This bodhisattva’s eyes are like the petals of a vast blue lotus; even if a hundred thousand million moons were gathered together, his countenance would be more upright and handsome than they.
His body is of a true golden color, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits.
His majestic power is blazing and his radiance shines brilliantly; he is fully endowed with all the primary marks, possessing a body as firm and solid as that of Nārāyaṇa.
(Jièhuán says: This refers to the marks and signs extending forty-two thousand *yojanas*. "Harmonious integration" (*héhé*) means gathering together.

(Meng). (Jie-huan said: "This demonstrates that the Dharma-body is adorned with the treasure of the Dharma.
He entered the seven-jeweled terrace and ascended into the void, remaining at a height of seven *tāla* trees above the ground.
Surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas who paid him respectful homage, he came to this Sahā world and Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Having arrived, he descended from the seven-jeweled terrace.
Taking a necklace worth hundreds of thousands [of gold pieces], he went to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he presented the necklace and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, the Buddha Viśuddhapuṣpadhvajarāja asks after the World-Honored One:
Are you free from illness and minor afflictions? Is your daily life light and easy? Do you dwell in peace and happiness? Are the four great elements in harmony? Can worldly matters be endured?”
"No. Are sentient beings easy to deliver? Do they not have much greed, anger, ignorance, jealousy, stinginess, or pride?
Do they not lack filial piety toward their parents or respect for śramaṇas? Do they not hold wrong views or harbor unwholesome minds? Do they restrain the five sensory faculties? "World-Honored One."
"Can sentient beings subdue all the māras and enemies? Has the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who entered parinirvāṇa long ago, come from within his stupa made of the seven treasures to hear the Dharma?
Furthermore, inquire after the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna: Is he at ease, free from affliction, and able to endure remaining for a long time?"
(He addressed the Buddha and asked about the matters of enduring [the world]. Greed, anger, delusion, pride, and so forth are all matters that must be endured and transcended.
The five faculties are called the five desires; the various demons are called the five aggregates.)
The Precept Ring said: "The above are all the words of the former King Śubhavyūha’s inquiry.

"Virtue. He possesses such supernormal powers.
