The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, for twelve thousand years, made offerings of one hundred thousand kinds of music to the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja,
and presented him with eighty-four thousand bowls made of the seven precious gems. By virtue of these causes and conditions and their karmic retribution,
he has now been born in the land of the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasamudgatajñāna and possesses such supernormal powers.

He delights in proclaiming the sound of the Dharma; the alms bowl is his appropriate vessel. He delights in offering a hundred thousand kinds of music to demonstrate his desire to widely proclaim the sublime Dharma;

he offers eighty-four thousand bowls to demonstrate his desire to respond to and transform the afflictions of sentient beings. Therefore, as a result, he now possesses a divine spirit who follows him and responds with sublime sounds.

"Śubhavyūha, what do you think? Was that Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara who, at the time of the Buddha Ghoṣadatta-rāja, made offerings of music and presented precious vessels, anyone else? It was this very Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara.
Śubhavyūha, this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara has already made offerings to and drawn near countless Buddhas over a long period of time."
They have planted roots of virtue. Furthermore, they have planted [roots of virtue] before hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Guṇakara, you see only that the bodhisattva Gadgadasvara’s body is here; however, this bodhisattva manifests various bodies and everywhere preaches this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings.
(Jie-huan said: "The wondrous voice and the responsive transformations of Avalokiteśvara can all manifest bodies within the ten realms.

From devas, humans, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras—these are called the six ordinary realms—to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas—these are called the four holy realms. These constitute the ten realms.")
“Śāriputra, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara is able to rescue and protect all sentient beings in the Sahā world.
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva manifests such various transformations and bodies here in this Sahā land to preach this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings;
yet, in his supernormal powers, transformations, and wisdom, there is no diminution whatsoever. This Bodhisattva, by means of...”
His manifold wisdom shines brightly throughout the Sahā world, causing all sentient beings to each attain what they need to know.
It is likewise so throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions.

(Xiangmai said: "To say that although there are various transformations, the divine wisdom remains undiminished, refers to what was previously called 'attaining the three virtues of the Tathāgata'—being able to remain as it always has been.
To say that 'wisdom shines with clear illumination' refers to the guidance provided through skillful means (*upāya*).
To say that 'each attains what they know' refers to understanding according to one's respective kind)."
Jiehuan said: "This consists of three sections. The first restates [the teaching] regarding the salvation of this Sahā world;

the second restates the power of spiritual transformations and the illumination of wisdom; the third restates that as it is in this direction, so it is in the ten directions. This is called 'extensive manifestation.'"
If there are those who are to be delivered by means of the form of a śrāvaka, he manifests the form of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.
If there are those who are to be delivered by means of the form of a pratyekabuddha, he manifests the form of a pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma for them.

If there are those who are to be delivered by means of the form of a bodhisattva, he manifests the form of a bodhisattva and preaches the Dharma for them. If there are those who are to be delivered by means of the form of a Buddha, he then manifests...

He manifests in the form of a Buddha to preach the Dharma. In this way, he manifests various forms according to what is appropriate for those to be saved, even manifesting his own parinirvāṇa for those who are to be saved by means of parinirvāṇa.
Flower Virtue, such is the manner in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara has accomplished the power of great supernormal knowledges and wisdom.
(Jie-huan said: "This corresponds to the four noble ones; 'Huade' and 'Miaoyin' are the concluding answers.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Huade addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Miaoyin has deeply planted roots of goodness."
“World-Honored One, in what samādhi does this bodhisattva abide, such that he is able to manifest transformations everywhere in this manner to deliver sentient beings?
(Jie-huan says: This is an inquiry concerning samādhi.)
The Buddha told Flower Virtue Bodhisattva: "Good son, this samādhi is named 'Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
Abiding within this samādhi, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings in such a manner."
(Jie-huan said: "Like a pure maṇi gem that reflects colors according to its surroundings, may these wondrous practices circulate until this goal is reached.

When this chapter on the coming and going of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara was being preached, forty-two thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the Bodhisattva Puṣpadatta attained the Lotus Samādhi (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*).
(Nan-yueh further said: "This is what is meant by 'accomplishing the virtue of the true mark through wondrous practice'").

the Lotus Samādhi is the attainment of the function of the true mark."
Chapter Twenty-five: The Universal Gate of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
A single utterance constitutes a sound; their combination constitutes a tone. Amidst the various sounds of suffering in the world, he observes them all equally and rescues them simultaneously.
He is titled Avalokiteśvara. His wondrous and perfect practice issues forth from the one mind; his responsiveness is all-pervading, and thus he is titled the Universal Gate (Samantamukha).

Jiehuan says: This refers to what was previously explained in the preceding chapter—how he manifests various forms through his wondrous voice to preach the Dharma and rescue beings from all manner of hardships.
It is no different from that of Avalokiteśvara; it is merely brief rather than universal, and subtle rather than perfect.

Yet Avalokiteśvara does not depart from these practices, for he is able to contemplate their sounds and respond according to each resonance, providing a perfect response throughout the great trichiliocosm without any marks of coming or going.
What is called the karma of sovereign mastery is manifested through the Universal Gate; thus, one advances toward Miaoyin (Gandhahasti).
In reality, these two sages share a single path, acting as beginning and end for one another.
(The Southern Inscription states: "The subsequent verses praise the virtue of Guanyin while also mentioning Miaoyin; thus we know that these two sages share one and the same Way.
That which is the practice of Miaoyin is manifested as the Universal Gate; thus we know that [the two] are identical from beginning to end.")
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One, for what causes and conditions is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara named 'Avalokiteśvara'?"
If a fool were to praise me, saying: "The world is boundless and its dust is turbulent; sentient beings are countless and their karma is vast.
The river of craving has no bottom and its waves flow on endlessly; therefore my name is 'Inexhaustible Intent. The practice of Avalokiteśvara is likewise so."
The Commentary on the Precepts Ring states: "That which is about to reveal the Universal Gate (Pumen) is initiated by Akṣayamati;
this signifies that the perfect practice of the Universal Gate manifests in inexhaustible ways."

The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati: "Good son, if there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings who undergo various sufferings and afflictions, and they hear of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon his name, then the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara..."
Immediately upon observing their voices, all attained liberation. (Jiehuan remarked:

"This refers to observing and rescuing all at once amidst the clamor of various sufferings. [Yu] Lin Dharma Master invoked the name [of the Buddha] for seven days and was spared from disaster in the Tang;
Sun Jingde recited the sutra a thousand times and preserved his life in the Wei. This is precisely it.
[To be] liberated [from all].
The Precept Ring says: Regarding "contemplation" (*guan*) within sound and speech, it refers to the wisdom of contemplation responding to phenomena.

Contemplation is true contemplation and pure contemplation; both are wisdom, compassion, and kindness. The essence of contemplating contemplation and the nature of hearing hearing are fundamentally without suffering.
Sentient beings are unable to turn their hearing inward; instead, they follow after sounds and wander through the cycle of existence, thereby undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
Avalokiteśvara does not follow after the objects of sound, nor does he give rise to false perceptions or views; thus, he is liberated in every respect.
He causes those sentient beings who suffer to hold his name, and those who behold him also attain liberation, because he is truly empowered by the force of genuine, pure compassion and contemplation.
Furthermore,
if there are those who hold the name of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, even if they enter a great fire, the fire shall not burn them,
by virtue of the majestic spiritual power of this Bodhisattva. If they are being swept away by a great flood, by invoking his name, they shall immediately find shallow ground.
[The commentary] says: (Jièhuán stated: "This refers to being liberated from external karma.
If there were hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions of sentient beings who, for the sake of seeking gold, silver, lapis lazuli, *śaṅkha* (conch), agate, and coral...
When treasures such as amber and pearls enter the great ocean, even if a black wind should blow their ship and cast them adrift into the realm of the rākṣasa demons,
if among those on board there is even a single person who invokes the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, [they shall be saved].
All these people have attained liberation from the peril of the rākṣasas. For this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara.

(Formerly, at the Prime Minister’s residence, [the minister] asked Ziyu about the meaning of being drifted and cast down by black winds. Ziyu called out his name and chanted it; the official’s face suddenly changed with alarm. Ziyu said:
"This is precisely what it means to be drifted and cast down by black winds; thus, ordinary people cannot escape [from] following the sound.")
"Transmigration; drifting and falling in a single thought—all is like this. Jiehuan said:
"The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* clarifies the merit of the fourteen kinds of fearlessness. The first is:
because I do not observe the sounds themselves, but rather observe the observer, I cause suffering sentient beings to observe their own sounds and thereby attain liberation. Now, as for 'not...'"
To observe the observer by means of the observation of Avalokiteśvara is the true contemplation that leaves behind defilements and restores one's original nature.

When defilements are left behind and the original nature is restored, all delusions naturally fall away; thus, it enables suffering sentient beings who receive this true contemplation to immediately attain liberation.
Second, when cognition and vision are revolved back, fire cannot burn them. Third, when seeing and hearing are revolved back, then...

Water cannot drown it. This is because seeing and cognition belong to the element of fire, while hearing and listening belong to the element of water. When seeing and cognition revolve back [to their source], one leaves the dust of fire;

when hearing and listening are bestowed [back to their source], one leaves the dust of water. Once these illusory objects are detached from, the true nature is thereby restored; thus, there is nothing that can burn or drown it.
When one is able to revolve the virtue of seeing, then the fire of afflictions and the water of craving and attachment both cease to exist.
It can burn and drown one. Fourth, by extinguishing delusions and severing killing, ghosts cannot cause harm;
all this is due to the empowerment of the contemplative power of leaving behind sensory dust and restoring one's true nature.
Akṣayamati, such is the majestic and sublime power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
(Jie-huan says: This refers to the formation of external karma.)

If there are sentient beings who are excessively prone to lustful desire, and who constantly mindfully revere and pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately become free from desire.
(Jiehuan says: This refers to liberation from internal karma. This arises from the cultivation of hearing and becoming detached from sensory objects, such that one is no longer plundered by forms.)
[He] applied force [to it].
The Precept Ring said: "Sentient beings are plundered by form because their habitual desires unite with sensory objects; thus they are 'plundered by form.

Once one is graced by this wondrous power, desire and love dry up, and the faculties and their objects no longer meet. Thus, even if there are seductive forms, they cannot plunder or disturb [the mind], and so one attains [liberation]."
Free from desire,
Ajita, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great majestic power and brings benefit to many. Therefore,
sentient beings should always keep him in mind.
(Śīlaka said: "This refers to the internal karma.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara travel through this Sahā world?

(Nan-yueh added: "These are the thirty-two transformations. Jiehuan said:

By virtue of this power, my body manifests thirty-two transformations to enter all lands, beginning with the Buddha-body and ending with humans and non-humans—
constituting these thirty-two forms— all of which are spontaneously and freely accomplished through the wondrous power of non-action.

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati: "Good son, if there are sentient beings in any land who are to be delivered by means of a Buddha-body, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately manifests a Buddha-body and preaches the Dharma for them.

If they are to be delivered by means of a Pratyekabuddha-body, he immediately manifests a Pratyekabuddha-body and preaches the Dharma for them. If they are to be delivered by means of a Śrāvaka-body..."
Regarding those who attain deliverance: he immediately manifests in the form of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.

(Jiehuan says: "Only the three sages are mentioned here; however, in the 'Chapter on the Wondrous Sound,' the stage of the bodhisattva is opened. This [manifestation] should actually belong to the stage of the Buddha.
It should be read as 'ying' (to respond), meaning that he responds to them according to their faculties)."
To those who are to be saved by the body of Brahmā, he manifests the body of Brahmā and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by the body of Śakra, he manifests the body of Śakra and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by the body of Maheśvara, he manifests the body of Maheśvara and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be saved by the body of a celestial general...
To those who are to be delivered through the body of a celestial general, he manifests as a celestial general and preaches the Dharma to them.
To those who are to be delivered through the body of Vaiśravaṇa, he manifests as Vaiśravaṇa and preaches the Dharma to them.
(Brahmā is the lord of the first dhyāna heaven; Śakra is the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
Īśvara dwells at the summit of the desire realm; Maheśvara dwells at the summit of the form realm; the Heavenly Great General commands the spirits and ghosts;
the Four Heavenly Kings govern the world; Vaiśravaṇa dwells in the north and is the most honored).
Akṣayamati, this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara has accomplished such meritorious virtues; assuming various forms, he wanders through all lands to deliver and liberate sentient beings.
(Jiehuan said: "This is what manifests from the bonds.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings..."
Those who hear this chapter on the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, his sovereign deeds, and his supernormal powers manifested through the Universal Gate,
should know that their merit will not be small.
(Xiangmai said: "Regarding the title of Guanyin, it is sometimes called Guanshiyin and sometimes called Guanzizai; its practice is sometimes called Pumen and sometimes called Yuantong.
It is called 'Guanshiyin' when speaking of its virtue in responding to things according to the contemplation of compassion and the contemplation of kindness.
It is called 'Guanzizai' when speaking of the power of illuminating the mind according to true contemplation and pure contemplation.")
When one issues forth from the single mind, there is nothing to which it does not respond; this is called the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*).
When one reflects back from the myriad things, there is nothing that is not harmonized; this is called Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*). In reality, they are but one.
The Precept Ring says: "In the past, when the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder (Dharaṇīdhara) encountered the Buddha Viśvabhū, he was instructed to maintain the ground of the mind;
thus, all things become level. This means that by employing the wondrous Dharma within one's own mind, external afflictions are naturally pacified so that they can no longer cause harm.
Therefore, upon hearing this chapter, [the Precept Ring] deeply praises its merit, intending to manifest the karma of sovereign mastery."
The practice of the Universal Gate is, in truth, the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground.

If those who hear and uphold this can maintain their mind-ground with equanimity, then external afflictions will naturally subside and be unable to cause harm; they will be able to bestow fearlessness upon all who are terrified.
Through this, the karma of mastery and the practice of the Universal Gate will become one's own possession. Therefore it is said:
If there are those who hear this, you should know that the merit of such persons is not small. Avalokiteśvara is sometimes designated by the title *Īśvara*, and sometimes by the name *Īśvarakarma*.

To be designated by the title *Īśvara* means that his mind has attained mastery (*vaśitā*), as is the case when the Heart Sūtra refers to him as "Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. To be named *Īśvarakarma* means that his speech has attained mastery.

This is as described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* regarding the "wondrous power of non-action. Nevertheless, all dharmas and practices are nothing other than demonstrations intended to cause one to maintain the ground of the mind;
therefore, this [sutra] ultimately concludes by extolling and manifesting the "Earth-Holding" Samādhi.
When the Buddha preached this "Universal Gate" chapter, eighty-four thousand sentient beings within the assembly all resolved to attain the peerless,
unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, [the Master] Nan said: "Avalokiteśvara embodies this principle to accomplish the practice of the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*). Adapting his manifestations according to the various classes of beings, he brings himself into equality with all things.
Therefore, those who hear of his reputation give rise to such a mind. These [practices] are called the 'perfect practice' (*paripūrṇa-caryā*) by which one accomplishes the most supreme virtue."
The Precept Ring says: "The Peerless" means that there is nothing peerless—that is, no object with which it can be equaled. "Peer" means that all objects are equal to it.
Since there is no object with which it can be equaled, yet it is able to be equal to all objects—this is the supreme virtue of the Tathāgata.
Chapter Twenty-Six: Dhāraṇī.
"Dhāraṇī" in the language of China means "total retention. It is the wondrous power of mindfulness and wisdom, the secret speech of all Buddhas.

By means of a single syllable, it can encompass immeasurable dharmas and sustain immeasurable beings. It subdues the heterodox, establishes the orthodox, eradicates evil, and gives rise to goodness—all of these it encompasses in their entirety.
This is what is meant by "upholding it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if there is a son of good family..."
“If there is one who can receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—whether by reciting it until they have mastered it, or by copying its scrolls—how much merit will they obtain?

The Buddha told Bhaisajyarāja: “If there were a son of good family who made offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in eight hundred million nayutas of Ganges Rivers, what do you think? Would the merit obtained by such a person be great? [He replied: “Very much so.”

"Much, World-Honored One. The Buddha said: "If a son of good family is able, regarding this sutra, to receive and uphold even a single four-line verse, reciting it, explaining its meaning, and practicing according to the teaching, his merit will be exceedingly great."

(Bhaiṣajyarāja is the later incarnation of Priyadarśana. Through his ascetic practices and upholding of the sutra, with his resolve set upon its propagation and protection, he has brought forth this chapter.

As for the merit of upholding the sutra, it has been clarified repeatedly in the preceding chapters; for example, compared to the merit described in the "Dharma-Teacher" chapter, it does not even equal that of making offerings to ten trillion buddhas.
Compared to the merit in the "Rejoicing" chapter, it does not even equal that of bestowing various external objects or attaining minor fruits. Until...)

This merit surpasses that of making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of eight hundred million *koṭis* of Ganges Rivers; it clarifies that the benefit of upholding and practicing [the precepts] is profound, and the merit obtained is even more excellent.
The *Jie-huan* (Ring of Precepts) states: "In order to extend broad protection, one first asks who attains blessings, so that future generations may know the nature of this practice."
It becomes ever more profound; the merit attained becomes ever more excellent, and they successively provide great protection for it.
Chapter Twenty-seven: The Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment.
Formerly, four bhikṣus made a pact to dwell in the mountain forests and diligently uphold the Sublime Dharma. One of them went out to beg for alms and saw the majesty of the king.
Staff. Suddenly, he gave rise to attachment; because of this, he was reborn as a king named Wondrous Adornment (*Sudarśana*).

Now I shall recount his original story, desiring to enable practitioners to protect themselves with the Way: externally to ward off the demons of perception, internally to sever evil thoughts, to eliminate false conditions, and to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly: "In the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there was a Buddha named Meghadundubhisvararājasaṃkusumitābhijña, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
His land was named Prabhāvyūha, and his kalpa was named Priyadarśana. This was the Dharma of that Buddha."
In the middle [of that land], there was a king named Wondrous Adornment (Sudarśana). The king’s consort was named Pure Virtue (Viśuddhaguṇā). They had two sons:
the first was named Pure Treasury (Viśuddhagarbha), and the second was named Pure Eye (Viśuddhanetra).
"Pure Virtue" means that although he manifests a defiled body, his fundamental virtues are pure. "Treasury" refers to that which contains the wondrous principle.

"Pure Eye" refers to that which is revealed by wondrous wisdom; these are all the virtues he possesses. Because he is endowed with this wondrously pure wisdom and principle, he is able to transform the heterodox into the virtue of a flower.
These two sons possess great supernormal powers, merit, and wisdom. For a long time they have cultivated the path practiced by Bodhisattvas, namely:

the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. And so forth...
One attains complete clarity and thorough penetration of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).

(Supplementary Note: Mindfulness is for contemplating the Dharma; diligence is for advancing in cultivation; effort is for proceeding toward realization; the faculties (*indriya*) ensure that abilities are not uprooted;

the powers (*bala*) ensure that one is not overcome; awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) enables decisive understanding; and the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) provide comprehensive integration. These are all established as mutually dependent conditions. The nature of the mind is like...)

The great earth is like the seed; the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are like the sowing; the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are like the planting; the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are like the sprouting of shoots;

the five faculties (*indriya*) are like the roots; the five powers (*bala*) are like the stalks; the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are like the flowers; and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) is like the fruit. One who possesses both of these [sets] is called one who is "endowed with the body" (*kāyasaṃpanna*).
Jie-huan said: "Skillful means are not included within the enumeration of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), yet they facilitate the realization of all six.

Compassion, mercy, joy, and equanimity are called the four immeasurable minds (catvāry apramāṇāni). In the practice of the Mahāyāna, these four minds constitute the essence, the six perfections the function, and the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) the assistance;
through this, one attains the fruit of Buddhahood. Both disciples have fully understood and mastered these thirty-seven [factors]."

The "categories" (skandhas) are the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, which constitute the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). The transformation of evil into good constitutes the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).

Desire, effort, mind, and investigation constitute the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom constitute the five faculties (*indriya*). When these five faculties subdue the Māras and external adversaries, they become the five powers (*bala*).
Wisdom, discernment, joy, tranquility, equanimity, and concentration constitute the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). [These include] vision, thought, and verbal action.
He was instructed to cultivate mindfulness and concentration as the Eightfold Noble Path.
Furthermore, he attained the Bodhisattva Pure Samādhi, the Sun and Star宿 Samādhi, the Pure Light Samādhi, and the Pure Color Samādhi.
The Samādhi of Pure Illumination, the Samādhi of Long Adornment, and the Samādhi of the Treasury of Great Majestic Virtue—one thoroughly penetrates all these samādhis as well.
(Supplementary Note: Pure light can manifest myriad forms; pure color is not congealed into shape; pure illumination clearly perceives the ten thousand phenomena.)
The Dharma is the eternally adorned, non-primitive Dharmakāya, the treasury of great majestic power endowed with great spiritual efficacy.
The "Ring of Precepts" states: "Pure Samādhi is the fundamental source of the Pure Treasury and the Pure Eye.
The sun and the stars represent the illuminating functions of fundamental wisdom and discriminative wisdom."
At that time, that Buddha, wishing to guide King Subhavyūha and out of compassion for sentient beings, preached this Lotus Sūtra.
(Jie Huan says: "This refers to the King of Constellations preaching the sūtra.")
Thereupon, the two sons addressed their parents, saying: "Excellent, O parents!
We pray that you will go at once to the presence of the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound King-Flower-Wisdom to attend upon and make offerings to him. Why is this?
Because a Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower, or like a one-eyed turtle encountering the hole of a floating log. Yet our own past merit is profound and vast."
We have been born at a time when we encounter the Buddha-dharma; therefore, our parents should grant us permission to go forth into homelessness. Why is this?
Because Buddhas are difficult to encounter, and such a time is likewise hard to meet.
The Āgamas state: Beneath Mount Sumeru in the great ocean, there is a one-eyed turtle and a log with a single hole.
If the turtle can place its head through the hole of the log, it may escape drowning; however, that log drifts around Mount Sumeru, and only once every three thousand years do they happen to meet.
"Furthermore, to direct a single eye toward a single aperture is considered extremely difficult.

Jiehuan said, "This metaphor illustrates how difficult it is to encounter the Buddha-dharma. This is because sentient beings are mired in their own biased views, and moreover, because the sages do not appear in the world every generation."
At that time, King Wonderful Adornment’s eighty-four thousand women of the inner palace were all capable of receiving and upholding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The Bodhisattva Pure Eye had long since attained mastery in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Samādhi*, as had the Bodhisattva Pure Treasury.
Having already, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, attained mastery in the samādhi of transcending all evil destinies,

he desires to cause all sentient beings to leave behind all evil destinies. The king’s consort has attained the samādhi of the assembly of all Buddhas and is able to know the secret treasury of all Buddhas.
(Xiang Mai said: "This account describes the virtuous assembly of the palace, making it easy to encourage and transform them.

The King and his harem constitute the receptive capacity (*adhikāra*), while Jingzang and Jingyan serve as the teachers. Because the capacity and the teaching are in harmony, transformation is easily achieved)."
The virtue of Kaihuan was that her spiritual faculties were pure and sharp. The virtue of Jingyan was that she had wondrously attained the true mark (*dharmatā*).
The virtue of Jingzang was that she was well able to provide relief and assistance. The virtue of the Lady was that she deeply understood the essentials of the Dharma.

As for the "Collection of Samādhis," it is the essential compendium of the assemblies of all Buddhas and the ultimate destination of the Three Vehicles. Therefore, by attaining this samādhi, one is able to know the secrets.

[The] *Zang* [edition] states: "At that time, that Buddha preached the Dharma for the king, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. The king was greatly delighted. (Xing Jianzi remarked:

"The preceding passage says the Buddha preached the Dharma for the king; the following passage says the king abandoned the Dharma and turned his mind [toward it]. This refers to the king's initial devotion to worldly matters and his subsequent transformation through the Buddha's teaching.)
At that time, King Wonderful Adornment and his consort took off from their necks pearl necklaces worth hundreds of thousands and scattered them over the Buddha.
In mid-air, these transformed into a precious four-pillared pavilion. Within the pavilion was a great jeweled couch, spread with hundreds of thousands of millions [of cloths].
Celestial robes. Upon them is a Buddha, seated in the full lotus posture, emitting great radiance.

(The bestowed pearl necklaces transform into a seat of the Dharma-emptiness; the garments of gentle patience and the body of precious awakening are manifested through the Buddha’s power to arouse right mindfulness.)
At that time, King Wonderful Adornment had this thought: "The Buddha’s body is rare and marvelous; it is upright, dignified, and extraordinary, having achieved the foremost and most subtle of forms."
[And Nan said: "This means that the deviant mind has been utterly severed and right mindfulness has appeared before one; therefore, one receives the prediction [of enlightenment].
Jiehuan said: "At that time, upon seeing the sublime marks, the king suddenly realized that the illusory and delusive forms of the world are not to be cherished or delighted in;
thus, he deeply praised the subtle and wondrous form of the Buddha’s body."]
At that time, the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja-pūrvayugaśrīcintāmanijñāna addressed the fourfold assembly, saying:

"Do you see this King Subhavyūha standing before me with palms joined? This king shall become a bhikṣu within my Dharma and, through diligent cultivation of the dharmas that assist the path to Buddhahood, he shall attain buddhahood.
His name shall be Śālarājā, his land shall be named Mahāprabha, and the kalpa shall be named..."
O Great King, that Sāla-tree King Buddha has an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas and an immeasurable number of śrāvakas.
His land is level and upright; such are his merits.
The Buddha’s name was Gathering the Vast Shading of Multitudes; his land was named Gathering the Destruction of All Evil Darkness; and the eon was named Gathering the Transcendence of All Nobility.
These all accorded with his causal practices. With the wind of a single thought of pure faith, he transformed his ministers and subjects, causing them all to obtain the benefits of the Dharma.
This refers to extensively practicing the conduct that destroys heterodox practices. By means of this, he relinquished the rank of king to attain the rank of Buddha;
that is, he transcended all noble and high positions.
Thereupon, the king immediately entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother, along with his consort, two sons, and all his attendants and possessions, [entrusting them] to the Buddha-dharma.

He left the household life to practice the Way within the kingdom. After the king had gone forth, he constantly applied himself with diligent vigor for eighty-four thousand years, practicing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Following this period, he attained the Samādhi Adorned with All Pure Merits.
(For eighty-four thousand years, he practiced the dharma of the Lotus Sutra. This was for the purpose of purifying the afflictions (*kleśa*).

After this period had passed—meaning that once the afflictions were purified—the samādhi manifested before him. Consequently, he transformed the defiled adornments of false views into the pure adornments of merit.)
When the Buddha spoke this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Subhavyūha," eighty-four thousand people were distanced from dust and freed from defilement,
attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
(Nan Yue added: "This means that the power of correctness assists in the accomplishment of virtuous conduct.

Jing Huan said: "Dust refers to false views; defilement refers to false attachments. To distance oneself from the dust of views externally and to remain free from the defilement of attachments internally."
Then the Dharma-eye will be perfectly clear and bright, with all flaws and obscurations utterly eliminated.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s Exhortation to Resolve.
This sutra begins with the questions and answers of Mañjuśrī and concludes with the exhortation to resolve by Samantabhadra. It consists of twenty-eight chapters.
The principle is one and pervasive. For wisdom can bring about awakening, which constitutes the beginning; for practice can perfect virtue, which constitutes the end.
Virtue is all-encompassing, aiding those above and benefiting those below. By thus accomplishing the constant practice after fruition, one exhausts the Way of Wondrous Enlightenment.
Therefore, it is named "Universal Good’s Exhortation to Awakening."
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, by means of his sovereign supernormal powers, majestic virtue, and renown,
arrived from the eastern direction accompanied by an immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable number of great bodhisattvas.
(Xiangmai said: "Because he does not depart from constant practice yet responds to things through non-action, he is called 'Mastery of Supernatural Powers.
Because his virtue is all-pervasive and his name is renowned everywhere, he is called 'Dignified Virtue and Renown.
That he comes together with boundless bodhisattvas demonstrates that the myriad practices are perfectly encompassed and inexhaustible.)

Jiehuan said: "Samantabhadra presides over the phenomena of the Dharma-realm and is perfectly endowed with the myriad practices; thus, within phenomena, there is reality. His response-body is nowhere not present.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the Dharma assembly, he manifested as one coming from the East.

The East is the place where the Lord of Thunder emerges. Because the Dharma assembly has reached this point, the wisdom of the causal stage is perfected and the enlightenment of the fruition stage is fulfilled."

When the practice of the eleven stages (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*) is perfected and complete, the merit of progressive cultivation has reached its consummation and the essence of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is fully realized.
Thereupon, relying on effortless action (*anābhoga-caryā*), one emerges to bring benefit to sentient beings; thus, it is shown that [the Buddha] comes from the East.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, after the exposition of the ocean-like merits of the Buddha concludes following the description of the stages beyond the eleventh, it then speaks of the appearance of the Tathāgata for the sake of benefiting others.
This refers to the "worldly conduct" mentioned above.
All the lands through which he passed trembled universally; precious lotus flowers rained down, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various kinds of music were played.
(Jie-huan said: "The arrival of the wondrous voice is likewise accompanied by rains of lotus flowers and the performance of music;
all of these serve to manifest sublime conduct and proclaim the flowing sound of the Dharma.")

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, from the land of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja, I have heard from afar that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is being preached in this Sahā world.
Together with immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas, I have come to hear and receive it.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach it for us."
Furthermore, the name "Supreme King of Jewel Splendor" (*Ratnaśrītejorāja*) is a title for mastery in beneficial conduct (*hitacaryā*).
Since Samantabhadra possesses both mastery and majestic virtue (*tejas*), the statement that he comes from the land of the Buddha Supreme King of Jewel Splendor clarifies his manifestation.
This is because he embodies the sovereign conduct for the benefit of all Buddhas.
Regarding the "ring of precepts," it says: "The mind-hearing of Samantabhadra can penetrate the ten directions; therefore, it is called 'hearing from afar.
If a good son, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, wishes to obtain this Lotus Sūtra, how can he do so?"
[Nan said: "To 'attain' means to attain it so as to perfect one's virtuous conduct.
Jiehuan said: "What you asked previously concerned only the practice, recitation, and exposition [of the sutra]. But this question asks how one can 'attain' this sutra;
it is because you wish for every person to attain it for themselves."
The Buddha told Samantabhadra Bodhisattva: "If a son of good family accomplishes four dharmas, he shall obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
First, being protected and remembered by all Buddhas; second, planting the roots of all virtues;
third, entering the stage of the right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*); and fourth, generating the mind to rescue all sentient beings. By thus accomplishing these four dharmas,"
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, one will certainly obtain this sutra.
"Being protected by the Buddha's mindfulness" means that one’s realization accords with the Buddha’s mind. "Planting the roots of all virtues" means that both merit and wisdom are perfected.

"Entering the stage of right determination" (samyaktva-niyāma) means embodying the wondrous essence of the Buddha. "Arousing the mind to save living beings" means practicing the wondrous conduct of the Buddha. These are the four dharmas.
Only through such accomplishment can one truly obtain this sutra (thereby fulfilling the constant practice of Samantabhadra).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, during the final five hundred years of the turbid and evil age..."
Whoever upholds this sutra, I shall protect and guard them;

I shall remove their misfortunes and afflictions, grant them peace and security, and ensure that no one seeks to find an opportunity to harm them—whether it be Māras, sons of Māra, daughters of Māra, followers of Māra, or those possessed by Māra;
or yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, or...
Whether they be *kimpuruṣas*, *pūtanas*, *vetālas*, or other such beings who afflict humans, none shall find an opportunity to harm them.
(Master Xingjian said: *yakṣas* are valiant and robust ghosts; *rākṣasas* are swift and agile ghosts;
*kumbhāṇḍas* are demonic ghosts whose forms resemble jars; *piśācas* are epileptic ghosts.)
The Precept Ring says: Samantabhadra’s constant practice is no longer for his own benefit, but is purely for the benefit of others;

therefore, from this point forward, all shall circulate the Dharma transformation and protect those who uphold the sutra, without any other distinct mode of conduct. As for the piśāca, the vexing and harmful ghost—
"Vedala, you who suppress and curse demons:
World-Honored One, by means of my supernatural powers, I shall now protect this sutra;
after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, I will cause it to be widely circulated within Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be interrupted. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised him, saying: "Excellent!"
Excellent, excellent, Samantabhadra! You are able to protect and assist this sutra, so that many sentient beings may attain peace, happiness, and benefit.
You have already accomplished inconceivable merit and profound, great compassion;
having long ago resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you are able to make such supernatural vows to guard and protect this [sutra].
Sūtra: "I shall, by means of my supernormal powers, protect those who are able to receive and uphold the name of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Samantabhadra, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, practice, and transcribe this Lotus Sūtra,"
One should know that such a person sees Śākyamuni Buddha; it should be known that such a person hears this sutra directly from the Buddha’s own mouth.
One should know that such a person makes offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha; one should know that such a person is praised by the Buddha as "Excellent!
One should know that such a person has the Buddha Śākyamuni stroke their head with his hand; one should know that such a person is [accepted] by Śākyamuni...
[The Buddha] is covered by the robes of a *bhikṣuṇī*.
[The *Jiehuan* (Vow-Ring) says: "This is the merit of assisting in the proclamation of right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), which fulfills what was previously stated regarding Samantabhadra.

Thus, seeing Śākyamuni as if hearing him directly from the mouth" and so forth, means that if one is able to maintain right mindfulness, then one sees the Buddha within the sutra itself. It is not... [as before].
To be hindered by names and forms is precisely to create the sublime within the Dharma; this is no different from hearing it directly from the Buddha himself.
This is called making offerings to the Buddha, performing the work of a Buddha, and being praised by the Buddha. It is called deeply acceding with the Buddha’s mind.

That he strokes one’s head and says the time for attaining the fruit is near, or that he covers one with his robe and says the practice of gentle patience is accomplished—all arises from the correctness of mindfulness; thus, the hidden realization is such as this.
Therefore, Samantabhadra, if you see one who receives and upholds this sutra, you should rise to welcome them from afar, treating them with the same reverence as you would the Buddha.

When this "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Exhortation" was being preached, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, immeasurable and boundless, attained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *dhāraṇīs*.
Bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms within a trichiliocosm became fully endowed [with these qualities].

The Path of Samantabhadra. (Jiehuan said: "This concludes the exhortation to revere [the practice]. (Xiangmai said: "From the 'Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta' up to this point, it is through practice that one accords with wisdom;
this is the gateway to the constant and great functioning [of the Dharma]. The *Avataṃsaka* teaching is now complete, and the 'Good Thief' appears once more.")
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra act so that practice may accord with wisdom; this is the gateway of the great function of the fruit-dharma, which is eternally thus. Their intent is the same as this.
(Furthermore, Nan says: "These are all final exhortations to inspire, so that one may attain the *parivarta* dhāraṇīs in the tens of billions and be fully endowed with this path of Samantabhadra.")
The *Jie-huan* (Circumambulation of the Precepts) states: "The *Dhāraṇī* of Ten Thousand Kotis of Revolutions is the practice that pervades all places;

the Path of Samantabhadra is the essence that pervades all places. To say that "immeasurable Bodhisattvas have all attained this practice" and "Bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust in a world-system all possess this essence" is the ultimate discourse on the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*: the unity of wisdom and practice, and of essence and function.

Everything is perfectly complete. Thus, upon hearing this chapter, one’s practice is perfected. When it reaches such a height, it is what is called "accomplishing the virtue of non-virtue through constant practice.
This is precisely the ultimate realization of the true aspect (*dharmatā*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
